title: Architectural Textured Proxy Generation
summary: Textured proxy models are a fundamental representation for architectural scenes, enabling efficient rendering while preserving visual fidelity. Existing approaches construct such proxies through a sequential pipeline in which geometry is first abstracted from a dense reconstruction and textures are later projected from input images. This geometry-only formulation neglects image evidence during proxy generation, leading to misalignment of structural features such as facades, edges, and their intersections across views. As a result, inconsistencies are deferred to a downstream correction stage during texturing, where the underlying geometric structure can no longer be reliably recovered. In this work, we introduce an image-guided proxy formulation in which proxy generation is jointly constrained by both the dense reconstruction and the input aerial images. By incorporating image derived structural cues directly into the construction process, the proxy is optimized to align with observed features across views from the outset, rather than relying on post hoc correction that may be infeasible. This shift from a geometry-only to an image-guided paradigm produces proxies that are inherently consistent with the input imagery, enabling more accurate geometry and more coherent texture mapping. We realize this formulation through a framework that extracts structural priors from images and dense geometry, and enforces their consistency during proxy optimization. The resulting proxies exhibit improved alignment of structural features, reducing artifacts such as edge duplication, texture drift, and cross view inconsistencies. Experiments on diverse architectural scenes demonstrate that our approach produces compact, geometry texture aligned proxies with substantially improved visual fidelity compared to existing methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes an image-guided formulation for generating textured proxy models of architectural scenes, in which proxy optimization is constrained by both the dense reconstruction and the input aerial images. This yields proxies better aligned with structural features and with fewer texture artifacts than geometry-only pipelines.
AI.motivation: Existing pipelines abstract geometry from a dense reconstruction first and project textures afterwards, so image evidence is ignored during proxy generation and misalignment of facades, edges and their intersections across views can only be corrected downstream, when the structure can no longer be reliably recovered.
AI.method: Image-guided proxy formulation in which proxy generation is jointly constrained by the dense reconstruction and the input aerial images; a framework extracts structural priors from images and dense geometry and enforces their consistency during proxy optimization.
AI.result: On diverse architectural scenes the proxies show improved alignment of structural features and fewer artifacts such as edge duplication, texture drift and cross-view inconsistencies, and are compact and geometry-texture aligned with substantially improved visual fidelity over existing methods; no specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Moving from a geometry-only to an image-guided paradigm produces proxies that are consistent with the input imagery from the outset, giving more accurate geometry and more coherent texture mapping than post hoc correction.

title: Real-Time Volumetric Light Transport Inference without a Path
summary: We present a real-time method for reconstructing fully integrated pixel radiance in rendered volumetric media under direct and ambient environmental illumination, using compact, low-cost scene features and statistics. Unlike Monte Carlo denoising pipelines for volumetric rendering, which depend on computationally expensive path-traced radiance estimates, our approach directly infers the final light-transport solution from inexpensive primary-ray and environment sample evaluations. We show that these features form a near-sufficient representation of the scene, enabling accurate reconstruction at substantially lower computational cost. Using an attention-augmented image-to-image network, we demonstrate that complete pixel radiance can be inferred directly from these auxiliary features, without requiring the original radiance signal. Operating in image space also provides a more stable computational cost as the camera zooms into or out of the volume, with substantially less dependence on volume density than approaches based on explicit multiple-scattering simulation. We demonstrate real-time performance and high reconstruction accuracy in challenging volumetric cloud scenarios.

AI.tldr: Presents a real-time method that reconstructs fully integrated pixel radiance in rendered volumetric media by inferring the final light-transport solution from cheap primary-ray and environment-sample features, without path-traced radiance estimates. An attention-augmented image-to-image network achieves high accuracy in challenging volumetric cloud scenes.
AI.motivation: Monte Carlo denoising pipelines for volumetric rendering depend on expensive path-traced radiance estimates, and explicit multiple-scattering simulation has a cost that depends strongly on volume density and camera distance.
AI.method: An attention-augmented image-to-image network that predicts complete pixel radiance directly from compact, low-cost scene features and statistics computed from primary-ray and environment sample evaluations, operating in image space.
AI.result: Real-time performance and high reconstruction accuracy in challenging volumetric cloud scenarios, with more stable computational cost as the camera zooms into or out of the volume and less dependence on volume density; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Complete pixel radiance can be inferred from inexpensive auxiliary features that form a near-sufficient representation of the scene, offering accurate reconstruction at substantially lower computational cost.

title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
summary: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.

AI.tldr: A state-of-the-art report on differentiable physics simulation that separates two questions the literature conflates: which mathematical object a returned derivative belongs to (the referent) and how the backward pass is organized (the realization). It classifies methods and engines along these axes, measures four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost on one testbed, and reviews when zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients.
AI.motivation: Differentiable simulators differ both in the physics they model and in the object they differentiate, and the literature merges these distinctions, obscuring claims about exactness and the apparent exactness-memory trade-off.
AI.method: A two-axis taxonomy of referent (finite executed computation, converged equation, or continuous dynamics) against realization (automatic differentiation, equation-level adjoint solve, or custom adjoint), plus an orthogonal taxonomy for contact, which is non-smooth; the work also covers model classes, systems techniques and applications, and releases a diagnostic tool that computes a reporting checklist.
AI.result: On one testbed the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and the review finds evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where the four mechanisms act.
AI.conclusion: The apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a fundamental constraint, and the report closes with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic and a research agenda.

title: Explicit LOD-Conditioned Anisotropic Filtering for Neural Texture Compression
summary: Neural texture compression (NTC) stores material textures compactly, but the dominant feature-pyramid design receives no filtering from the GPU texture unit: it learns each material at a fixed UV and level of detail and has no explicit anisotropic-filtering (AF) mechanism. Setting the filter from the footprint aspect ratio alone is not enough: a single input cannot carry both the shape of the footprint and its size, so the image is too blurry near the camera by the same amount at every distance. Our method, AF-NTC, instead conditions the decoder on the same three bounded values a hardware sampler uses: minor-axis scale (LOD), aspect ratio, and major-axis orientation. These drive a tap line along the major axis and a level blend across the minor axis, and we train against anisotropically filtered ground truth. At $25\%$ of a full BC7 mip chain, AF-NTC beats the no-AF trilinear-BC7 baseline on all ten material--scene pairs we compare ($+1.3$ to $+7.6$\,dB), and it is $0.0$ to $3.4$\,dB below the $4\times$-larger anisotropic-BC7, depending on the material.

AI.tldr: Introduces AF-NTC, a neural texture compression method that conditions the decoder on the same three bounded values a hardware sampler uses (minor-axis scale, aspect ratio and major-axis orientation) to add explicit anisotropic filtering. At 25% of a full BC7 mip chain it outperforms the trilinear-BC7 baseline on all ten material-scene pairs.
AI.motivation: The dominant feature-pyramid design in neural texture compression receives no filtering from the GPU texture unit and has no explicit anisotropic-filtering mechanism, and a single input cannot carry both the shape and the size of the footprint, so images are too blurry near the camera at every distance.
AI.method: The decoder is conditioned on minor-axis scale (LOD), aspect ratio and major-axis orientation, which drive a tap line along the major axis and a level blend across the minor axis; training uses anisotropically filtered ground truth.
AI.result: At 25% of a full BC7 mip chain, AF-NTC beats the no-AF trilinear-BC7 baseline on all ten material-scene pairs by 1.3 to 7.6 dB, and is 0.0 to 3.4 dB below anisotropic BC7 that uses a mip chain 4x larger, depending on the material.
AI.conclusion: Explicit conditioning on the hardware sampler's anisotropic-filtering parameters lets a compact neural texture representation approach the quality of a much larger anisotropic BC7 texture.

title: From Video to Digital Twin: An Exploratory Study of World Models and Gaussian Splatting on In-the-Wild Video
comment: 35 pages, 14 figures. Supplementary movies and code: this https URL
summary: Generative world models and 3D Gaussian Splatting promise to turn ordinary video into explorable 3D scenes, but little is reported on how they behave on uncurated, in-the-wild footage. We study what these models recover when the only input is a publicly available news walkthrough of a food bank warehouse, with presenters walking through every shot and no drawings, scans or site visit, and we use the result as the geometry of a digital twin. A commercial world model given 20 frames recovered camera poses and metric depth for three areas, which we fused into about 747,000 Gaussian splats for 200 credits (20 US cents). Splat models optimized locally on a CPU, at no credit cost, were photorealistic near the filmed path but degraded quickly away from it. On held-out frames, scored in pixels not covered by people, they reached 21.2 and 23.1 dB PSNR from 64 and 43 training frames, and lost 3.8 and 5.4 dB when given only the 8 frames a world model accepts. Removing the trainer's background fill and person-hull carving raised held-out PSNR, showing that cleaning the space behind moving people costs fidelity in observed pixels while its gain lies where no ground truth exists. Asking the world model to generate views of areas the video never showed failed on the provider's side twice, so extrapolation could not be evaluated and unseen space was filled by a scripted model instead. We also describe the corrections needed to turn world-model output into a valid, metric Universal Scene Description (OpenUSD) asset with its native splat schema, which serves as the only interface to a data layer, a browser viewer, Blender and NVIDIA Omniverse. The findings suggest that today's models recover the observed parts of a real scene cheaply and at metric scale, while few-view fidelity and extrapolating unobserved space remain open. The work is an exploration of these methods, not a deployed product.

AI.tldr: An exploratory study of whether a commercial world model and 3D Gaussian Splatting can turn an uncurated in-the-wild news walkthrough video of a food bank warehouse into a metric digital twin. The models recover observed parts of the scene cheaply and at metric scale, while few-view fidelity and extrapolation to unseen space remain open.
AI.motivation: Generative world models and 3D Gaussian Splatting promise to turn ordinary video into explorable 3D scenes, but little has been reported on how they behave on uncurated in-the-wild footage.
AI.method: A commercial world model given 20 frames recovered camera poses and metric depth for three areas, which were fused into about 747,000 Gaussian splats; splat models were optimized locally on a CPU, the trainer's background fill and person-hull carving were ablated, and the result was converted into a valid metric OpenUSD asset with a native splat schema.
AI.result: On held-out frames scored in pixels not covered by people, the splat models reached 21.2 and 23.1 dB PSNR from 64 and 43 training frames, and lost 3.8 and 5.4 dB when given only the 8 frames a world model accepts; removing background fill and person-hull carving raised held-out PSNR, and the fused reconstruction cost 200 credits (20 US cents). Extrapolation to unseen areas could not be evaluated because the provider's world model failed twice.
AI.conclusion: Cleaning the space behind moving people costs fidelity in observed pixels while its gain lies where no ground truth exists, and few-view fidelity and extrapolation of unobserved space remain open problems for world-model-based digital twins.

title: Same Pixels, Different Documents: Measuring Part-Level Editability in Image Vectorization
summary: Image vectorization is often evaluated by rendering fidelity, which cannot distinguish documents that render identically but support different edits. Edit-based evaluation tests outcomes, but an oracle that gathers a part's fragments can conceal the cost of selecting them. We introduce Pass@k, which tests whether a prescribed edit can succeed using objects selectable within k clicks under a specified interaction model. Eight document diagnostics characterize properties relevant to editing beyond these tasks. We assess structural sensitivity through controlled perturbations, practical relevance through designer operations, and reference dependence through alternative drawings. We evaluate twelve open and commercial methods on 211 references, with 635 edit tasks on 93 of them. In each of four reference sets, including two drawn by designers, 64-88% of oracle-passed tasks on parts composed of multiple shapes fail at Pass@1, against 6-40% for single shapes, pooling counts over configurations. Higher fidelity does not guarantee higher Pass@1, while selected diagnostics are associated with designers' effort in our study.

AI.tldr: Introduces Pass@k, an edit-based metric for image vectorization that tests whether a prescribed edit can succeed using objects selectable within k clicks under a specified interaction model, together with eight document diagnostics. Evaluating twelve methods shows that higher rendering fidelity does not guarantee higher Pass@1 on editing tasks.
AI.motivation: Image vectorization is usually evaluated by rendering fidelity, which cannot distinguish documents that render identically but support different edits, while oracle-based edit evaluation conceals the cost of selecting the fragments that make up a part.
AI.method: Pass@k tests edit success under a bounded click budget; eight document diagnostics characterize editing-relevant properties, assessed through controlled structural perturbations, designer operations and alternative reference drawings.
AI.result: Across four reference sets (two drawn by designers) with 211 references and 635 edit tasks on 93 of them, 64-88% of oracle-passed tasks on parts composed of multiple shapes fail at Pass@1, compared with 6-40% for single shapes; higher fidelity does not guarantee higher Pass@1, and selected diagnostics are associated with designers' effort.
AI.conclusion: Editability is a distinct property from rendering fidelity, and the proposed click-bounded evaluation with diagnostics reveals editing failures that fidelity and oracle-based measures miss.

title: Action Transfer Across Character Body Plans in Latent-Action World Models: An Empirical Study of Animated Characters
comment: 28 pages, 13 figures, 8 tables. Dataset: this https URL
summary: Latent-action world models learn actions from video without labels, and recent methods aim to share these actions across bodies. Transfer between 2D characters with different body structures remains underexplored. In this paper, we study whether an action learned from one character can make a character with a different body perform the same action. A cat, a blob and a human can all jump, but each moves its body in its own way. The usual transfer gain mixes body motion with screen movement and can assign a perfect score to a model that ignores its action. To address this, we introduce a transfer score that compares the correct action with wrong ones from the same source. We test five training objectives on a new synthetic benchmark of 2D cartoon characters with six body plans, the standard Sprites benchmark, and 431 selected animal and human animations from DeformingThings4D. With a fixed camera, a baseline that only copies the source's screen movement scores 0.71, as high as most learned models. In contrast, with a camera that follows the body, the best model reaches only 0.46 for an unseen animal family and 0.20 for humans. With this camera, a linear probe identifies the action class of unseen animal families with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy (chance 17%). The learned actions therefore retain information about which action is performed, but the correct action closes only part of the prediction error gap for a new character.

AI.tldr: Studies whether an action learned by a latent-action world model from one 2D character can make a character with a different body plan perform the same action, and proposes a transfer score that controls for screen movement. With a camera that follows the body, the best learned models transfer poorly to unseen animal families and humans.
AI.motivation: Transfer gains between characters with different bodies are usually measured in ways that mix body motion with screen movement, so a model that ignores its action can still score perfectly, and transfer between 2D characters with different body structures remains underexplored.
AI.method: A transfer score that compares the correct action against wrong actions from the same source; five training objectives are tested on a new synthetic benchmark of 2D cartoon characters with six body plans, the standard Sprites benchmark, and 431 selected animal and human animations from DeformingThings4D, with a linear probe used to check action information.
AI.result: With a fixed camera, a baseline that only copies the source's screen movement scores 0.71, as high as most learned models; with a body-following camera the best model reaches 0.46 for an unseen animal family and 0.20 for humans, while a linear probe identifies the action class of unseen animal families with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy (chance 17%).
AI.conclusion: Learned actions retain information about which action is performed, but the correct action closes only part of the prediction error gap for a new character, so cross-body action transfer remains limited.

title: PLS-GS: Probabilistic Lidar Scaffolds for Compact, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Main paper and supplementary material. Code: this https URL
summary: While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is typically optimized from images only, many robotics and mapping applications provide both camera and high-definition LiDAR data, combining rich visual appearance with accurate geometric structure. We introduce PLS-GS, a probabilistic LiDAR scaffold for Gaussian Splatting that exploits this complementary sensing setting to construct a compact 3DGS representation aligned to the measured surface. PLS-GS fits a Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model jointly over position and color, yielding a continuous and adaptive scaffold that eliminates the need for discrete scene partitioning such as voxel grids or octrees. The fitted mixture then guides the renderable 3DGS Gaussians: each rendering Gaussian is associated with a GMM component and constrained in the local surface frame induced by that component's covariance. A Mahalanobis support loss bounds the deviation of the rendering Gaussians from the corresponding LiDAR-derived surface. Across five large outdoor scenes, PLS-GS places primitives markedly closer to the LiDAR measurements than both image- and LiDAR-initialized baselines, while employing substantially fewer primitives, yielding a considerably more compact model and faster rendering. At matched capacity, PLS-GS places primitives closer to the LiDAR measurements, with comparable rendering quality. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents PLS-GS, a probabilistic LiDAR scaffold that fits a Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model over position and colour to guide 3D Gaussian Splatting in compact, surface-aligned form. Across five large outdoor scenes it places primitives closer to LiDAR measurements with fewer primitives and faster rendering.
AI.motivation: Many robotics and mapping applications have both camera and LiDAR data, yet 3DGS is typically optimized from images only, and discrete scene partitions such as voxel grids or octrees are needed to organize the primitives.
AI.method: A Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model fitted jointly over position and colour serves as a continuous, adaptive scaffold; each rendering Gaussian is associated with a mixture component and constrained in the local surface frame given by that component's covariance, with a Mahalanobis support loss bounding its deviation from the LiDAR-derived surface.
AI.result: Across five large outdoor scenes PLS-GS places primitives markedly closer to LiDAR measurements than image- and LiDAR-initialized baselines using substantially fewer primitives, giving a more compact model and faster rendering; at matched capacity it still places primitives closer to LiDAR with comparable rendering quality.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting complementary LiDAR geometry yields a compact, surface-aligned 3DGS representation without discrete scene partitioning, at comparable rendering quality.

title: Quadratic Bezier Splatting with Structural Initialization for Efficient Painting Rendering
summary: Stroke-based rendering is often optimized as a pixel-level reconstruction task. This over-reliance on global error reduction not only degrades strokes into fragmented curves due to a lack of structured planning, but also allows locally defective primitives to be concealed by overlapping layers. To address these issues, we introduce a model-guided framework for stroke-audited rendering. Our framework uses Quadratic Bezier Splatting to analytically model continuous curved strokes with efficient differentiable alpha compositing. Built on this renderer, a feedforward multi-scale stroke decoder provides a structural initialization with learned stroke-scale allocation, while test-time stroke optimization supplies the reconstruction capacity needed for high-fidelity refinement. We further propose a single-stroke audit mechanism that explicitly evaluates local stroke quality, preventing defective primitives from surviving optimization through layer-wise compensation. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves coherent layouts, improves PSNR by up to 5.46 dB, yields a 16% more compact representation, and accelerates combined renderer forward and backward computation by a factor of 220.3.

AI.tldr: Proposes a model-guided framework for stroke-based painting rendering that combines Quadratic Bezier Splatting with a feedforward multi-scale stroke decoder and a single-stroke audit that removes locally defective strokes. It reports coherent layouts, up to 5.46 dB PSNR gain, a 16% more compact representation and a 220.3x speed-up of combined forward and backward computation.
AI.motivation: Stroke-based rendering is usually optimized as pixel-level reconstruction, which fragments strokes into curves lacking structured planning and lets locally defective primitives be hidden by overlapping layers.
AI.method: Quadratic Bezier Splatting provides analytic, differentiable alpha-composited curved strokes; a feedforward multi-scale stroke decoder gives structural initialization with learned stroke-scale allocation; test-time stroke optimization refines reconstruction, and a single-stroke audit evaluates each stroke's local quality.
AI.result: Compared with existing methods the approach achieves coherent layouts, improves PSNR by up to 5.46 dB, yields a 16% more compact representation, and accelerates the combined renderer forward and backward computation by a factor of 220.3.
AI.conclusion: Structural initialization combined with per-stroke quality auditing gives stroke-based rendering that is coherent, compact and much faster than pixel-driven optimization.

title: SoftPAT3D: Physics-Augmented Text-to-3D Scene Generation with Deformables
summary: We present SoftPAT3D, a physics-augmented framework for text-to-3D scene generation in which deformable objects, such as cloth, stuffed toys and ropes, are generated as physically valid, simulation-ready bodies and placed in intersection-free contact with the furniture that supports them, with one another and with themselves. Existing physics-augmented pipelines simulate rigid bodies only and cannot accommodate a generated deformable object, which text-to-3D generation returns as a geometrically invalid mesh, sometimes self-intersecting, that has no rest shape, no material model and no admissible initial state. These are the inputs a deformable simulation requires, and we construct each from information already in the pipeline. The rest shape comes from how the object is manufactured rather than from the generated physically inconsistent deformed configuration, and a material library assigns each deformable object its initial elastic parameters, which can then be optimized. The occluded support is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, each object is released from an optimizable placement above the supporting part that the prompt specifies, and the complete scene is driven to static equilibrium under one unified contact model, with completion verified by geometric checks and a vision-language model. When a scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, and the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same contact energy reaches the targets the grid does not, places several bodies jointly and recovers and optimizes material parameters. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in a single simulation, and the pipeline also runs from the text prompt alone. On all sixty-five prompts, SoftPAT3D produces no undesired interpenetration of any kind, whereas every other system does, and its scenes directly support scene editing and robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: Presents SoftPAT3D, a physics-augmented text-to-3D scene pipeline that generates deformable objects such as cloth, stuffed toys and ropes as simulation-ready bodies and places them in intersection-free contact with supporting furniture and with each other. On sixty-five prompts it produces no undesired interpenetration, where every other system does.
AI.motivation: Existing physics-augmented pipelines simulate only rigid bodies, while text-to-3D generation returns deformable objects as geometrically invalid meshes, sometimes self-intersecting, with no rest shape, material model or admissible initial state.
AI.method: The rest shape comes from how the object is manufactured, a material library assigns initial elastic parameters that can be optimized, the occluded support is regenerated as a watertight collision mesh, and the scene is driven to static equilibrium under one unified contact model, with failed scenes corrected by a grid search over placements and a differentiable simulation adjoint.
AI.result: On all sixty-five prompts SoftPAT3D produces no undesired interpenetration of any kind, whereas every other system does; multi-body scenes equilibrate in a single simulation, the pipeline also runs from the text prompt alone, and the scenes support scene editing and robotic manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Constructing rest shapes, material models and admissible initial states from information already in the pipeline makes deformable objects usable in physics-augmented text-to-3D scene generation.

title: From Sketch to Design: A Cross-scale Workflow for Procedural Generative Urban Design
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures. Author version of a paper published at CAADRIA 2024
summary: Urban designers use sketches and symbols to express spatial intentions, while many generative urban design tools rely on numeric parameters that are difficult to relate to this visual process. We propose a cross-scale workflow and a web-based prototype that translates symbolic sketches into controllable procedural urban generation. A vocabulary of shapes, informed by examples of urban design diagrams and sketching exercises with graduate urban design students, encodes attributes such as network structure, density, and program. The prototype uses the \$1 Unistroke Recognizer to map gestures to symbols and translates their locations and sizes into tensor-field attractors and weighted parameter grids. Grid and radial tensor fields guide street-network generation, while the parameter grids control building heights and programs. Implemented in JavaScript and TypeScript with React and this http URL, the prototype supports interactive sketching, visualization, and urban massing generation. We describe the methodology and illustrate prototype interactions, then discuss downstream integration with architectural-scale generative tools for further refinement and analysis. The work connects designers' symbolic input with an explicit procedural generation process.

AI.tldr: Presents a cross-scale workflow and web-based prototype that translates symbolic urban design sketches into controllable procedural urban generation, with street networks guided by tensor fields and building heights and programs set by parameter grids. It connects designers' symbolic input to an explicit procedural generation process.
AI.motivation: Urban designers express spatial intentions through sketches and symbols, whereas many generative urban design tools rely on numeric parameters that are hard to relate to this visual process.
AI.method: A vocabulary of shapes, informed by urban design diagrams and sketching exercises with graduate urban design students, encodes network structure, density and program; the $1 Unistroke Recognizer maps gestures to symbols, whose locations and sizes become tensor-field attractors and weighted parameter grids that guide street generation and massing.
AI.result: The prototype, implemented in JavaScript and TypeScript with React, supports interactive sketching, visualization and urban massing generation, and the abstract illustrates prototype interactions; no quantitative evaluation is reported.
AI.conclusion: The workflow links designers' symbolic input to procedural generation and is intended for downstream integration with architectural-scale generative tools for further refinement and analysis.

title: Feel My Focus: Gaze-Triggered Digital Twin Creation for Remote Collaboration
summary: We present Feel My Focus, a gaze-triggered mixed reality (MR) demonstration that enables rapid creation and sharing of lightweight 3D digital twins during remote collaboration. Unlike systems that use gaze primarily as a referential pointer, Feel My Focus treats sustained visual attention as a generative action: a fixation on a physical object initiates single-image capture, attention-guided segmentation, and one-shot 3D reconstruction, allowing a remote partner to inspect and discuss the object in situ. The system integrates gaze-tracking glasses, modular segmentation and reconstruction services, and an MR client for runtime streaming and interaction. This design prioritizes responsiveness and experiential continuity over photometric fidelity. We report observations from a public demonstration, highlighting design trade-offs, failure modes, and user control considerations for deploying gaze-triggered generative systems in real-world collaborative settings.

AI.tldr: Presents Feel My Focus, a mixed reality demonstration in which a sustained fixation on a physical object by a user wearing gaze-tracking glasses triggers single-image capture, attention-guided segmentation and one-shot 3D reconstruction, so that a remote partner can inspect the object in situ. Observations from a public demonstration highlight design trade-offs, failure modes and user control considerations.
AI.motivation: Gaze in remote collaboration is typically used as a referential pointer, whereas the authors treat sustained visual attention as a generative action that can create shareable 3D digital twins during collaboration.
AI.method: The system integrates gaze-tracking glasses, modular segmentation and reconstruction services, and a mixed reality client for runtime streaming and interaction, prioritizing responsiveness and experiential continuity over photometric fidelity.
AI.result: The paper reports observations from a public demonstration rather than quantitative measurements, describing design trade-offs, failure modes and user control considerations for deploying gaze-triggered generative systems in real-world collaborative settings.
AI.conclusion: Gaze-triggered generation of lightweight 3D twins is feasible for remote collaboration, with responsiveness favored over fidelity, but it raises open questions about failure handling and user control.

title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.

AI.tldr: Identifies severe SM-level load imbalance in GPU-based 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering caused by uneven per-tile workloads and proposes a software-defined scheduler that mitigates the resulting execution tail. It accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x per scene averaged and up to 5.6x on the most imbalanced frames, without retraining or specialized hardware.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS optimizations either change the algorithm and require retraining or rely on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants, and the imbalance leaves most SMs idle while a few process heavy tiles, especially in large urban scenes.
AI.method: A persistent kernel schedules heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs, with a lightweight per-frame policy that decides when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline.
AI.result: Averaged per scene the approach accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.
AI.conclusion: A scheduling-level fix that is orthogonal to existing optimizations and works across diverse 3DGS variants can remove the execution tail without retraining or new hardware.

title: Spaghetti Splatting: Differentiating Curvilinear Dirac Masses via Convolution
summary: In production systems, 3D geometry is represented by primitives such as points, lines, and triangles, as rendering hardware is optimized to generate images from them very efficiently. Learning such primitives from images by volume rendering is challenging, as they are Dirac masses defined at infinitesimal locations in space. EWA splatting, Poisson reconstruction, and 3D Gaussian Splatting overcome this by convolving Dirac masses with a low-frequency kernel, a recipe that generalizes along two axes: the kernel and the primitive. As points and triangles have already received significant attention, we investigate this recipe for curvilinear primitives, and introduce Spaghetti Splatting. We approximate curves by polylines whose convolution converges to that of the continuous curve, and volume render each segment so that connected segments composite without overcounting at their joints. For fast training and inference, we linearize the camera projection per segment, which also accommodates kernels beyond Gaussians, such as Beta kernels. As a point is a curve of zero length, our representation is a strict superset of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It remains competitive with the state-of-the-art on general scenes, outperforms methods specialized to line-like geometry, natively supports anti-aliasing, and produces long connected strands that are directly amenable to physics simulation.

AI.tldr: Introduces Spaghetti Splatting, which extends the convolution-based differentiable rendering recipe of EWA splatting, Poisson reconstruction and 3D Gaussian Splatting to curvilinear primitives by approximating curves with polylines. It remains competitive on general scenes, outperforms methods specialized to line-like geometry, and produces long connected strands suitable for physics simulation.
AI.motivation: Points and triangles have received most attention for learning primitives from images, while curvilinear primitives, which are Dirac masses at infinitesimal locations, are hard to learn by volume rendering without the low-frequency convolution that makes points and Gaussians tractable.
AI.method: Curves are approximated by polylines whose convolution converges to that of the continuous curve; each segment is volume rendered so that connected segments composite without overcounting at joints, and the camera projection is linearized per segment to allow fast training and inference and kernels beyond Gaussians such as Beta kernels.
AI.result: The method remains competitive with the state of the art on general scenes, outperforms methods specialized to line-like geometry, natively supports anti-aliasing, and produces long connected strands directly amenable to physics simulation; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A point is a curve of zero length, so the representation is a strict superset of 3D Gaussian Splatting, extending the splatting recipe to curvilinear geometry.

title: Adaptive Budgeted Data Acquisition for Robust Off-Policy Evaluation from Multiple Loggers
summary: We consider off-policy evaluation when additional data can be purchased from several existing logging policies (or loggers) with heterogeneous costs per observation. While existing work on multiple loggers presumes a fixed number of observations from each logger, we study how to allocate a limited budget across them sequentially to evaluate a finite class of target policies. We propose Adaptive Greedy, an algorithm that purchases observations sequentially from the affordable logger that has the most cost-normalized variance reduction across the target policies. It turns out that each such purchase is an 'approximate conditional-gradient step' for the corresponding design problem. Under mild assumptions, we establish that the empirical allocation converges almost surely to the optimal design at an explicit rate. We also derive the asymptotic normality of the final pooled estimator and show that it attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Simulations and a semi-synthetic application based on the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 show that Adaptive Greedy outperforms standard allocation strategies, remains accurate if stopped early, and matches the final accuracy of repeated integer programming at a fraction of its computational cost.

AI.tldr: Proposes Adaptive Greedy, an algorithm for off-policy evaluation that sequentially buys observations from several loggers with heterogeneous costs, choosing at each step the affordable logger with the largest cost-normalized variance reduction across target policies. It converges to the optimal design and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound while matching integer programming at a fraction of its computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing work on multiple loggers assumes a fixed number of observations from each logger, whereas a limited budget must be allocated across loggers sequentially when additional data can be purchased.
AI.method: Each purchase is interpreted as an approximate conditional-gradient step for the corresponding design problem; the paper proves almost-sure convergence of the empirical allocation to the optimal design at an explicit rate and derives asymptotic normality of the final pooled estimator.
AI.result: In simulations and a semi-synthetic application based on AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175, Adaptive Greedy outperforms standard allocation strategies, remains accurate if stopped early, and matches the final accuracy of repeated integer programming at a fraction of its computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Sequential cost-aware purchasing of observations from multiple loggers can be both statistically efficient and computationally cheap for off-policy evaluation.

title: Spiking Sensory Networks
summary: Effective sensory reception is critical for survival, yet the computational mechanisms behind how peripheral sensory neurons (SNs) transduce external signals into spiking representations for downstream brain circuits remain to be fully understood. Numerous theoretical frameworks have been proposed to model sensory processing, with Bayesian approaches among the most prominent. However, existing machine learning attempts to apply Bayesian theory to spiking neurons remain largely phenomenological, disconnected from empirical biology, and poorly validated on non-stationary temporal data. Conversely, neuroscientific models often rely on strong inductive experimental biases or explicit kinetic dynamics fit post hoc to match spiking data. Here, we introduce a class of recurrent Poisson VAE models, termed Spiking Sensory Networks (SSNs), that bridge these paradigms by reconciling variational inference with biologically inspired spike transduction for time-varying stimuli. Evaluated on real-world odor plume recordings from locust olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs), SSNs match or exceed the reconstruction fidelity of Spiking Neural Network (SNN) and GLM baselines while exhibiting superior representational characteristics. Furthermore, SSNs are well-suited for neuroscientific investigation, learning empirical in vivo ORN response motifs and exhibiting emergent spike-frequency adaptation under unsupervised reconstruction without manual tuning. Moreover, we theoretically link the recurrent decoding objective to mutual information maximization, and derive a formal thermodynamic lower bound connecting the Poisson Kullback-Leibler regularizer to the excess non-equilibrium metabolic power of biophysical homeostasis. Ultimately, our work synthesizes principles from machine learning theory and empirical neuroscience, providing a viable bridge that concretizes Bayesian models with biological mechanisms.

AI.tldr: Introduces Spiking Sensory Networks, recurrent Poisson variational autoencoders that reconcile variational inference with biologically inspired spike transduction for time-varying stimuli. On locust olfactory receptor neuron recordings they match or exceed the reconstruction fidelity of spiking neural network and GLM baselines while learning empirical response motifs and spike-frequency adaptation.
AI.motivation: Existing machine learning attempts to apply Bayesian theory to spiking neurons are phenomenological and poorly validated on non-stationary temporal data, while neuroscientific models rely on strong experimental biases or post hoc fitted kinetic dynamics.
AI.method: A class of recurrent Poisson VAE models that perform variational inference over spike transduction of time-varying odor plume stimuli, with the recurrent decoding objective linked theoretically to mutual information maximization and the Poisson Kullback-Leibler regularizer linked to a thermodynamic lower bound on excess non-equilibrium metabolic power.
AI.result: Evaluated on real-world odor plume recordings from locust olfactory receptor neurons, the models match or exceed the reconstruction fidelity of SNN and GLM baselines and exhibit superior representational characteristics, learn empirical in vivo ORN response motifs, and show emergent spike-frequency adaptation without manual tuning.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a bridge between machine learning theory and empirical neuroscience that concretizes Bayesian models with biological mechanisms, linking variational inference to both information-theoretic and metabolic principles.

title: Information-Theoretic Generalization for Set-Input Optimization-Valued Objectives
summary: Modern machine learning is increasingly evaluated using criteria such as multicalibration, CVaR, and Cressie-Read DRO, which target subgroup reliability, tail risk, and distributional robustness rather than averages of fixed per-example losses. Existing information-theoretic generalization bounds for pointwise losses do not directly apply, because these empirical criteria depend on the entire batch and involve a post-hoc auxiliary optimization over witnesses, thresholds, or reweightings. We formalize this structure as set-input optimization-valued objectives. In the balanced supersample setting, we bound the expected optimized validation-training gap in terms of an objective-dependent sub-Gaussian parameter and the square root of the prediction-based conditional mutual information (fCMI) between the learned supersample prediction table and the selector vector. Combining this with fixed-predictor population-validation comparisons yields unified algorithm-dependent generalization bounds. We verify sub-Gaussianity of the selector gap using stability and convex L2-Lipschitz certificates, obtaining concrete bounds for multicalibration, CVaR, and Cressie-Read DRO, with a stability-based single-index refinement.

AI.tldr: Derives information-theoretic generalization bounds for set-input optimization-valued objectives, such as multicalibration, CVaR and Cressie-Read DRO, whose empirical value depends on the whole batch and on a post-hoc optimization. The bounds are obtained through a sub-Gaussian parameter and the conditional mutual information between the learned prediction table and the selector vector, with concrete certificates for the three criteria.
AI.motivation: Existing information-theoretic generalization bounds apply to pointwise losses, but criteria targeting subgroup reliability, tail risk and distributional robustness depend on the entire batch and involve auxiliary optimization over witnesses, thresholds or reweightings.
AI.method: The objective structure is formalized as set-input optimization-valued objectives; in the balanced supersample setting the expected optimized validation-training gap is bounded in terms of an objective-dependent sub-Gaussian parameter and the square root of the prediction-based conditional mutual information (fCMI), combined with fixed-predictor population-validation comparisons; sub-Gaussianity is certified via stability and convex L2-Lipschitz conditions.
AI.result: The abstract reports unified algorithm-dependent generalization bounds with concrete instances for multicalibration, CVaR and Cressie-Read DRO, plus a stability-based single-index refinement; no empirical numbers are given.
AI.conclusion: Generalization analysis can be extended to batch-dependent, optimization-valued criteria, yielding bounds for several fairness, risk and robustness objectives.

title: Beyond Discrete Ancestry Groups: Distribution-Aware In-Context Learning for Cancer Outcome Prediction Across the Genetic Ancestry Continuum
summary: Machine learning models for omics-based prediction of cancer outcomes are commonly built on aggregated data without distinguishing ancestry groups, or under an ancestry-discrete design, which partitions samples into ancestry groups and fits a separate model within each group. Recent evidence shows that this approach is inherently limited: predictive accuracy declines with genetic distance from the training samples, even within a single ancestry group, because the data distribution shifts continuously rather than only between predefined categories. In this paper, we propose distribution-aware in-context learning (DA-ICL) for ancestry-continuum modeling. Our method extends conventional ancestry-discrete modeling to ancestry-continuum modeling, capturing the nonstationary omics-endpoint relationship across the genetic continuum while enabling efficient modeling through an in-context learning foundation model. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating the superiority of the ancestry-continuum over ancestry-discrete modeling, along with empirical results supporting the proposed framework. Source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes distribution-aware in-context learning (DA-ICL) for omics-based cancer outcome prediction across the genetic ancestry continuum, extending ancestry-discrete modeling to ancestry-continuum modeling with an in-context learning foundation model. The paper gives theoretical analysis of its advantage over ancestry-discrete modeling and reports supporting empirical results.
AI.motivation: Models built on aggregated data or on an ancestry-discrete design lose accuracy as genetic distance from the training samples grows, even within one ancestry group, because the data distribution shifts continuously rather than only between predefined categories.
AI.method: Distribution-aware in-context learning that captures the nonstationary omics-endpoint relationship across the genetic continuum, enabling efficient modeling through an in-context learning foundation model rather than separate models per ancestry group.
AI.result: The abstract reports theoretical analysis demonstrating the superiority of ancestry-continuum over ancestry-discrete modeling together with empirical results supporting the framework; no specific numbers are given.
AI.conclusion: Modeling outcomes along the genetic ancestry continuum rather than in discrete groups is a better formulation for omics-based cancer prediction, and source code is released.

title: Group-Conditional Conformal Risk Control: Exact Guarantees, Limits, and Overlapping Extensions
summary: We study group-conditional conformal risk control (CRC) for disjoint and overlapping groups under bounded monotone losses. For disjoint groups, we establish exact finite-sample conditional risk control, two-sided bounds on the group-restricted risk, and fundamental limitations arising from local support and calibration-rank granularity. For overlapping groups, we study two exactly valid approaches: group-restricted calibration followed by union deployment, and direct calibration of the deployed prediction-set family. We characterize the union's limiting reconciliation gap, identify conditions for its disappearance, and establish sharp lower bounds for structured losses in specified product-form models. We also demonstrate a strict size advantage for direct calibration in an ordinal model. Experiments show that direct calibration can reduce prediction-set size, but its efficiency depends on group structure, loss type, and shape fitting. Results on historical diabetic-retinopathy scores further illustrate these tradeoffs. Overall, local support, reconciliation slack, and threshold heterogeneity determine efficiency, with neither approach uniformly dominating.

AI.tldr: Studies group-conditional conformal risk control for disjoint and overlapping groups under bounded monotone losses, establishing exact finite-sample conditional risk control for disjoint groups and comparing two exactly valid approaches for overlapping groups. Direct calibration can reduce prediction-set size, but its efficiency depends on group structure, loss type and shape fitting, so neither approach uniformly dominates.
AI.motivation: Conditional risk guarantees for prediction sets must hold for groups that may overlap, and the efficiency of the available constructions depends on local support, calibration-rank granularity and how the union of group-restricted sets reconciles across groups.
AI.method: For disjoint groups the work gives exact conditional risk control and two-sided bounds on group-restricted risk; for overlapping groups it compares group-restricted calibration followed by union deployment with direct calibration of the deployed prediction-set family, characterizing the union's limiting reconciliation gap.
AI.result: Direct calibration can reduce prediction-set size and shows a strict size advantage in an ordinal model, while efficiency depends on group structure, loss type and shape fitting; experiments on historical diabetic-retinopathy scores illustrate these trade-offs, and the abstract gives no further numbers.
AI.conclusion: Local support, reconciliation slack and threshold heterogeneity determine efficiency in group-conditional conformal risk control, and neither the union nor the direct approach uniformly dominates.

title: Deep backward multistep high-order regression methods for high dimensional nonlinear parabolic partial differential equations
summary: We propose a deep backward multistep high-order regression (MHDBR) method for semilinear parabolic partial differential equations through their backward stochastic differential equation representations. The method combines multistep time discretization with regression targets formed by conditional expectations. Under explicit regularity, starting-value, forward-approximation and network-moment assumptions, we prove an error bound separating time discretization, conditional Monte Carlo sampling and neural-network approximation. The analysis assumes exact population minimization; finite-training-sample generalization and optimization errors are not included. For generators independent of the gradient variable, suitably constrained GroupSort networks and sufficiently large conditional sample sizes give order $J$ in the stated nodal $L^2$ error norm. The required network sizes depend on dimension, so this result does not establish dimension-independent complexity. We present a reproducible time-discretization test satisfying the analytical assumptions and three broader neural-network benchmarks, whose relation to the assumptions is discussed explicitly.

AI.tldr: Proposes the deep backward multistep high-order regression method (MHDBR) for semilinear parabolic PDEs in high dimensions, built on their backward stochastic differential equation representations, and proves an error bound that separates time discretization, conditional Monte Carlo sampling and neural-network approximation. The bound gives order J under stated assumptions, with the network size depending on dimension.
AI.motivation: Deep solvers for high-dimensional nonlinear parabolic PDEs need accurate, high-order time discretization together with regression targets that can be estimated reliably, and their error analysis is needed to separate these sources of error.
AI.method: Multistep time discretization combined with regression targets formed by conditional expectations, estimated with neural networks (constrained GroupSort networks for generators independent of the gradient variable) and conditional Monte Carlo sampling.
AI.result: Under explicit regularity, starting-value, forward-approximation and network-moment assumptions, and assuming exact population minimization, the method attains order J in the stated nodal L2 error norm with sufficiently large conditional sample sizes; a reproducible time-discretization test satisfies the analytical assumptions and three broader neural-network benchmarks are reported, though finite-sample generalization and optimization errors are not included.
AI.conclusion: The analysis establishes a high-order error bound for the method, but because network sizes depend on dimension it does not establish dimension-independent complexity.

title: Matchability-Aware Conformal Prediction for Open-Ended Language Model Generation
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often do not produce calibrated uncertainty estimates for their answers. We propose CAELUM, a framework that builds semantic prediction sets while separating aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty. CAELUM samples answers using an ensemble of clarification prompts, clusters them by semantic equivalence, and estimates the aleatoric and epistemic components via kernel-based von Neumann entropy before calibrating nonconformity scores with split conformal prediction. We use a weight $w_\lambda(x)=1+U_{\mathrm{ale}}(x)+\lambda\,U_{\mathrm{epi}}(x)$ to control for the contribution of the epistemic uncertainty of each instance and fit a coefficient $\lambda^\star$ to minimize prediction set size. When the objective is nonflat and selection is stable across splits, $\lambda^\star$ could be a diagnostic, where large values may indicate epistemic dominance (retrieve, abstain) and $\lambda^\star\to 0$ aleatoric dominance (clarify). For individual queries, a log ratio $R(x)$ compares the weighted epistemic component with the aleatoric component. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the coverage is capped by matchability, the fraction of items whose reference answer appears in any sampled cluster. Empirically, this matchability can be predicted from the original question features using a lightweight classifier. We use those predictions to define a stratum and derive a conformal coverage bound within it. Across 30 LLM and dataset combinations (4-32B), mean coverage is 0.74 in the learned stratum versus 0.65 overall, averaged over the 78 evaluations using the learned classifier. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CAELUM, a conformal prediction framework that builds semantic prediction sets for open-ended LLM answers and separates aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty. Across 30 LLM and dataset combinations, mean coverage is 0.74 in a learned stratum versus 0.65 overall.
AI.motivation: LLMs often do not produce calibrated uncertainty estimates for their answers, and open-ended generation makes it hard to separate uncertainty due to ambiguous questions from uncertainty due to lack of knowledge.
AI.method: CAELUM samples answers from an ensemble of clarification prompts, clusters them by semantic equivalence, and estimates aleatoric and epistemic components via kernel-based von Neumann entropy. It weights nonconformity scores with a coefficient lambda fitted to minimise prediction set size, calibrated with split conformal prediction, and predicts matchability from question features with a lightweight classifier to define a stratum with a conformal coverage bound.
AI.result: Across 30 LLM and dataset combinations (4-32B parameters), mean coverage is 0.74 in the learned stratum versus 0.65 overall, averaged over 78 evaluations with the learned classifier. The paper also proves coverage is capped by matchability, the fraction of items whose reference answer appears in any sampled cluster.
AI.conclusion: The lambda coefficient and the log ratio R(x) are proposed as diagnostics that indicate whether an instance is dominated by epistemic uncertainty (retrieve or abstain) or aleatoric uncertainty (clarify), and matchability is identified as the limiting factor on coverage.

title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement with Statistical Guarantees
summary: Recursive self-improvement offers a promising path toward AI agents that improve through experience by refining their own harnesses without retraining their underlying large language models (LLMs). Making this self-improvement process reliable, however, requires more than generating new updates: agents must decide which changes are worth keeping. A greedy gate that accepts updates based solely on higher validation scores can mistake an observed gain for genuine progress and lead to performance degeneration, whereas overly conservative statistical gates may reject beneficial updates and hinder performance improvement. We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a framework that adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, with an LLM analyzing historical context to help determine how much evidence is required to update the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, we prove that TRUST limits the proportion of accepted updates that result in unacceptable performance loss. We further derive a lower bound on the final performance gain. Across the benchmarks HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with the models DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate's 45.59% to 2.78%, while achieving higher final scores than the state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines for recursive self-improvement. These findings demonstrate that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TRUST, a framework that applies online multiple hypothesis testing to decide which self-improvement updates an LLM agent should accept, controlling the rate of harmful updates. On HotpotQA, DROP and APPS, it reduces the ratio of accepted inferior updates from 45.59% for a greedy gate to 2.78%.
AI.motivation: Recursive self-improvement of agent harnesses needs a gate that decides which updates to keep. A greedy gate accepts updates that only look better on validation and can cause performance degradation, while overly conservative statistical gates reject beneficial updates.
AI.method: TRUST adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, and an LLM analyses historical context to decide how much evidence is needed to replace the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, the authors prove a bound on the proportion of accepted updates causing unacceptable loss and derive a lower bound on final performance gain.
AI.result: Across HotpotQA, DROP and APPS with DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate's 45.59% to 2.78%. It also achieves higher final scores than state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines.
AI.conclusion: TRUST balances statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement, avoiding both the false gains of greedy acceptance and the missed improvements of overly conservative gates.

title: On Generalization in Bilevel Least Squares with Overparameterized Neural Networks
summary: Bilevel optimization addresses machine learning problems in which the outer objective is a value function implicitly defined through the solution of an inner problem. While its algorithmic aspects are well developed, its generalization properties remain much less understood. In this paper, we study the generalization of inexact gradient methods when both objectives are least-squares regression problems and when the estimator of the value function's gradient, or hypergradient, is obtained by implicit differentiation in function space. This approach allows us to derive stationarity bounds for these methods in terms of the uniform generalization errors of the two regression functions needed to estimate the hypergradient. When these regression functions are defined as overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient flow with early stopping, we obtain explicit finite-sample bounds on these generalization errors in the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime. Combining these with our general inexact gradient analysis shows the effect of sample size on the overall convergence of the bilevel method. Numerical experiments on synthetic data illustrate our results. Beyond the NTK regime, further experiments reveal an initialization-dependent implicit bias induced by the bilevel structure, which can lead to feature learning at the inner level and overall performance improvements.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the generalisation of inexact gradient methods for bilevel optimisation when both levels are least-squares problems and the hypergradient is estimated by implicit differentiation in function space. It gives finite-sample generalisation bounds for overparameterised two-layer ReLU networks in the NTK regime.
AI.motivation: Bilevel optimisation is well understood algorithmically, but its generalisation properties are much less understood.
AI.method: The authors derive stationarity bounds for inexact gradient methods in terms of the uniform generalisation errors of the two regression functions used to estimate the hypergradient. The regression functions are overparameterised two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient flow with early stopping.
AI.result: Explicit finite-sample bounds on the generalisation errors are obtained in the NTK regime, and combining them with the inexact gradient analysis shows how sample size affects overall convergence. Numerical experiments on synthetic data illustrate the results.
AI.conclusion: Beyond the NTK regime, experiments reveal an initialisation-dependent implicit bias induced by the bilevel structure, which can lead to feature learning at the inner level and overall performance improvements.

title: Bayesian transfer for offline Q-learning with multi-task Gaussian processes
summary: Offline reinforcement learning can benefit from data collected in related tasks, yet indiscriminate knowledge transfer may lead to negative transfer under task mismatch and limited target-data coverage. We propose a target-aware Bayesian transfer framework for offline Q-learning based on multi-task Gaussian processes that jointly model task-specific Q-functions. Source tasks are assessed using target predictive evidence and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), while posterior uncertainty and behavior-supported action sets guide conservative Bellman updates and policy extraction. To account for the dependence induced by Bellman bootstrapping, we distinguish Bellman innovations from bootstrap errors and establish stability and predictive source-selection results under explicit regularity conditions. We further derive selection-adaptive posterior contraction and offline policy-performance bounds, identifying the structural conditions under which source information can be pooled to achieve minimax-optimal rates in a shared-function Gaussian sequence experiment. Simulation studies with heterogeneous source tasks demonstrate improved target Q-function estimation and reduced material negative transfer compared with indiscriminate source pooling. An application to human decision-making data further shows higher average expected immediate payoff than both target-only learning and matched-size random source selection. These results highlight the benefits of combining target-aware source selection with uncertainty-aware conservative learning for reliable and sample-efficient offline reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a target-aware Bayesian transfer framework for offline Q-learning based on multi-task Gaussian processes that selectively pools source tasks. It shows improved target Q-function estimation and reduced negative transfer compared with indiscriminate source pooling.
AI.motivation: Offline reinforcement learning can benefit from related-task data, but indiscriminate knowledge transfer can cause negative transfer under task mismatch and limited target-data coverage.
AI.method: Multi-task Gaussian processes jointly model task-specific Q-functions. Source tasks are assessed using target predictive evidence and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), while posterior uncertainty and behaviour-supported action sets guide conservative Bellman updates and policy extraction. Bellman innovations are distinguished from bootstrap errors to handle the dependence induced by Bellman bootstrapping.
AI.result: Simulation studies with heterogeneous source tasks show improved target Q-function estimation and reduced negative transfer relative to indiscriminate pooling. On human decision-making data, the method achieves higher average expected immediate payoff than both target-only learning and matched-size random source selection.
AI.conclusion: Combining target-aware source selection with uncertainty-aware conservative learning gives reliable and sample-efficient offline reinforcement learning. The paper also gives selection-adaptive posterior contraction and policy-performance bounds, identifying conditions under which source information attains minimax-optimal rates.

title: Identifiable alignment of unpaired representations
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Aligning two models without paired data requires a distance that both share, yet existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry. This is either an arbitrary choice or imposed by their loss function. We show that, under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of one data-generating process. This holds whether the models are encoders, decoders or both, and whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment map preserves this distance and the distribution of representations, and is identifiable if and only if the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold. We show that this symmetry breaking holds generically. Identifiability makes the alignment coupling the unique optimum of Gromov--Wasserstein and of its weighted combinations with a linear program. The linear program alone has the same optimum if almost every data point has a distinct distribution of distances. The coupling, and with it the alignment map, is recovered exactly from permuted samples, even without identifiability, and consistently from independent ones. Our method, Neural Gromov--Monge Alignment (NGMA), uses no pairs or labels and outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It relies on pullback distances to align image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, where Euclidean distances fail.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Neural Gromov-Monge Alignment (NGMA), which aligns two unpaired models using the pullback of the data metric as a shared distance. It uses no pairs or labels and outperforms unpaired and label-informed baselines.
AI.motivation: Aligning two models without paired data needs a distance both models share, but existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry, which is either arbitrary or dictated by the loss function.
AI.method: Under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of the same data-generating process, whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment is the unique optimum of Gromov-Wasserstein and of its weighted combination with a linear program, and it is recovered from permuted samples and consistently from independent ones.
AI.result: NGMA outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It aligns image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, cases where Euclidean distances fail.
AI.conclusion: Pullback distances give a principled, identifiable geometry for unpaired representation alignment, provided the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold, which the authors show holds generically.

title: Amortized Bayesian Experimental Design with In-Context Knowledge Conditioning
comment: 38 pages, 25 figures. Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Amortized Bayesian experimental design (BED) enables real-time design strategies by shifting acquisition cost offline, but existing methods remain tied to the prior and task distribution they were trained on and cannot exploit additional information available at deployment. We introduce in-context amortized BED with unified knowledge encoding (IMBUE), a BED framework that admits external knowledge at deployment through a unified in-context interface. IMBUE accepts two forms of such knowledge without retraining, namely user-specified prior knowledge and observations from previous instances of the experiment. Both are encoded as additional input tokens and processed in-context with the accumulated observations by a shared Transformer, and a learned reliability filter scores each external token against the observations and excludes inconsistent ones. Across four benchmarks, IMBUE accelerates early-stage information acquisition when the external knowledge is reliable, and remains close to the no-external baseline when it is not.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IMBUE, an amortised Bayesian experimental design framework that accepts external knowledge at deployment without retraining. It encodes user-specified priors and observations from previous experiments as in-context tokens, filtered by a learned reliability filter.
AI.motivation: Existing amortised Bayesian experimental design methods are tied to the prior and task distribution used in training and cannot exploit extra information available at deployment.
AI.method: External knowledge is encoded as additional input tokens and processed in-context with accumulated observations by a shared Transformer. A learned reliability filter scores each external token against the observations and excludes inconsistent ones.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, IMBUE accelerates early-stage information acquisition when the external knowledge is reliable, and stays close to the no-external-knowledge baseline when it is not.
AI.conclusion: IMBUE makes amortised experimental design adaptable to deployment-time knowledge while remaining robust to unreliable knowledge.

title: Query- and Candidate-Aware Long User Sequence Modeling for Sponsored Product Ranking in Search
comment: Accepted to ACM RecSys 2026 Workshop on Context-Aware Recommender Systems (CARS)
summary: User sequence modeling is widely used in recommendation and advertising. Search ranking presents an additional challenge: the current query expresses immediate intent, while a candidate product determines which parts of a user's long-term history are relevant. We present a production sequence framework for sponsored-product ranking that augments recent behavior with two retrieval channels over long-term history: candidate-nearest-neighbor retrieval and query-nearest-neighbor retrieval. The selected actions are encoded together with dedicated query and candidate context tokens, while candidate-aware early fusion injects the candidate into every history token. Offline ablations show that dual retrieval improves major ranking metrics relative to the production baseline. In an online A/B test on sponsored-product search traffic, the model increased CTR, attributed conversion rate, and orders per impression.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a production sequence model for sponsored-product ranking in search that retrieves relevant long-term user history using both the candidate product and the current query. In an online A/B test it increased CTR, attributed conversion rate and orders per impression.
AI.motivation: In search ranking, the current query expresses immediate intent while the candidate product determines which parts of a user's long-term history are relevant, a combination that standard recommendation sequence models do not address.
AI.method: Recent behaviour is augmented with two retrieval channels over long-term history: candidate-nearest-neighbour retrieval and query-nearest-neighbour retrieval.
