AI.method: PFNs predict through in-context learning and model propensity scores and outcome regressions within doubly robust estimators, with and without cross-fitting. Synthetic and semi-synthetic settings vary confounding complexity and effect heterogeneity, and conventional learners include parametric regressions and Super Learner ensembles.
AI.result: Under simple parametric data-generating processes PFNs are competitive with correctly specified parametric regressions. In complex settings they outperform all conventional learners for accuracy and uncertainty quantification. As sample size grows only TabPFN and Mitra consistently approach nominal coverage. At n=200 and in higher-dimensional semi-synthetic settings, PFNs show poor coverage without cross-fitting, apparently due to propensity score overfitting.
AI.conclusion: PFNs are promising in-context nuisance learners for causal estimation, but evaluation in more challenging settings is still needed, particularly for small samples without cross-fitting.

title: What Travels Across Languages? Reading, Transfer and Erasure of Cross-Lingual Concept Subspaces in Bangla Idioms
comment: 73 pages, 21 figures, 52 tables. Code, frozen analysis plans and aggregate results: this https URL
summary: Cross-lingual concept analysis requires distinguishing the information that a subspace retains from the classifiers and erasers that transfer through it. We study these operations in six frozen encoders using 10,359 Bangla (Bengali) idiom senses, eight input conditions, and figurative-class and sentiment labels. Class-mean directions provide the most consistent evidence of shared coarse meaning: in post hoc analyses, they outperform random-subspace, permuted-label and covariance-matched nulls in all 12 model-label tests under balanced accuracy. A prospective internal re-split supports idiom-alone sharing in 10 of 12 tests, spanning five encoders. The original confirmatory logistic-regression family rejects both planned nulls in 4 of 12 tests, where English directions gain only a few accuracy points above the majority-class floor (3.0-7.3). Classifier transfer depends on the input map and regularization: English-trained class-mean readouts beat both zero-shot nulls in 8 of 12 discovery tests, and stronger source-selected penalties improve transfer through logistic and LEACE directions. These readouts use Bangla-validation-selected layers and unlabeled target preprocessing. Input controls show greater coarse-class sharing for explicit glosses than for idiom counterparts. Reading, however, does not imply effective erasure: English-fitted LEACE removes less than one percentage point of Bangla figurative-class accuracy, compared with 4-11 points for Bangla-fitted LEACE; INLP shows a similar asymmetry. Pattern-filter analysis, covariance-weighted input maps and a binary Gaussian overlap bound explain how these operations can diverge. The analogous multiclass ordering is an empirical diagnostic, observed in 11 of 12 cells. The results support an estimator-sensitive account of cross-lingual concept sharing and motivate evaluating reading, classifier transfer, erasure and overlap separately.

AI.tldr: The study examines how Bangla idiom meaning is encoded across frozen multilingual encoders, separating what a subspace reads, what classifiers transfer through it, and what can be erased. Class-mean directions show the most consistent evidence of shared coarse meaning, but reading does not imply effective erasure.
AI.motivation: Cross-lingual concept analysis needs to distinguish what a subspace retains from what transfers through classifiers and erasers, because these operations can diverge.
AI.method: Six frozen encoders are evaluated on 10,359 Bangla idiom senses under eight input conditions, with figurative-class and sentiment labels. Class-mean directions, logistic regression, LEACE and INLP are compared against random-subspace, permuted-label and covariance-matched nulls, with pattern-filter and covariance-weighted analyses and a binary Gaussian overlap bound.
AI.result: Class-mean directions beat the nulls in all 12 post hoc model-label tests under balanced accuracy, and a re-split supports idiom-alone sharing in 10 of 12 tests. In the confirmatory family, both nulls are rejected in 4 of 12 tests, where English directions gain only a few points above the majority floor. English-trained class-mean readouts beat zero-shot nulls in 8 of 12 discovery tests. English-fitted LEACE removes less than one point of Bangla figurative-class accuracy, compared with 4 to 11 points for Bangla-fitted LEACE.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual concept sharing depends on the estimator, so reading, classifier transfer, erasure and overlap should be evaluated separately rather than treated as one property.

title: Orthogonal Updates for the Win: Towards Accelerated Adaptive Minimax Optimization
summary: Single-loop minimax methods are appealing for modern machine learning, but standard stochastic gradient updates can be unstable and oscillatory under tightly coupled primal-dual dynamics, making performance notoriously sensitive to stepsizes. To fundamentally improve stability, we develop an orthogonal update framework tailored to minimax optimization, which applies updates along orthogonalized directions to reduce update anisotropy. However, orthogonalization reshapes the optimization geometry and makes coordinating primal-dual stepsizes even more delicate. To overcome this challenge, we develop AdaSGDA, which equips orthogonal updates with an adaptive stepsize rule driven by accumulated gradient norms. This mechanism automatically balances coupled primal-dual progress under orthogonalization, yielding an effectively parameter-free method for nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization. We prove that AdaSGDA avoids problem-dependent tuning while attaining the state-of-the-art $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/4}\right)$ convergence rate. We further propose AdaSGDA-VR, which incorporates a carefully designed variance reduction scheme and achieves the faster $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/3}\right)$ rate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods deliver competitive performance compared to existing minimax optimization methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes orthogonal updates for single-loop minimax optimization and an adaptive stepsize method, AdaSGDA, that is effectively parameter-free. A variance-reduced variant, AdaSGDA-VR, achieves a faster rate.
AI.motivation: Standard stochastic gradient updates for minimax problems can be unstable and oscillatory under tightly coupled primal-dual dynamics, and performance is sensitive to stepsizes.
AI.method: Updates are applied along orthogonalized directions to reduce anisotropy. The resulting primal-dual geometry is balanced by an adaptive stepsize driven by accumulated gradient norms. AdaSGDA-VR adds a variance reduction scheme.
AI.result: For nonconvex-strongly-concave problems AdaSGDA avoids problem-dependent tuning and attains the state-of-the-art O(T^(-1/4)) rate. AdaSGDA-VR attains O(T^(-1/3)). Experiments show competitive performance against existing minimax methods.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonalized updates with norm-driven adaptive stepsizes give a stable, nearly parameter-free approach to minimax optimization with provable rates.

title: Causal Machine Learning for Multilevel Studies with Unmeasured Cluster-Level Covariates via Variational Autoencoders
summary: Unmeasured confounders are a key obstacle to accurately estimating treatment effects in observational studies, and in multilevel data, they often arise at the cluster level. Flexible machine learning methods cannot directly resolve such unmeasured confounding. To address this, we propose the variational autoencoder-augmented R-learner (VAE-R), which leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to infer unmeasured cluster-level covariates from the within-cluster dependence of outcome and treatment residuals, and uses the resulting adjustments to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and the average treatment effect (ATE). The VAE decoder is specified through an offset likelihood so that the latent variables capture only the cluster-level variation left unexplained by measured covariates. VAE-R accommodates unmeasured cluster-level confounders in observational studies and unmeasured cluster-level predictors of the outcome in multisite randomized trials. We also provide data-driven strategies for selecting the two hyperparameters of the VAE, the latent dimension size and the Kullback-Leibler weight. Our simulation study shows that VAE-R nearly eliminates the bias of the ordinary R-learner's CATE and ATE estimates in multilevel observational data and improves their precision in multisite randomized trials. Finally, we illustrate VAE-R with two datasets, one from a multilevel observational study and the other from a multisite randomized trial.

AI.tldr: VAE-R combines a variational autoencoder with the R-learner to infer unmeasured cluster-level confounders in multilevel data and estimate CATE and ATE. Simulations show it nearly removes the bias of the ordinary R-learner in multilevel observational data.
AI.motivation: Unmeasured confounders at the cluster level bias treatment effect estimates in multilevel observational studies, and flexible machine learning methods cannot resolve this by themselves.
AI.method: VAEs infer unmeasured cluster-level covariates from the within-cluster dependence of outcome and treatment residuals. The decoder uses an offset likelihood so that latent variables capture only variation not explained by measured covariates. Two VAE hyperparameters, the latent dimension and the KL weight, are selected with data-driven strategies.
AI.result: In simulations VAE-R nearly eliminates the bias of the ordinary R-learner's CATE and ATE estimates in multilevel observational data, and it improves precision in multisite randomized trials. It is illustrated on one multilevel observational dataset and one multisite trial.
AI.conclusion: VAE-R handles unmeasured cluster-level confounding in observational studies and unmeasured cluster-level outcome predictors in multisite trials, improving causal estimation in multilevel settings.

title: Learning through Capacity Awareness to Minimize Hospital Readmissions
summary: Predictive algorithms are increasingly used to guide hospital discharge decisions, yet these models can exhibit censoring bias for vulnerable patients due to insufficient historical data or past discharge decisions. When biased readmission risk predictors are used to inform discharges, the training data generated by discharge decisions may perpetuate similar biases when predictors are re-trained, leading to a vicious cycle. We extend a queueing-based Markov decision process for hospital discharge to incorporate periodically retrained readmission risk predictors. Our key insight is that cost-optimal, "capacity-aware" operational decision policies can naturally diversify the lengths of stay at which patient outcomes are observed, enabling consistent estimation of readmission risk without explicit fairness constraints. We prove that repeated retraining under discharge-up-to policies converges to unbiased risk estimates under well-specification. In synthetic experiments and calibrated simulations based on patient-level data from a partner hospital, we find that where commonly used threshold-on-risk policies can remain persistently biased, discharge-up-to policies reduce learning error over status quo decision policies (such as thresholding on risk) by 24%-25%. These improvements to estimation also mitigate some forms of bias, reducing readmission cost disparities (adjusted for baseline risk differences between demographic groups) by 38%-63%. Our results demonstrate how capacity-aware decision policies can improve both predictive performance and fairness by addressing censoring bias.

AI.tldr: The paper extends a queueing-based Markov decision process for hospital discharge to periodically retrained readmission risk models, and shows that capacity-aware discharge-up-to policies reduce censoring bias. Such policies improve learning error and reduce readmission cost disparities without explicit fairness constraints.
AI.motivation: Readmission risk predictors can be biased against vulnerable patients because of censoring, and retraining on data generated by biased discharge decisions can create a vicious cycle.
AI.method: The queueing MDP is extended with periodic retraining of risk predictors. Discharge-up-to policies, which are cost-optimal and capacity-aware, are compared with threshold-on-risk policies. The authors prove that repeated retraining under these policies converges to unbiased risk estimates under well-specification.
AI.result: In synthetic experiments and calibrated simulations based on patient data from a partner hospital, discharge-up-to policies reduce learning error relative to status quo policies by 24% to 25%, where threshold-on-risk policies can stay persistently biased. Readmission cost disparities adjusted for baseline risk differences fall by 38% to 63%.
AI.conclusion: Capacity-aware decision policies that diversify observed lengths of stay can improve both predictive performance and fairness by addressing censoring bias.

title: A Stability Analysis of AdamW: Unstable Equilibria and Non-Convergence
summary: AdamW is ubiquitous in deep learning, yet its behavior remains poorly understood. We analyze its dynamics through the lens of dynamical systems and show that AdamW admits an implicit fixed-point objective: its fixed points coincide with the stationary points of a constrained and regularized optimization problem. However, not all of these fixed points are stable under AdamW's dynamics, and stability depends sensitively on curvature, weight decay, and momentum parameters. Even in one-dimensional settings, equilibria may be unstable, and trajectories can exhibit persistent oscillations rather than convergence to them. We further extend the analysis to higher dimensions, deriving sufficient conditions for local stability of the continuous-time dynamics, and propose a convergent modification that preserves AdamW's fixed points. These results clarify what optimization problem AdamW is associated with, when its convergence can be expected, and how its dynamics could inspire more reliable optimizers.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes AdamW as a dynamical system and shows that its fixed points coincide with stationary points of a constrained, regularized problem. Stability depends on curvature, weight decay and momentum, and some fixed points are unstable.
AI.motivation: AdamW is ubiquitous in deep learning, but its dynamics and the optimization problem it solves were poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors identify an implicit fixed-point objective for AdamW, analyze stability of equilibria in one dimension and of the continuous-time dynamics in higher dimensions, and derive sufficient local stability conditions.
AI.result: Some equilibria are unstable even in one dimension, and trajectories can oscillate persistently rather than converge. A convergent modification is proposed that preserves AdamW's fixed points.
AI.conclusion: The analysis clarifies which optimization problem AdamW is associated with and when its convergence can be expected, and suggests how more reliable optimizers could be designed.

title: Robust Gaussian process regression: posterior contraction
summary: Gaussian processes form a popular and flexible class of prior distributions with principled uncertainty quantification, but the Gaussian likelihood on which the corresponding posterior relies makes them highly sensitive to outliers and contaminated observations. We study Gaussian process regression when among the $n$ observations, $m$ of these are possibly contaminated. A generic framework to obtain posterior contraction rates in this setting is considered, from a frequentist perspective as the sample size $n$ and the number of corrupted observations $m$ grow. We adopt a generalized Bayes approach in which the log--likelihood is replaced by a robustified version; we discuss various choices thereof, such as one recently proposed by Altamirano et al. that preserves conjugacy. We investigate the minimax rate of estimation under adversarial contamination in terms of the Sobolev smoothness $\beta$ of the regression function and $m$. The question of building adaptive procedures to both $\beta$ and $m$ is investigated, and we show that a polynomial loss for adaptation must be paid in general. We instantiate our results for Matérn Gaussian process and deep ReLU network priors. Numerical experiments for existing and new robust algorithms are provided, illustrating the practical applicability of our results.

AI.tldr: The paper studies posterior contraction for Gaussian process regression when some observations may be adversarially corrupted, using a generalized Bayes approach with robustified likelihoods. It derives minimax rates in terms of Sobolev smoothness and the number of corrupted observations.
AI.motivation: The Gaussian likelihood makes Gaussian process posteriors highly sensitive to outliers and contaminated observations, which is a problem for their standard uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: Among n observations, m may be contaminated. A generic framework yields posterior contraction rates from a frequentist perspective as n and m grow, using robustified log-likelihoods such as one proposed by Altamirano et al. that preserves conjugacy. Adaptation to both smoothness and m is investigated, and results are instantiated for Matern and deep ReLU network priors.
AI.result: The minimax rate under adversarial contamination is characterized in terms of the Sobolev smoothness beta and m. Adaptation to both beta and m requires a polynomial loss in general. Numerical experiments for existing and new robust algorithms illustrate the results.
AI.conclusion: Robust Gaussian process posteriors can achieve contraction under contamination, but adaptive procedures must pay a polynomial price in general.

title: A Trust Region Approach for Learning Schrödinger Bridges
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026; Takeshi Koshizuka and Lorenz Richter contributed equally
summary: We study the numerical approximation of Schrödinger Bridges in the setting where samples from the target distribution are unavailable and only an unnormalized target density is given. In this regime, the widely used iterative proportional fitting (IPF) procedure (and its variants) often exhibits severe numerical instabilities, stemming from ill-conditioned underlying control problems and from the fact that the optimal solution may lie far from the initialization. To address these issues, we propose a trust region variant of IPF that constrains successive updates to remain at a fixed Kullback-Leibler divergence from the current iterate. This restriction significantly improves numerical stability. Moreover, we show that the resulting method admits an interpretation as a mirror descent scheme with an adaptively chosen step size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging sampling tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a trust region variant of iterative proportional fitting (IPF) for learning Schrödinger Bridges when only an unnormalized target density is available. Successive updates are constrained to a fixed KL divergence from the current iterate, which substantially improves numerical stability.
AI.motivation: Standard IPF and its variants are numerically unstable in the unnormalized-density setting because the control problems are ill-conditioned and the optimal solution can lie far from the initialization.
AI.method: Each IPF update is constrained to stay at a fixed Kullback-Leibler divergence from the current iterate, a trust region variant of IPF. The authors show it can be interpreted as a mirror descent scheme with an adaptively chosen step size.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the restriction significantly improves numerical stability and that the method is effective on several challenging sampling tasks. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Trust region constraints offer a stable and principled route to Schrödinger Bridge learning from unnormalized densities, linked to mirror descent with adaptive step sizes.

title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization
summary: We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper gives finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees for learning DAG structure from observational data under generalized linear models at each node. It analyzes a nonsmooth objective with an exact acyclicity constraint and a quasi-minimax concave penalty, solvable by standard gradient-based methods.
AI.motivation: Gradient-based causal structure learning in nonlinear models is widely used, but statistical guarantees for it are missing from the literature.
AI.method: Under a generalized linear model for each node, the method minimizes a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, optimized with standard gradient-based solvers.
AI.result: Finite-sample guarantees are established for this model, including the widely used logistic and Poisson cases. Experiments show accurate structure recovery and good computational performance on standardized data, with negative controls used as baselines.
AI.conclusion: The work fills a theoretical gap by showing that gradient-based DAG learning in generalized linear models comes with nonasymptotic guarantees, supported by experiments.

title: When Should AI Overturn a Human Decision? Controversy at the 2026 World Cup and a $\sqrt{2/π}$ Solution
comment: This paper is intended for educational purposes
summary: We study how to combine a human binary call (a referee's offside or onside decision) with an AI numerical measurement (VAR's estimate of an attacker's position relative to the offside line). We derive an explicit maximum-likelihood rule that determines when the referee's call should stand and when a conflicting VAR measurement should overturn it. Our model treats the true offside margin as fixed and unknown and assumes independent additive Gaussian errors in the human's perception and the AI measurement. When both errors have zero means and known standard deviations $\sigma_H$ and $\sigma_{AI}$, respectively, the reversal threshold is $\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\sigma^2_{AI}/\sigma_H$. An onside call is overturned precisely when VAR's measured offside margin exceeds this threshold---not merely because VAR places the attacker beyond the offside line. We also derive the rule when either source has a systematic bias. We prove that the maximum-likelihood estimate of the true margin exists and is unique, while the final binary decision requires only a threshold comparison, without computing that estimate numerically. We illustrate the rule through numerical examples and show how to estimate the error parameters from calibration data. The same analysis applies beyond soccer to binary classification problems in which a human call and an AI measurement satisfy the stated model. This paper is intended for educational purposes: we aim to illustrate how undergraduate students and advanced high school students familiar with basic probability and calculus can investigate research questions in AI and its applications.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a maximum-likelihood rule for deciding when a referee's binary human call should be overturned by a conflicting AI numerical measurement, using the 2026 World Cup offside controversy as the motivating case. Under independent Gaussian errors, an onside call is overturned only when the VAR-measured offside margin exceeds sqrt(2/pi) times sigma_AI squared over sigma_H.
AI.motivation: The paper asks how to combine a human binary decision with an AI measurement that carry different error levels, a question that arises in offside review and more broadly in binary classification with human and AI inputs.
AI.method: The model treats the true offside margin as fixed and unknown, with independent additive Gaussian errors in the human perception and the AI measurement. The reversal threshold is derived in closed form, and extensions cover systematic bias in either source. The authors prove the maximum-likelihood margin estimate exists and is unique, and show that the final decision needs only a threshold comparison.
AI.result: The rule is illustrated with numerical examples, and the paper shows how the error parameters can be estimated from calibration data. The abstract notes that an onside call is overturned precisely when the measured margin exceeds the threshold, not merely because VAR places the attacker beyond the offside line.
AI.conclusion: The analysis gives a simple, explicit decision rule for combining human and AI calls, and it applies beyond soccer. The paper is written for educational use with undergraduate and advanced high school students.

title: How Path Integral Diffusion Decides a Finite Spin Glass
summary: When an AI diffusion-type generator samples a frustrated spin glass, which macroscopic alternatives does it decide first, and when? We study this for bridge-diffusion models of the Path Integral Diffusion (PID) type started from a point source. We show that every isotropic PID is a time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization, and conversely every signal-to-noise schedule is realized by a PID protocol. What a continuous-time generator decides therefore does not depend on the protocol, which only sets when and at what cost. We describe the generator's state by its partial commitments: the probabilities it assigns, at each moment, to nested classes of configurations fixed by the target. The partial commitments are martingales that move only along class contrasts. Their ensemble average gives the information about each level at an exact rate set by squared magnetization contrasts. Each split is decided, approximately, like a binary Gaussian channel at signal-to-noise ratio 1.04/\lambda_P, with \lambda_P the leading eigenvalue of the parent's correlation matrix. The theory is applied to Bethe-lattice and Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) glasses with up to 64 spins. It is observed generically that a trajectory first shifts its weight to one of the two mirror halves of the zero-field measure and then to the glassy classes inside it. These classes appear near the glass transition and keep their identity on cooling. Nested glassy levels have similar \lambda_P and are decided together, so a trajectory commits in one or two distinct events---the mirror choice and a compound glassy decision---which separate further with coupling and size, as the spectra predict. For a generator that takes finitely many steps, the protocol matters through the late, local stage rather than the macroscopic decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that every isotropic Path Integral Diffusion protocol is a time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization, and it analyzes which macroscopic decisions a diffusion generator makes when sampling a frustrated spin glass. Each split is decided approximately like a binary Gaussian channel with signal-to-noise ratio 1.04 divided by lambda_P, where lambda_P is the leading eigenvalue of the parent's correlation matrix.
AI.motivation: The question is which macroscopic alternatives a diffusion-type generator decides first, and when, when it samples a frustrated spin glass.
AI.method: The generator state is described by partial commitments, which are probabilities assigned to nested classes of configurations fixed by the target. These commitments are martingales that move only along class contrasts, and their ensemble average gives an exact information rate set by squared magnetization contrasts.
AI.result: Applied to Bethe-lattice and Sherrington-Kirkpatrick glasses with up to 64 spins, trajectories first shift weight to one of the two mirror halves of the zero-field measure and then to glassy classes inside it. Nested glassy levels with similar lambda_P are decided together, so a trajectory commits in one or two distinct events.
AI.conclusion: What a continuous-time generator decides is independent of the protocol, which affects only timing and cost, while for finite-step generators the protocol matters in the late, local stage.

title: Severity-Controlled Prediction Sets for Medication Recommendation
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version. Code: this https URL
summary: Medication recommendation is a multi-label prediction task. However, existing prediction-set evaluation and calibration methods rely mainly on exact-overlap metrics and therefore treat all missed medications as equally severe, overlooking how closely the prediction set matches them within the medication hierarchy. To address this, we introduce Conformal Severity Control (CSC), a post-hoc framework for calibrating medication prediction sets under hierarchy-aware mismatch severity. CSC uses the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) hierarchy to quantify mismatch severity and controls patient-level severity without retraining the predictor, supporting both average severity and upper-quantile severity for the highest-severity mismatches. Experiments on MIMIC-IV show that CSC tracks user-specified severity tolerances and shifts prediction sets away from distant mismatches toward exact or close matches.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Conformal Severity Control (CSC), a post-hoc method that calibrates medication prediction sets so that mismatches are weighted by their severity in the ATC hierarchy. It controls patient-level severity without retraining the predictor.
AI.motivation: Existing prediction-set evaluation and calibration for medication recommendation rely on exact-overlap metrics, so all missed medications count as equally severe, even when a predicted medication is close to the true one in the hierarchy.
AI.method: CSC uses the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) hierarchy to quantify mismatch severity. It supports control of either average severity or upper-quantile severity for the most severe mismatches, and it works post hoc on a trained predictor.
AI.result: Experiments on MIMIC-IV show that CSC tracks user-specified severity tolerances and shifts prediction sets away from distant mismatches toward exact or close matches.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchy-aware severity control gives clinically more meaningful calibration of medication prediction sets than exact-overlap approaches, without changing the underlying model.

title: Identifiable but Hard to Estimate: Rotation in Equally Spaced Overcomplete ICA
summary: How many observations are needed to estimate a common rotation in two-dimensional overcomplete independent component analysis? We study equally spaced mixing columns with known source count, common source law, and column norm. For a fixed non-Gaussian fourth-order Gram-Charlier source law, the rotation is identifiable modulo the column spacing. Yet the sample size for fixed relative angular accuracy grows exponentially with the source count. We characterize this sample size, up to absolute constants, by the reciprocal of the squared Hellinger distance between two rotations separated by half the column spacing. An explicit radially weighted phase estimator attains this scale uniformly over the rotation family, using the observation radius to prevent cancellation in the mean of an angular harmonic. We also determine the exact exponential decay rate of single-observation total variation for the same pair. This gives bounds on the sample size exponent; its exact value remains open. Finally, a noisy binary-source example shows how an exact zero line of the observed characteristic function can have an exponentially small normal derivative.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how many observations are needed to estimate a common rotation in two-dimensional overcomplete ICA with equally spaced mixing columns. The required sample size grows exponentially with the number of sources, and the authors characterize it up to absolute constants.
AI.motivation: Rotation is identifiable in this setting, but it is unclear how many samples are needed to estimate it to a fixed relative angular accuracy.
AI.method: The authors fix a non-Gaussian fourth-order Gram-Charlier source law and analyze equally spaced mixing columns with known source count, common source law and column norm. They give an explicit radially weighted phase estimator that uses the observation radius to avoid cancellation in the mean of an angular harmonic.
AI.result: The sample size is characterized by the reciprocal of the squared Hellinger distance between two rotations separated by half the column spacing, and the estimator attains this scale uniformly over the rotation family. The exact exponential decay rate of single-observation total variation for the same pair is determined, but the exact exponent of the sample size remains open. A noisy binary-source example shows an exponentially small normal derivative of the observed characteristic function at an exact zero line.
AI.conclusion: Identifiability does not imply practical estimability, since sample requirements grow exponentially with source count, and the exact sample-size exponent is left as an open problem.

title: Deep-Learning-Assisted Bayesian Inference for Extreme-Mass-Ratio Inspirals
summary: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) pose a major challenge to Bayesian parameter inference because of their complex, highly multimodal likelihood surfaces. Locating narrow high-likelihood regions is particularly difficult without knowledge of the true source parameters, which is unavailable in real observations. We develop a deep-learning-assisted Bayesian inference framework that combines neural-network-guided parameter-space localization, particle swarm optimization, and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Applied to simulated six-month EMRI signals, the framework recovers posterior distributions in close agreement with reference MCMC analyses initialized near the true parameter values, without requiring such knowledge for initialization. Once the neural network has been trained, the complete inference pipeline takes approximately 10 hours per signal.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a deep-learning-assisted Bayesian inference framework for extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs), combining neural-network-guided localization, particle swarm optimization and MCMC. On simulated six-month EMRI signals it recovers posteriors close to reference MCMC analyses that were initialized near the true parameters.
AI.motivation: EMRI likelihood surfaces are complex and highly multimodal, so locating narrow high-likelihood regions is hard without knowing the true source parameters, which real observations do not provide.
AI.method: A neural network guides localization in parameter space, particle swarm optimization is applied, and MCMC sampling follows. The pipeline does not need the true parameters for initialization.
AI.result: On simulated six-month EMRI signals, the recovered posterior distributions agree closely with reference MCMC analyses initialized near the true values. Once the network is trained, the full pipeline takes about 10 hours per signal.
AI.conclusion: The framework makes EMRI parameter inference feasible without prior knowledge of the true source parameters, at a cost of roughly 10 hours per signal after training.

title: Characterizing Underrepresentation when Generalizing Causal Survival Estimates
comment: To appear in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
summary: Randomized trial findings are routinely generalized to broader target populations to inform decisions in medicine and public policy. When the trial sample is misaligned with the target population, generalized effect estimates can yield suboptimal decisions. We characterize the target subgroups that are underrepresented in the trial cohort in time-to-event settings. Here, underrepresentation arises in two distinct ways: baseline underrepresentation, when a subgroup's covariate profile is rare in the trial relative to the target, and time-varying underrepresentation, when differential censoring erodes a subgroup over follow-up. Existing diagnostics either conflate these mechanisms or apply only to the baseline case. We show that the asymptotic variance of the efficient generalizability estimator admits a decomposition in which only two terms can diverge as representation weakens: a sampling-weight term capturing baseline misalignment and a censoring-weight term capturing differential loss to follow-up. Underrepresented subgroups are therefore those with imprecise generalized estimates, and the larger of the two terms gives the responsible channel. We use this decomposition in TRACE (Temporal Rashomon Analysis of CEnsored data), which combines a self-normalized variance objective with a tree-based search to localize underrepresented subgroups, attribute each to baseline mismatch or censoring, and find the follow-up intervals where censoring drives the variance inflation. We solve the joint problem with a parametric dynamic program nested inside a Rashomon ensemble of near-optimal trees. In synthetic benchmarks, TRACE recovers the planted underrepresented regions. In a case study generalizing the National Job Training Partnership Act (JTPA) Study to U.S. JTPA-eligible adults, restricting to reliably generalizable subgroups narrows the 95% confidence interval for the refined estimand by 60%.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes which target subgroups are underrepresented when generalizing causal survival estimates from a randomized trial, and it introduces TRACE to localize them. Variance is decomposed into a baseline sampling-weight term and a censoring-weight term, so each underrepresented subgroup is attributed to one of these channels.
AI.motivation: Existing diagnostics either conflate baseline and time-varying underrepresentation or apply only to the baseline case, which limits their use for time-to-event generalization.
AI.method: The asymptotic variance of the efficient generalizability estimator is decomposed so that only a sampling-weight term and a censoring-weight term can diverge. TRACE combines a self-normalized variance objective with a tree-based search, solved by a parametric dynamic program nested in a Rashomon ensemble of near-optimal trees.
AI.result: In synthetic benchmarks TRACE recovers the planted underrepresented regions. In a case study generalizing the National Job Training Partnership Act Study to U.S. JTPA-eligible adults, restricting to reliably generalizable subgroups narrows the 95% confidence interval for the refined estimand by 60%.
AI.conclusion: The decomposition gives a practical way to identify where generalized survival estimates are imprecise and to attribute the cause, whether baseline mismatch or differential censoring.

title: Conformal Prediction for Multi-Step Forecasting: Conditional Coverage and Sharp Score Calibration Rates
summary: Uncertainty quantification in prediction is a central problem in statistics and machine learning. Conformal prediction provides a flexible approach to constructing prediction sets with valid marginal coverage under exchangeability. In this paper, we investigate conformal prediction for both one-step and multi-step forecasting from a single stationary time series, addressing temporal dependence and the additional challenges of joint prediction across multiple horizons. We propose a kernel-based framework, called Time series Residual Analysis for Calibration with Kernels (TRACK), for estimating conditional quantiles of residual scores and constructing prediction sets from rolling-window forecasters. The framework accommodates heterogeneous uncertainty across horizons and accounts for dependence induced by rolling estimation, while allowing predictor memory and forecast horizons to grow with the sample size. Our finite-sample bounds quantify how temporal dependence and overlapping score windows affect calibration and coverage. We further derive bounds for conditional quantile estimation and pointwise conditional coverage discrepancy. The guarantees extend to more general predictors that admit an accurate rolling-window approximation. We also derive matching minimax bounds over classes of known score maps, clarifying how overlapping score windows affect calibration accuracy. Experimental results from simulations and applications to wind energy generation and bike sharing demand show that our methods improve regional conditional coverage while maintaining competitive interval widths.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TRACK, a kernel-based conformal prediction framework for one-step and multi-step forecasting from a single stationary time series. It gives finite-sample bounds on calibration and coverage and improves regional conditional coverage while keeping competitive interval widths.
AI.motivation: Standard conformal prediction assumes exchangeability, whereas forecasting from one time series involves temporal dependence, joint prediction across horizons, and dependence induced by rolling estimation.
AI.method: TRACK estimates conditional quantiles of residual scores and constructs prediction sets from rolling-window forecasters. It allows heterogeneous uncertainty across horizons and lets predictor memory and forecast horizons grow with the sample size.
AI.result: Finite-sample bounds quantify how temporal dependence and overlapping score windows affect calibration and coverage, and bounds are given for conditional quantile estimation and pointwise conditional coverage discrepancy. Matching minimax bounds are derived over classes of known score maps. Simulations and applications to wind energy generation and bike sharing demand show improved regional conditional coverage with competitive interval widths.
AI.conclusion: The results give theoretical guarantees and minimax-optimal calibration rates for conformal forecasting under temporal dependence, with practical gains in conditional coverage.

title: Scale-Invariant Empirical-Bayes Laplace Approximation for ReLU Networks
summary: ReLU networks are well-known to have continuous scale symmetries; infinitely many reparameterized weight vectors that represent the same function. Dinh et al. (2017) have shown that, by reparameterizing, the geometry of the loss landscape (e.g., curvature) of these networks can be changed arbitrarily without affecting the underlying function. Thus, any quantity that depends on the network's geometry should be defined with care. In this paper, we show that the Empirical Bayes (EB) Laplace's approximation is not well-defined for ReLU networks, mainly due to Hessian dependence in computing the marginal likelihood, which is not invariant under ReLU scale symmetries. Thus, we can get different prior precisions, posterior covariances, and predictive uncertainties for a network having identical predictions under ReLU scaling. We define family of prior precision fields indexed by $\gamma$ and introduce $\gamma$-canonicalization, which first converts the network to its canonical representation by balancing the ratio of incoming to outgoing weights, and then fits the Empirical Bayes (EB) Laplace to the canonical representation. This procedure is equivalent to transporting the isotropic Gaussian prior from the canonical representation to the original coordinates, by producing a ReLU-scale-compatible precision field. This makes the marginal likelihood invariant under ReLU scaling, while allowing $\gamma$ to be selected by maximizing the marginal likelihood. The resulting EB Laplace approximation is well-defined on ReLU scale-equivalence classes and yields consistent prior precision selection and predictive uncertainties across functionally identical parameterizations.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the Empirical Bayes Laplace approximation is not well defined for ReLU networks because the marginal likelihood depends on the Hessian and is not invariant under ReLU scale symmetries. It introduces gamma-canonicalization, which yields predictive uncertainties that are consistent across functionally identical parameterizations.
AI.motivation: ReLU scale symmetries allow the same function to be written with different weights, and the geometry-dependent quantities used in EB Laplace then change, so prior precisions, posterior covariances and predictive uncertainties can differ for identical predictions.
AI.method: A family of prior precision fields indexed by gamma is defined. The network is first converted to a canonical representation by balancing incoming and outgoing weight ratios, and the EB Laplace approximation is fit there. This is equivalent to transporting the isotropic Gaussian prior from the canonical form back to the original coordinates, giving a ReLU-scale-compatible precision field.
AI.result: The marginal likelihood becomes invariant under ReLU scaling, gamma can be selected by maximizing it, and the resulting EB Laplace approximation is well defined on scale-equivalence classes. The abstract does not report numerical experiments.
AI.conclusion: Canonicalization makes EB Laplace well defined for ReLU networks and gives consistent prior precision selection and predictive uncertainty across equivalent parameterizations.

title: A method to automatically discover symbolic local learning rules
summary: We present a general method for discovering symbolic local learning rules that can replace backpropagation, applicable, in principle, to any deep learning architecture and task. The method automatically discovers local loss functions specific to each layer by (1) constructing a dictionary of monomials of local tensor variables, inspired by Penrose diagram notation, (2) regressing over coefficients weighting these monomials to build layerwise polynomial losses whose gradients together minimize a target global loss. We test the method on classification, reconstruction, and self-supervised learning tasks with small multilayer networks and minimal datasets. Across all tasks, the discovered rules induce non-trivial interactions between layers, which lead to significant reductions in the corresponding global losses. Furthermore, the method selects sparse combinations of monomials, finding local rules that are more interpretable than those generated by MLP-based alternatives. The potential implications of our method range from energy-efficient deep learning to the discovery of biologically plausible learning mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method that automatically discovers symbolic local learning rules, layerwise polynomial losses, that can replace backpropagation. The discovered rules induce non-trivial interactions between layers and reduce the corresponding global losses on small networks.
AI.motivation: Backpropagation is the standard training method, and the authors seek interpretable, local learning rules that could be more energy efficient or closer to biological learning mechanisms.
AI.method: The method builds a dictionary of monomials of local tensor variables, inspired by Penrose diagram notation, and then regresses over coefficients weighting these monomials. The result is layer-specific polynomial losses whose gradients together minimize a target global loss.
AI.result: The method is tested on classification, reconstruction and self-supervised learning with small multilayer networks and minimal datasets. Across tasks the discovered rules significantly reduce the global losses, and the method selects sparse monomial combinations that are more interpretable than those from MLP-based alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Automatically discovered symbolic local rules are an interpretable alternative to backpropagation, with potential implications for energy-efficient deep learning and biologically plausible learning.

title: Odds-Structured Distributional Regression for Interpretable Time-to-Event Prediction
summary: Time-to-event prediction is fundamentally challenged by partial observability and aleatoric uncertainty. In clinical medicine, for instance, the timing of disease progression or acute readmission is contingent on highly dynamic and largely latent health trajectories. Rather than forcing a deterministic point forecast, distributional regression offers a principled means to address this complexity by predicting a probability distribution over time. However, explaining these distributional predictions presents a key obstacle: raw distribution parameters output by the model are abstract mathematical quantities that do not align well with domain concepts. To gain interpretability, we propose a novel paradigm where output parameters are designed to be additive in log-odds---a widely established measure in clinical risk modeling. Our approach, called ODDS-DR, moves beyond technical convenience to deliver clear domain alignment as well as the layer-wise computational structure required for robust, time-dependent feature attribution. Validated across two real-world clinical cohorts, our framework matches state-of-the-art predictive performance while resolving distributional outputs into interpretable risk markers across flexible prognostic horizons.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ODDS-DR, a distributional regression method for time-to-event prediction in which output parameters are additive in log-odds. This makes the predicted distribution interpretable and supports time-dependent feature attribution, with predictive performance matching state-of-the-art methods on two clinical cohorts.
AI.motivation: Raw distribution parameters from distributional regression are abstract and do not align with clinical concepts, which hinders explanation of time-to-event predictions.
AI.method: Output parameters are designed to be additive in log-odds, a standard measure in clinical risk modeling. The framework has a layer-wise computational structure that supports time-dependent feature attribution.
AI.result: Validated on two real-world clinical cohorts, ODDS-DR matches state-of-the-art predictive performance and resolves distributional outputs into interpretable risk markers across flexible prognostic horizons.
AI.conclusion: Log-odds-additive distributional outputs give interpretable, clinically aligned explanations of time-to-event predictions without sacrificing predictive accuracy.

title: Optimal Rates for Adaptive Private $k$-PCA
summary: Given $n$ i.i.d. random matrices $A_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ with common expectation $\Sigma$, the goal of \emph{Differentially Private Stochastic PCA} is to identify a $k$-dimensional subspace capturing the leading variance directions of $\Sigma$, while preserving differential privacy~(DP) for each individual sample $A_i$. \citet{dungler2025iterative} introduced \kdppca, the first algorithm to simultaneously (1) achieve sample complexity $n=\widetilde O(d)$ for sub-Gaussian data, (2) adapt its privacy noise to the intrinsic randomness of the data, and (3) extend seamlessly to any target dimension $k\le d$. However, its sample complexity has a suboptimal dependence on $k$. We propose the first algorithm that achieves optimal sample complexity in both $d$ and $k$, while retaining properties (2) and (3) of \kdppca. Additionally, prior utility guarantees require a minimum sample size with exponential dependence on the eigengap. Our method removes this dependence. It also improves the dependence on spectral parameters, matching known lower bounds for the spiked covariance model. Unlike deflation-based approaches like \kdppca, our algorithm updates the full $d\times k$ subspace jointly rather than one eigenvector at a time. This non-deflation structure simplifies the algorithm, reduces the number of hyper-parameters, and improves computational efficiency, particularly when using block linear algebra libraries.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the first differentially private stochastic PCA algorithm that achieves optimal sample complexity in both the dimension d and the subspace dimension k, while keeping the adaptive noise and arbitrary-k properties of the earlier kDP-PCA method. It also removes the exponential eigengap dependence in prior utility guarantees.
AI.motivation: The earlier kDP-PCA method has suboptimal dependence on k, its utility guarantees need a sample size exponential in the eigengap, and its deflation-based design is complex.
AI.method: The algorithm updates the full d-by-k subspace jointly rather than one eigenvector at a time, which removes deflation, simplifies the procedure, reduces hyperparameters and improves computational efficiency with block linear algebra.
AI.result: The method matches known lower bounds for the spiked covariance model in its dependence on spectral parameters. The abstract reports these theoretical improvements and does not give experimental numbers.
AI.conclusion: A non-deflation, jointly updated private PCA method attains optimal sample complexity and is simpler and faster to run than the prior approach.

title: Two-Phase Rapid Simulation-Based Inference with Differentiable Simulators
summary: We introduce Rapid Simulation Based Inference (RSBI), a diffusion-based variational approach to likelihood-free Bayesian inference that achieves high sampling efficiency under large prior-to-posterior volumes. RSBI builds on advances in Schrödinger Bridge (SB) diffusion sampling to handle multi-modal posteriors, with an initial likelihood supplied by a distance measure via a differentiable simulator. The key innovation of this initial surrogate likelihood is that it gives a highly efficient proposal distribution, replacing sequential rounds of other methods with an efficient one-shot proposal. Subsequent refinement then transports the proposal to the true posterior as specified by the simulator and the original prior. The SB sampler is warm-started from the proposal, and its energy is corrected by a neural likelihood ratio that is learned only where the proposal places mass. As a variational method, RSBI does not suffer from prior leakage commonly observed in standard sequential posterior estimation methods. To improve mode coverage we optionally utilize the well-tempered meta-dynamics framework, which also encourages exploration of the prior volume. We observe strong performance on standard SBI benchmarks, particularly when the prior volume is increased relative to the ground truth posterior, achieving a performance degradation of only $\sim5\%$ on Two Moons under a highly constrained simulation budget. Additionally, we evaluate RSBI's performance for gravitational wave ring-down posterior estimation, in a real-world physics benchmark inspired by black hole spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Rapid Simulation-Based Inference (RSBI), a diffusion-based variational method for likelihood-free Bayesian inference that uses a differentiable simulator to build a one-shot proposal and refines it with a Schrödinger Bridge sampler. It targets efficient inference when the prior volume is much larger than the posterior.
AI.motivation: Sequential posterior estimation methods can suffer from prior leakage and need multiple rounds of simulation, and large prior-to-posterior volumes make sampling inefficient.
AI.method: A distance-based surrogate likelihood, computed through a differentiable simulator, provides a proposal distribution in one shot. A Schrödinger Bridge sampler is warm-started from this proposal, and its energy is corrected by a neural likelihood ratio learned only where the proposal places mass. Optionally, well-tempered meta-dynamics improves mode coverage and encourages exploration of the prior.
AI.result: The method performs strongly on standard SBI benchmarks, especially when the prior is widened relative to the posterior. On Two Moons under a highly constrained simulation budget, performance degrades by only about 5%. It is also evaluated on gravitational wave ring-down posterior estimation.
AI.conclusion: RSBI offers an efficient one-shot-plus-refinement route to multimodal likelihood-free posteriors, and as a variational method it avoids prior leakage.

title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
comment: Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 19 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates two tabular foundation models, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models for Bayesian optimization in materials discovery. They are competitive with Gaussian processes, random forests and CatBoost on two standard materials science benchmarks without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Gaussian processes are the default surrogate for Bayesian optimization in materials active learning, but they need task-dependent kernel choices and may lack capacity for complex relationships.
AI.method: TabPFN and TabICL are used directly as surrogate models, with no bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning, and are compared against a broad set of baselines including Gaussian processes, random forests and CatBoost.
AI.result: The tabular foundation models are highly competitive across the two benchmarks. The abstract reports no specific numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Tabular foundation models are promising out-of-the-box surrogates for active learning in materials discovery and merit further development.

title: Graph-Guided Bayesian Factor Analysis: A Fast Integrated EFA-CFA Approach for High-Dimensional Data
summary: Factor analysis has been central to the analysis of high-dimensional biomedical data. However, existing exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis methods face several limitations: less interpretable factor findings, difficulty in identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors, challenges in estimating the covariance among factors, and maximum-likelihood fits that break down when variables outnumber subjects. We propose graph-guided Bayesian factor analysis (gg-BFA) to address these gaps. We first use a Bayesian model to explore and learn the latent graph structure, identifying which variables can and cannot be represented by low-dimensional factors and how many factors are needed. A dense-subgraph search proposes partitions of the variables into communities, each defining one factor, and a forward stepwise search compares their fractional variational posteriors and stops when the evidence lower bound first decreases. We show that this search recovers the true communities even when the number of variables grows much faster than the sample size. We then develop a confirmatory Bayesian model whose variational posterior of the covariance contracts at the parametric rate up to a logarithmic factor, yielding posterior inference for the factors and their covariance, as well as predictions of missing values. Its four members range from a community mask to several cross-loadings per variable. In five biomedical panels, the complete analysis took under ten minutes each on one GPU, and cross-loadings improved held-out covariance and the prediction of masked measurements. In TCGA Kidney, six of the first eight factors were enriched for known pathways, and 190 of the 210 factor correlations had 95% credible intervals excluding zero. Overall, gg-BFA is computationally fast and provides interpretable factor analysis findings and reliable inference results.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes graph-guided Bayesian factor analysis (gg-BFA), a fast integrated framework that combines exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis for high-dimensional biomedical data. It learns a latent graph to decide which variables fit low-dimensional factors, and it provides posterior inference for factors and their covariance.
AI.motivation: Existing EFA and CFA methods give less interpretable factors, struggle to identify which variables can be represented by low-dimensional factors, have difficulty estimating factor covariance, and break down when variables outnumber subjects.
AI.method: A Bayesian model learns the latent graph, and a dense-subgraph search proposes variable partitions into communities, each defining one factor. A forward stepwise search compares fractional variational posteriors and stops when the evidence lower bound first decreases. A confirmatory Bayesian model then gives variational posterior inference for factors and covariance, with four variants ranging from a community mask to several cross-loadings per variable.
AI.result: The search is shown to recover the true communities even when variables grow much faster than the sample size. Across five biomedical panels the full analysis takes under ten minutes each on one GPU, and cross-loadings improve held-out covariance and prediction of masked measurements. On TCGA Kidney, six of the first eight factors are enriched for known pathways, and 190 of 210 factor correlations have 95% credible intervals excluding zero.
AI.conclusion: gg-BFA is computationally fast and gives interpretable factor findings with reliable inference in high-dimensional biomedical settings.

title: Generalized Adaptive Boosting and the Geometry of Mistakes
summary: Not all mistakes are alike. For example, in medical diagnosis, false positive and false negative mistakes have a different impact and should not be aggregated. By revisiting the classical theory of boosting through this lens, we introduce the notion of $Z$-learner, which returns weak hypotheses achieving joint false-positive/false-negative guarantees $(\mathrm{FP},\mathrm{FN})$ from some set $Z \subseteq [0,1]^2$. This formulation generalizes the standard notion of $\gamma$-weak learning--recovered by taking $Z=\{(z_1,z_2): z_1+z_2<1/2-\gamma\}$--and allows for more flexible notions of weak learnability that account for the impact of the distribution on the achievable learning guarantees. This raises a natural question: which sets $Z$ are boostable? We answer this by giving a complete geometric characterization that unifies, as special cases, both the classical boosting dichotomy and the recent multi-objective extension of Bressan et al. (COLT 2025). We also present an adaptive algorithm for boosting $Z$-learners without relying on the prior knowledge of $Z$, generalizing AdaBoost's ability to handle unknown margin parameters. Finally, we demonstrate that $Z$-learners can achieve confidence amplification. However, the analysis is significantly more involved than in classical boosting and relies on the centerpoint theorem from discrete and computational geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes boosting to Z-learners that guarantee a joint false-positive and false-negative pair (FP, FN) from a set Z in [0,1] squared, and it gives a complete geometric characterization of which Z are boostable. The classical gamma-weak learning setting is recovered as a special case.
AI.motivation: Classical boosting aggregates all mistakes equally, but in applications such as medical diagnosis false positives and false negatives have different impacts, so a more flexible notion of weak learnability is needed.
AI.method: The authors define Z-learners and characterize boostable sets Z geometrically, which unifies the classical dichotomy with the multi-objective extension of Bressan et al. They also give an adaptive boosting algorithm that does not need to know Z in advance, generalizing AdaBoost's handling of unknown margin parameters. The analysis relies on the centerpoint theorem.
AI.result: The abstract reports theoretical results only: the geometric characterization, the adaptive algorithm, and confidence amplification for Z-learners. It gives no experimental numbers.
AI.conclusion: Boosting extends to asymmetric or multi-objective error notions through a geometric criterion, though the analysis is considerably more involved than in classical boosting.

title: Fisher-Glass Learning: Classification Bounds and Subpopulation Audits
summary: Accurate classifiers can fail when background cues change without altering the correct labels. Predictive performance alone does not quantify how much task information remains after accounting for such nuisance variation. Here we extend the Fisher-glass framework to connect nuisance-adjusted information with local classification difficulty and subpopulation auditing. We derive lower bounds on local minimax excess classification risk under explicit distinguishability and decision-separation conditions, alongside statistical audits accounting for estimation error and regularization. On Waterbirds, a feature-based diagnostic of task-background alignment selects an accurately classified group, with selection frozen before held-out evaluation. Across five training seeds, background replacements preserving the extracted bird foreground and labels yield 93.2% accuracy when background type is preserved and 40.6% when it changes, a controlled difference of 52.6 percentage points. Separately, search using task labels and a fixed nuisance direction identifies an independently evaluated population with 98.8% membership-weighted accuracy and low estimated projected predictive Fisher information. Training and acquisition experiments show that information gains and predictive gains can diverge. These findings support joint assessment of predictive performance, information under declared nuisance models and controlled sensitivity when diagnosing vulnerability and evaluating model improvements.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the Fisher-glass framework to link nuisance-adjusted information with local classification difficulty and subpopulation auditing. On Waterbirds, background replacements that keep the bird foreground and labels yield 93.2% accuracy when the background type is preserved and 40.6% when it changes.
AI.motivation: Predictive accuracy alone does not show how much task information remains after nuisance variation, such as background cues that change without altering the correct labels.
AI.method: The authors derive lower bounds on local minimax excess classification risk under explicit distinguishability and decision-separation conditions, and they add statistical audits that account for estimation error and regularization. A feature-based diagnostic of task-background alignment selects a group before held-out evaluation, and a search using task labels and a fixed nuisance direction identifies a subpopulation.
AI.result: Across five training seeds the background-change experiment shows a controlled difference of 52.6 percentage points, from 93.2% to 40.6% accuracy. The identified subpopulation reaches 98.8% membership-weighted accuracy in independent evaluation and has low estimated projected predictive Fisher information. Training and acquisition experiments show that information gains and predictive gains can diverge.
AI.conclusion: Predictive performance, information under declared nuisance models, and sensitivity to controlled changes should be assessed jointly when diagnosing vulnerabilities and evaluating model improvements.

title: Clique Constraints for Exact Causal Structure Learning
summary: Exact score-based causal structure learning supports explicit structural constraints and optimisation certificates, but its branch-and-cut search can be computationally demanding. We augment exact causal structure learning methods with an upper bound on the maximum clique size of the learned undirected skeleton, enforced at integer candidates through lazy cycle and clique constraints. On static linear-Gaussian Erdős-Rényi and scale-free DAGs, we evaluate callback order, alternative clique-cut policies, incumbent repair, fractional separation, and Big-M bounds. We report causal-recovery metrics jointly with optimality gaps, primal and dual bounds, node throughput, MIPSOL events, and callback cost. Two variants receive particular attention: B3 selects the most violated minimal (k+1)-clique inequality at each callback, whereas C3 repairs an infeasible integer candidate by deleting violating edges and refitting affected regression columns using QR-based least squares. The results do not indicate that clique constraints uniformly accelerate optimisation. However, their benefit depends on graph density, sample size, and cut-management policy, while large collections of correlated constraints can reduce node throughput. Tighter valid Big-M bounds reduced the fixed-budget optimality gap in most tested settings, without necessarily changing SHD or F1 at a fixed time limit. These findings characterize the computational trade-offs of clique-constrained exact causal learning, and identify selective separation and incumbent repair as promising directions.

AI.tldr: The paper adds an upper bound on the maximum clique size of the learned undirected skeleton to exact score-based causal structure learning, enforced via lazy cycle and clique constraints. The benefit depends on graph density, sample size and cut management, and it does not uniformly accelerate optimization.
AI.motivation: Exact causal structure learning gives optimality certificates and supports explicit structural constraints, but its branch-and-cut search can be computationally demanding.
AI.method: Clique-size upper bounds are enforced at integer candidates through lazy cycle and clique constraints. The authors evaluate callback order, clique-cut policies, incumbent repair, fractional separation and Big-M bounds, including variant B3, which adds the most violated minimal (k+1)-clique inequality, and variant C3, which repairs infeasible candidates by deleting violating edges and refitting with QR-based least squares.
AI.result: Results on static linear-Gaussian Erdos-Renyi and scale-free DAGs show that clique constraints do not uniformly accelerate optimization. Large collections of correlated constraints can reduce node throughput, and tighter valid Big-M bounds reduce the fixed-budget optimality gap in most tested settings without necessarily changing SHD or F1.
AI.conclusion: Clique-constrained exact causal learning has computational trade-offs that depend on graph density, sample size and cut policy, and selective separation and incumbent repair are identified as promising directions.

title: BIBIMBAP: A Benchmark for Instructional BIM-Based Automated Programming
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are emerging as natural-language interfaces for Building Information Modeling (BIM), successfully achieving information retrieval, but no benchmark exists to evaluate their ability to edit Industry Foundation Classes (IFC). We introduce BIBIMBAP, a Text-to-BIM benchmark with 100 curated tasks covering Create-Read-Update-Delete (CRUD) operations across spatial, geometric, topological, numeric, and conceptual categories. Each task includes a natural-language prompt, an IFC model, expected structured outputs, and test scripts for automated evaluation. Baseline results show limited performance (best: 50.2%) and frequent failures in constraint preservation and spatial reasoning, with some correct outputs achieved despite flawed reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BIBIMBAP, a benchmark of 100 curated tasks for evaluating whether LLMs can edit Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) building models through CRUD operations. Baseline results are limited, with the best model reaching 50.2%.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used as natural-language interfaces for Building Information Modeling and succeed at information retrieval, but no benchmark exists for evaluating their ability to edit IFC models.
AI.method: Each task covers Create-Read-Update-Delete operations across spatial, geometric, topological, numeric and conceptual categories, and includes a natural-language prompt, an IFC model, expected structured outputs and test scripts for automated evaluation.
AI.result: The best baseline reaches 50.2%. Frequent failures occur in constraint preservation and spatial reasoning, and some correct outputs are produced despite flawed reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Text-to-BIM editing remains hard for current LLMs, and the benchmark provides a testbed for measuring progress on constraint preservation and spatial reasoning.

title: How Many Examples, and Which Ones? A Study of In-Context Learning for Natural Language Inference
summary: Natural language inference (NLI) is a fundamental task of natural language processing and crucial for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of AI methods. Research has mostly focused on encoder or encoder-decoder architectures. However, the field of decoder-only Large Language Models (LLMs) remains underexplored. While prior work has mainly investigated complex sampling and prompting techniques, the effectiveness of a minimalistic prompting approach is yet to be examined in decoder-only LLMs. In this work, we examine and provide a comprehensive benchmark of LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Phi 4) in this domain, across the MNLI, QNLI and SciTail datasets. The performance of these models was evaluated using zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies with simple and direct prompts. The results of the article indicate that LLMs generally perform exceptionally well when they are provided with a simple, straightforward prompt, challenging the notion that complex prompting techniques are always required for NLI tasks. Additionally, we find that the choice of demonstration label in one-shot prompting significantly affects performance for most models, with entailment-primed examples performing best. Our findings also show that the use of a few representative examples, in the case of few-shot, produced performance comparable or superior to prompts with higher example counts, although the efficacy of the prompting techniques is model and dataset-dependent. Moreover, our simple prompting approach consistently matched or outperformed more elaborate methods such as ICS and MCQ-based prompting.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks decoder-only LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Phi 4) on natural language inference with minimal zero-shot and few-shot prompts on MNLI, QNLI and SciTail, finding that simple prompts work well and that demonstration label choice matters.
AI.motivation: NLI has been studied mostly with encoder or encoder-decoder models, and the effect of minimalistic prompting on decoder-only LLMs had not been examined, while prior work focused on complex sampling and prompting techniques.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four decoder-only LLM families under zero-shot and few-shot prompting with simple, direct prompts, and vary the label of the demonstration in one-shot prompting and the number of examples in few-shot prompting.
AI.result: Simple prompts perform very well, and one-shot performance depends strongly on the demonstration label, with entailment-primed examples performing best for most models. A few representative examples match or beat prompts with more examples, and the simple prompt matched or outperformed ICS and MCQ-based prompting consistently, though effects vary by model and dataset.
AI.conclusion: Complex prompting techniques are not always needed for NLI with LLMs, and careful choice of a few representative demonstrations can be as effective as using more examples.

title: DramaGrow: A Regime-Aware Benchmark for Auditing LLM Judges of Multi-Episode Drama
summary: LLMs can now draft complete multi-episode dramas, and LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate them. Assessing the reliability of these judges is difficult because drama quality encompasses specification-backed errors, reproducible preferences, and legitimate disagreement among human raters. Most existing evaluations reduce these cases to a single score from one judge call and leave tie calibration, call-to-call variation, and the vote margin underlying the human reference unreported. We introduce DramaGrow, a regime-aware benchmark and audit protocol for AI-generated Chinese five-episode drama. The benchmark assigns verifiable constraint violations, four-of-five preferences, and within-panel disagreements to separate denominators and evidence rules. It contains 800 episodes, 120 byte-preserving interventions, and 1,155 blinded five-rater records, including a frozen extension with 114 supermajority pairs and 21 disagreement pairs. On the frozen sets of 114 preference pairs and 35 constraint interventions, the repeated absolute-score rubrics yield overlapping performance, with mean accuracies of 53.8-55.8% and three-call agreement of 29.8-32.5%, and their accuracy falls from 71.6-71.9% to 34.8-37.1% as the tie band widens. DirectPair-GLM reaches 85.1% preference accuracy, 89.5% constraint F1, and 81.9% Detect+Locate on the same items, and exact subpanel enumeration identifies four-of-five as the smallest stable human vote margin. Evaluation protocol, tie calibration, judge-call variation, and panel margin therefore affect performance as much as rubric design. We will release the specification packages, scripts, interventions, anonymized human votes and rationales, frozen judge runs, and analysis code.

AI.tldr: DramaGrow is a regime-aware benchmark and audit protocol for LLM judges of AI-generated five-episode Chinese dramas, showing that evaluation protocol, tie calibration, call-to-call variation and vote margin affect judge accuracy as much as rubric design.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM judges for drama quality reduce assessments to a single score from one judge call and do not report tie calibration, call-to-call variation or the human vote margin, even though drama quality mixes verifiable errors, reproducible preferences and legitimate human disagreement.
AI.method: The authors build a benchmark of 800 episodes with 120 byte-preserving interventions and 1,155 blinded five-rater records, separating constraint violations, four-of-five preferences and within-panel disagreements into different denominators and evidence rules, and compare repeated absolute-score rubrics with a DirectPair-GLM model on frozen sets.
