title: YRC-Bench: Benchmarking Culturally Aware Machine Translation for Historical Heritage via Tri-Level Semantic Bridging
summary: Translating historical cultural heritage poses profound challenges for machine translation systems due to the acute semantic asymmetry across eras and cultures, where terse classical syntax frequently obscures domain-specific cultural knowledge. While Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable prowess in generic translation benchmarks, they struggle to negotiate Culturally-Specific Items and diachronic shifts in domain-rich historical texts, such as Yellow River cultural records. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce YRC-Bench, the first human-curated, multi-parallel benchmark dedicated to historical heritage translation across Classical Chinese, Modern Chinese, and nine target foreign languages. YRC-Bench establishes a tri-level parallel corpus incorporating modern explanatory glosses as explicit semantic bridges and operationalizes translation strategies through paired conserved versus substituted CSI variants categorized by cultural translatability. Systematic evaluations of nine leading LLMs across bidirectional translation directions reveal that leveraging modern Chinese glosses - especially human-curated ones - dramatically elevates both lexical fidelity and semantic adequacy. Furthermore, multidimensional human preference audits by native experts unveil distinct cross-cultural preferences between Sinographic-tradition and non-Sinographic language groups.

AI.tldr: YRC-Bench is a human-curated multi-parallel benchmark for translating historical Yellow River cultural heritage texts across Classical Chinese, Modern Chinese and nine target foreign languages. Modern Chinese glosses, especially human-curated ones, markedly improve lexical fidelity and semantic adequacy of LLM translations.
AI.motivation: LLMs perform well on generic translation benchmarks but struggle with culturally-specific items and diachronic shifts in historical texts, where terse classical syntax obscures domain-specific cultural knowledge.
AI.method: The benchmark provides a tri-level parallel corpus with modern explanatory glosses as explicit semantic bridges, and operationalizes translation strategies through paired conserved versus substituted CSI variants categorized by cultural translatability. Nine leading LLMs are evaluated in bidirectional translation directions, with multidimensional human preference audits by native experts.
AI.result: Leveraging modern Chinese glosses, especially human-curated ones, dramatically elevates both lexical fidelity and semantic adequacy. Expert audits reveal distinct cross-cultural preferences between Sinographic-tradition and non-Sinographic language groups.
AI.conclusion: Cultural and diachronic knowledge is a bottleneck for historical heritage translation, and explicit glosses plus cross-cultural human preference audits are needed to evaluate it.

title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
summary: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

AI.tldr: onóna is a weight-tying variant that uses two embedding tables, with the input embedding as their average and the output head combining both softmax distributions under a token-conditioned gate. It lowers validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons at matched token budgets, at the cost of one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.
AI.motivation: Weight tying cuts the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax, which restricts output expressiveness.
AI.method: The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token sets the mixture weight, and its values can be precomputed for inference. The Transformer body is unchanged. Evaluation covers Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M and 1B scales.
AI.result: Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one loss exception is the 1B MoE model.
AI.conclusion: onóna increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing, at the modest cost of one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

title: Large Language Models without QK-Normalization
comment: Code is available at this https URL
summary: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.

AI.tldr: QK-MAP replaces query-key normalization with a magnitude-aware projection that encodes vector magnitude as bounded periodic phase patterns using multiple learnable frequencies. It achieves lower training and validation loss than standard attention and QK-Norm for models from 190M to 7B parameters.
AI.motivation: QK-Norm stabilizes training but also suppresses the token-specific magnitude information in query and key norms, which carries attention selectivity and token importance.
AI.method: QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns with fixed norm. Magnitude is thus represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone, and multiple frequencies help reduce periodic ambiguity.
AI.result: Across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters, QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both standard attention and QK-Norm. It preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and gives stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests.
AI.conclusion: Query-key scale can be controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information, so normalization is not the only route to stable attention.

title: Global Context Guidance for Diffusion Large Language Models
summary: Diffusion large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, enabling parallel generation through iterative denoising. Recent guidance methods improve diffusion LLMs by introducing a weak model to guide the prediction of the base model during denoising. However, the influence of the weak model during denoising remains less clear, and computing its prediction requires an additional forward pass at each denoising step. We present in this paper an in-depth analysis of how diffusion LLMs use contextual information during denoising. Our analysis reveals that diffusion LLMs rely more heavily on local context while often underutilizing global context. Based on this observation, we introduce Global Context Guidance (GCG), a feature-space guidance method that enhances global-context utilization without constructing an explicit weak model. Extensive experiments on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that GCG consistently outperforms existing guidance methods, while incurring much lower inference overhead.

AI.tldr: Global Context Guidance (GCG) is a feature-space guidance method for diffusion LLMs that strengthens use of global context without building an explicit weak model. It consistently outperforms existing guidance methods on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B and LLaDA-1.5 while adding much lower inference overhead.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs rely more heavily on local context and often underuse global context during denoising. Existing guidance methods use a weak model whose influence is unclear and which needs an extra forward pass at each step.
AI.method: The authors analyse how diffusion LLMs use contextual information during denoising, then introduce GCG, which enhances global-context utilization in feature space instead of constructing a weak model.
AI.result: GCG consistently outperforms existing guidance methods on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B and LLaDA-1.5 across diverse benchmarks, while incurring much lower inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Enhancing global-context use in feature space is an effective and cheap alternative to weak-model guidance for diffusion LLMs.

title: AI in the Clinical Documentation Loop: Effects of LLM-Induced Note Bloat and Diagnostic Overcall on Downstream LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to process medical records for healthcare tasks such as clinical documentation. Because these tools also generate documentation, the relationship is now bidirectional: models both read from and write to the record. Understanding how LLMs behave when reading records that already contain LLM-authored content is therefore critical for their safe deployment. In this study, we examine how LLM-authored content in the medical record affects downstream LLMs that read the same record. We consider two types of LLM-induced artifacts: bloat, in which LLM-generated summaries accumulate in the record and change the length and provenance of its content over time; and distortion, in which LLMs subtly alter clinical findings rather than fabricating facts outright. As a case of distortion, we study diagnostic overcall (documenting an unconfirmed differential diagnosis in the record) and test whether it propagates to the reader LLM's output. Across seven reader models from four families, we find evidence of both effects. First, LLM-generated summary notes modestly but consistently degraded downstream hospital-course generation compared with copy-forward and templated text of matched length. Second, injected overcalls reappeared in downstream outputs at rates that varied by reader model, without detectable changes in standard quality metrics. These findings show the need to monitor AI-generated content in medical records and to account for it when those records are later processed by AI.

AI.tldr: Using seven reader models from four families, the paper shows that LLM-authored content in medical records degrades downstream LLMs. LLM-generated summaries degrade hospital-course generation, and injected diagnostic overcalls reappear in outputs at model-dependent rates without detectable change in standard quality metrics.
AI.motivation: LLMs now both read and write clinical records, so the safety of downstream LLMs that read records already containing LLM-authored content needs study.
AI.method: The authors examine two artifacts: bloat, where LLM-generated summaries accumulate and change the length and provenance of record content, and distortion, where LLMs subtly alter clinical findings. For distortion they study diagnostic overcall, documenting an unconfirmed differential diagnosis, and test whether it propagates to reader LLM outputs. LLM summaries are compared with copy-forward and templated text of matched length.
AI.result: LLM-generated summary notes modestly but consistently degrade downstream hospital-course generation compared with copy-forward and templated text of matched length. Injected overcalls reappear in downstream outputs at rates that vary by reader model, without detectable changes in standard quality metrics.
AI.conclusion: AI-generated content in medical records needs to be monitored, and it must be accounted for when those records are later processed by AI.

title: On the Geometric Bottlenecks of Cross-Lingual Knowledge Editing
summary: Transformer-based autoregressive multilingual language models (LMs) are often assumed to store factual knowledge in an interlingua: a language-agnostic latent space. If this assumption holds, a parameter update applied in a source language during knowledge editing should inherently propagate to its semantic equivalents in target languages. However, empirical benchmarks show that cross-lingual propagation of edits often degrades substantially, a degradation that prior work treats largely as an algorithmic symptom rather than a structural bottleneck. In this work, we investigate whether representational anisotropy creates a structural bottleneck for source-only associative-memory editing, and perform a geometric dissection of the cross-lingual propagation gap. Using associative memory-based "locate-then-edit" methods, including ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit, as analytical frameworks, we derive a closed-form decomposition of this gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch. Our empirical findings show that cross-lingual propagation is primarily bottlenecked by a large orthogonal residual component, indicating that source-language edits often fail to span the target-language update directions required for successful transfer. Furthermore, we show that post-hoc correction using only source-language residual statistics encounters a large residual-prediction barrier. Finally, we perform a structural realignment via a targeted contrastive alignment objective and find that it substantially improves key-space propagation and partially improves cross-lingual edit transfer, while leaving value-space mismatch as a remaining bottleneck.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that cross-lingual propagation of knowledge edits is bottlenecked by a large orthogonal residual component, indicating that source-language edits often fail to span target-language update directions. Post-hoc correction from source-language residual statistics faces a large prediction barrier, and contrastive alignment improves key-space propagation and partly improves transfer.
AI.motivation: Knowledge edits often fail to propagate across languages, and prior work treats this mainly as an algorithmic symptom, while the authors ask whether representational anisotropy creates a structural bottleneck.
AI.method: Using associative-memory locate-then-edit methods (ROME, MEMIT and AlphaEdit) as analytical frameworks, the authors derive a closed-form decomposition of the cross-lingual propagation gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch and orthogonal residual mismatch. They then test post-hoc correction and a targeted contrastive alignment objective.
AI.result: Cross-lingual propagation is primarily bottlenecked by a large orthogonal residual component. Post-hoc correction using only source-language residual statistics encounters a large residual-prediction barrier. Contrastive structural realignment substantially improves key-space propagation and partially improves cross-lingual edit transfer, while value-space mismatch remains a bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: The gap is structural rather than purely algorithmic, and value-space mismatch is the remaining obstacle after key-space realignment.

title: TransMem: Transition-Aware Retrieval for Evolving Personal Memory
summary: Long-term personalized agents are increasingly expected to answer queries over user histories in which preferences, goals, and constraints evolve across interleaved conversations. Existing retrieval-based and structured-memory systems can surface relevant facts, but often return isolated memory units that do not explain which earlier preference was refined, contradicted, or superseded by later evidence. We introduce TransMem, a transition-aware memory retrieval framework that stores preference updates as explicit retrieval units alongside ordinary factual memories. During memory construction, TransMem routes user interaction history into topic-structured memory graphs, detects shift events, and grounds them as transition records. At inference time, TransMem first retrieves factual anchors and then adaptively expands over transition records, producing a compact context of factual anchors and accepted transition records. Experiments on PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones show that TransMem outperforms representative retrieval-based and structured-memory baselines. Controlled analyses further show that transition records and adaptive expansion contribute beyond factual anchoring, chronological expansion, flat transition retrieval, and fixed-hop traversal. These results suggest that preference-update records are useful retrieval units for long-term personalization.

AI.tldr: TransMem is a retrieval framework for evolving personal memory that stores preference updates as explicit transition records alongside factual memories, so it can explain which earlier preference was refined, contradicted or superseded. It outperforms retrieval-based and structured-memory baselines on PersonaMem and PersonaBench with two Qwen backbones.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval and structured-memory systems surface relevant facts but return isolated memory units that do not show how preferences, goals and constraints changed across interleaved conversations.
AI.method: During construction, TransMem routes interaction history into topic-structured memory graphs, detects shift events and grounds them as transition records. At inference it retrieves factual anchors first, then adaptively expands over transition records to produce a compact context of anchors and accepted transitions.
AI.result: On PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones, TransMem outperforms representative retrieval-based and structured-memory baselines. Controlled analyses show that transition records and adaptive expansion contribute beyond factual anchoring, chronological expansion, flat transition retrieval and fixed-hop traversal.
AI.conclusion: Preference-update records are useful retrieval units for long-term personalization of agents.

title: Behavioral Evaluation of Large Language Models Under Cognitive Biases in HAZOP Studies
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to IFAC for possible publication. Supplementary material available at this https URL
summary: Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies safeguard industrial processes against catastrophic accidents. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist HAZOP drafting, yet evaluations rely on lexical overlap. Because LLMs internalize human heuristics, prompts may trigger biased judgments. Whether frontier LLMs withstand cognitive perturbations in safety-critical workflows remains unknown. Here we show across 420 trials that three frontier LLMs resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations, rendering overall susceptibility statistically inconclusive. Contrary to assumed broad fragility, models rejected confirmation and availability cues. However, safety-critical risk downgrades emerged under low anchors and gain frames. Thus, automated hazard analysis requires disciplined human-in-the-loop validation.

AI.tldr: Across 420 trials, three frontier LLMs resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations in HAZOP studies, so overall susceptibility is statistically inconclusive. Safety-critical risk downgrades still appeared under low anchors and gain frames, so automated hazard analysis needs human-in-the-loop validation.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly assist HAZOP drafting, yet evaluations rely on lexical overlap, and LLMs may inherit human heuristics that prompts can trigger, so their robustness to cognitive perturbations in safety-critical work was unknown.
AI.method: The authors run 420 trials with three frontier LLMs, applying cognitive manipulations to HAZOP prompts, including confirmation and availability cues, low anchors and gain frames.
AI.result: The three models resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations, and overall susceptibility is statistically inconclusive. Models rejected confirmation and availability cues, but safety-critical risk downgrades emerged under low anchors and gain frames.
AI.conclusion: Automated hazard analysis requires disciplined human-in-the-loop validation, because the residual susceptibility to anchors and framing matters in safety-critical settings.

title: Evaluating Physically Grounded Procedural Reasoning in VLMs through Real-World Execution: Crochet as a Testbed
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.

AI.tldr: FoundationChain tests whether VLMs can infer how a crochet object was made from an image and write a pattern that reproduces it, with success verified by hand-crocheting the patterns. Of 40 patterns from four VLMs, only four are free of errors, exposing weaknesses in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.
AI.motivation: VLMs can write convincing procedures, but whether they work in practice is unclear, and automated simulation is unreliable for crochet, so physical execution is the only faithful check.
AI.method: The authors propose crochet as a testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning. Given an image of a basic crochet object, VLMs must infer how it was made and generate a pattern producing the same result. The authors crocheted 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand and diagnosed the causes of failure.
AI.result: Only four of the 40 patterns are free of errors. Physical execution reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect and allows a more precise diagnosis of deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Physical execution is a cheap and informative way to evaluate procedural reasoning in VLMs, and the results show that fluent, convincing patterns are not evidence of correctness.

title: Cascading Circle Loss: Order-Preserving Contrastive Learning for Graded Legal Retrieval
summary: This paper introduces Cascading Circle Loss (CasCL), a contrastive learning framework for legal retrieval tasks with graded relevance. CasCL combines an InfoNCE objective for positive-negative separation with a cascade of ranking boundaries that model ordered relevance levels between queries and legal clauses. The framework also includes a negative-aware self-paced optimization mechanism and a relevance gain weighting strategy to improve ranking quality. Experiments on legal passage retrieval benchmarks show that CasCL consistently outperforms existing methods, including InfoNCE, Circle Loss, MNRL and Margin MSE, across both binary retrieval and graded ranking metrics.

AI.tldr: Cascading Circle Loss (CasCL) is a contrastive learning framework for graded-relevance legal retrieval that combines InfoNCE with a cascade of ranking boundaries for ordered relevance levels. It consistently outperforms InfoNCE, Circle Loss, MNRL and Margin MSE on legal passage retrieval benchmarks for binary and graded ranking metrics.
AI.motivation: Legal retrieval involves graded relevance between queries and legal clauses, and existing contrastive losses do not model ordered relevance levels directly.
AI.method: CasCL combines an InfoNCE objective for positive-negative separation with a cascade of ranking boundaries that model ordered relevance levels. It adds a negative-aware self-paced optimization mechanism and a relevance gain weighting strategy to improve ranking quality.
AI.result: On legal passage retrieval benchmarks, CasCL consistently outperforms InfoNCE, Circle Loss, MNRL and Margin MSE across both binary retrieval and graded ranking metrics.
AI.conclusion: Modelling ordered relevance levels within a contrastive objective improves ranking quality for graded legal retrieval.

title: Adapting Large Language Models via Multi-Task Learning for Mental Health Problem, Emotion, and Sentiment Detection
summary: This study investigates sequential multi-task learning using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), LoRA, and 4-bit quantization on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct for mental health problem detection, emotion detection, and sentiment analysis. Using 4,243 English social media posts, it compares two task sequences and demonstrates that task ordering significantly affects knowledge transfer and task interference. The MHP-first sequence achieves the best mental health problem detection (Micro-F1: 0.7624), while the Emotion-first sequence performs better in emotion (F1: 0.6052) and sentiment analysis (F1: 0.9459). A Joint-MTL baseline further highlights the challenges of simultaneous learning, including task interference and generative format collapse. Overall, the findings demonstrate the effectiveness of sequential PEFT for mental health NLP while showing that task order is critical to balancing performance across related tasks. The integration of LoRA and 4-bit quantization also reduces computational and memory requirements, supporting the adaptation of large language models in resource-constrained environments.

AI.tldr: Sequential multi-task PEFT with LoRA and 4-bit quantization on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct shows that task order strongly affects transfer and interference in mental health problem detection, emotion detection and sentiment analysis. The MHP-first sequence gives the best mental health detection, while the Emotion-first sequence performs better on emotion and sentiment.
AI.motivation: Multi-task learning across related mental health NLP tasks may involve task interference, and the effect of task ordering on knowledge transfer was not established.
AI.method: The study uses sequential multi-task learning with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) and 4-bit quantization on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct over 4,243 English social media posts, comparing two task sequences and a Joint-MTL baseline.
AI.result: The MHP-first sequence achieves the best mental health problem detection (Micro-F1 0.7624), while the Emotion-first sequence performs better on emotion (F1 0.6052) and sentiment analysis (F1 0.9459). Joint-MTL shows task interference and generative format collapse.
AI.conclusion: Sequential PEFT is effective for mental health NLP, and task order is critical for balancing performance across related tasks. LoRA with 4-bit quantization also reduces compute and memory needs.

title: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Turkish Large Language Models with Search-Based Inference and Model Merging
summary: We improve Turkish mathematical reasoning in Large Language Models by combining LoRA fine-tuning, weight-space model merging, and search-based inference. Using Turkish-Llama 8B-DPO with Turkish translations of MetaMath, NuminaMath, and TigerLab, we find data quality beats scale (Mix-30k best among fine-tuned; large MetaMath underperforms). Linear merging delivers the largest gains (GSM8K up to 0.63), while Ties is modest and Breadcrumbs/Slerp degrade. Search with MCTS and Tree of Thoughts improves mean LLM-judge scores for reasoning quality on a 0-100 scale. Limitations include machine translation, limited scale, and search stochasticity.

AI.tldr: The paper improves Turkish mathematical reasoning in LLMs by combining LoRA fine-tuning, weight-space model merging and search-based inference on Turkish-Llama 8B-DPO. It finds that data quality matters more than data scale, and that linear merging gives the largest gains.
AI.motivation: The abstract gives no explicit motivation beyond improving mathematical reasoning for Turkish, a language with fewer resources than English.
AI.method: LoRA fine-tuning of Turkish-Llama 8B-DPO on Turkish translations of MetaMath, NuminaMath and TigerLab, followed by weight-space merging (Linear, Ties, Breadcrumbs, Slerp) and search at inference time with MCTS and Tree of Thoughts.
AI.result: Mix-30k is the best fine-tuned set and large MetaMath underperforms. Linear merging reaches GSM8K up to 0.63, Ties is modest, and Breadcrumbs and Slerp degrade. MCTS and Tree of Thoughts improve mean LLM-judge reasoning-quality scores on a 0-100 scale.
AI.conclusion: Data quality outweighs data scale for Turkish math reasoning, and linear merging with search is a useful combination. The authors note limitations from machine translation, limited scale and search stochasticity.

title: Evaluating Jev on Arabic: Comparing Decision Models and LLMs Across Arabic Tasks and Dialects
summary: How does Jev compare with other systems on Arabic tasks, and how does its performance change between Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and dialects? We evaluate 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 large language models (LLMs), on 43 tasks across 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol. The Arabic-focused frozen suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, which we also remove in a separate descriptive comparison. Jev 1.14.0 achieves a mean task-primary metric of 69.24 on a scale multiplied by 100, compared with 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, the highest-scoring system on this aggregate. Removing the recorded English controls, repeated cross-task items or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Relative performance and gains between Jev versions vary across task families. In content-matched comparisons within Jev 1.14.0, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets; dialect-specific results show larger variation, and SIB-200's source-clustered interval includes zero. Paired contrasts with Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B show a larger Palestinian banking penalty for Jev 1.14.0 than for either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty; the other gap contrasts remain inconclusive. These descriptive findings show why aggregate scores should be read alongside task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. They do not establish a general model ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.

AI.tldr: The paper compares 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 LLMs, on 43 Arabic tasks across 9 task families under a shared zero-shot protocol. It reports how Jev performs on Modern Standard Arabic and on dialects.
AI.motivation: The authors ask how Jev compares with other systems on Arabic tasks and whether its performance changes between Modern Standard Arabic and dialects.
AI.method: A shared zero-shot evaluation protocol over an Arabic-focused frozen suite that includes English control items, with a separate descriptive comparison that removes these controls. Content-matched dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps are computed within Jev 1.14.0, and paired contrasts are run against Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B.
AI.result: Jev 1.14.0 scores a mean task-primary metric of 69.24, against 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, which is the top system on the aggregate. Pooled dialect-minus-MSA gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets, and SIB-200's interval includes zero. Jev 1.14.0 shows a larger Palestinian banking penalty than either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty. Removing controls or repeated items leaves the system order unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate scores should be read together with task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. The findings do not establish a general ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.

title: Simple Test-Time Refinement for Plot-to-Code Generation via Visual-Code Diagnostics
summary: Plot-to-code generation has been greatly advanced by recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing studies mainly focus on one-pass generation or iterative sampling guided by verifier-based filtering, which does not align with the typical human programming workflow of generate first, then iteratively error-location and fix. This naturally motivates a test-time refinement paradigm for plot-to-code generation. In this work, we present the first study on plot-to-code generation via iterative test-time refinement. We propose a Visual-Code Diagnostics framework that enables refinement through visual feedback from source code. Specifically, we first categorize generation errors into four coarse-grained types, and then train lightweight discriminators to recognize and localize these errors based on the rendered visual outputs and corresponding code. Unlike traditional compiler- or debugger-based verification, our approach performs iterative refinement guided by one diagnostics system, enabling more effective semantic and visual correction during test time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves generation quality across diverse generators and significantly outperforms strong test-time scaling baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Visual-Code Diagnostics, a test-time refinement framework for plot-to-code generation that corrects code using visual feedback from rendered outputs. It is presented as the first study of iterative test-time refinement for this task.
AI.motivation: Existing plot-to-code work focuses on one-pass generation or iterative sampling with verifier-based filtering, which does not match the human workflow of generating first and then locating and fixing errors.
AI.method: Generation errors are grouped into four coarse-grained types. Lightweight discriminators are trained to recognize and localize these errors from the rendered visual output and the corresponding code, and refinement is guided by this diagnostics system rather than by a compiler or debugger.
AI.result: The method consistently improves generation quality across diverse generators and significantly outperforms strong test-time scaling baselines.
AI.conclusion: Visual feedback from source code offers an effective route to semantic and visual correction at test time, without relying on compiler or debugger verification.

title: MultiTurnRoute: A Platform for Building and Evaluating Multi-Turn LLM Routers
summary: In a multi-turn conversation, the choice of language model at one turn can affect which model should answer the next. The selected model's reply shapes the context for the next query, and its cached prompt prefix can reduce the cost of using that model again. We introduce MultiTurnRoute, a platform for building and evaluating multi-turn LLM routers. A shared interface gives built-in and user-defined routers the current query, dialogue history, and an estimate of each model's reusable prefix length. Our routing algorithm, Chain-of-Route (CoR), uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent dialogue history to predict response quality and estimates cost from each model's reusable prefix. MultiTurnRoute Arena ranks routers on recorded conversations and compares session quality and cost in interactive runs where a simulated user responds to each reply. On a benchmark drawn from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M with per-turn quality annotations for five LLMs, CoR reduces the normalized cost required to match the strongest model's quality by up to 20.3% relative to the strongest routing baseline, while matching or improving peak response quality.

AI.tldr: MultiTurnRoute is a platform for building and evaluating multi-turn LLM routers, together with the Chain-of-Route algorithm (CoR). CoR uses a learned gate over dialogue history and estimates cost from each model's reusable cached prefix.
AI.motivation: In multi-turn dialogue, the model chosen at one turn changes the context for later turns and its cached prefix changes the cost of reuse, so single-turn routing ignores these effects.
AI.method: A shared interface gives routers the current query, dialogue history and an estimate of each model's reusable prefix length. CoR predicts response quality with a learned gate over recent and recurrent dialogue history and estimates cost from the reusable prefix. MultiTurnRoute Arena ranks routers on recorded conversations and in interactive runs with a simulated user.
AI.result: On a benchmark built from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M with per-turn quality annotations for five LLMs, CoR cuts the normalized cost needed to match the strongest model's quality by up to 20.3% relative to the strongest routing baseline. It matches or improves peak response quality.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for cached prefixes and dialogue history in routing can reduce cost in multi-turn use without sacrificing peak quality.

title: KeyASRBench: Measuring Whole-Phrase Keyword Preservation in Real-World ASR
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Bilingual ASR evaluation with a 10-hour model-conditioned challenge set and a disjoint 30-minute model-blind control
summary: Public automatic speech recognition (ASR) benchmarks increasingly report low sequence error rates, yet production systems still use hotword lists, contextual biasing, retrieval, and post-correction. This motivates a complementary question: does a transcript preserve selected names, products, technical terms, versions, and relational phrases? We present KeyASRBench, a bilingual pilot that operationalizes occurrence-based Keyword Error Rate (KER) over frozen whole-phrase annotations. The 10-hour model-conditioned challenge set contains 1,501 Chinese and English clips with 4,723 keyword occurrences. Across five locally inferred checkpoints and two official API systems, language-specific MER/WER ranges from 5.31% to 12.91%, while KER ranges from 13.61% to 33.81%. A disjoint 30-minute model-blind control yields KER of 10.65%-27.31%. The control confirms that selected-phrase errors extend beyond challenge-set selection.

AI.tldr: KeyASRBench is a bilingual pilot benchmark that measures whether an ASR transcript preserves selected whole-phrase keywords such as names, products and technical terms. It uses an occurrence-based Keyword Error Rate (KER) over frozen annotations.
AI.motivation: Low sequence error rates on public ASR benchmarks do not show whether production-critical phrases such as names and technical terms are preserved, and production systems rely on hotword lists and post-correction for this reason.
AI.method: A 10-hour model-conditioned challenge set of 1,501 Chinese and English clips with 4,723 keyword occurrences, scored with occurrence-based KER over frozen whole-phrase annotations. A disjoint 30-minute model-blind control set is used to check selection effects.
AI.result: Across five locally inferred checkpoints and two official API systems, language-specific MER and WER range from 5.31% to 12.91%, while KER ranges from 13.61% to 33.81%. The model-blind control gives KER of 10.65% to 27.31%.
AI.conclusion: Errors on selected phrases are substantially larger than sequence-level error suggests, and the control shows this gap is not an artifact of how the challenge set was selected.

title: SCorPion: A Strategic, Controllable and Personified Conversational Companion
summary: Fixed prompt-based language models face challenges in open-domain conversations, where versatile topics require different expert advice or demonstrations to maximize their universal performance. Motivated by the dynamic prompt studies in language generation, we extract different chatting strategies from varied forms of text corpus, which steer the language model to different styles based on human principles. We design and deploy a conversational companion called SCorPion, which uses GraphRAG to extract and summarize the knowledge graph globally, yield community-summarized strategies, and produce query-focused optimal strategies. SCorPion has strategic thinking, yields personified and stylized responses, and can be controlled by explicit factors. Code and further results can be found in this https URL.

AI.tldr: SCorPion is a conversational companion that improves open-domain chat by extracting chatting strategies from text corpora and using GraphRAG to select query-focused strategies. It produces personified, stylized responses that can be controlled by explicit factors.
AI.motivation: Fixed prompt-based language models struggle in open-domain conversation, where varied topics call for different expert advice or demonstrations.
AI.method: Chatting strategies are extracted from varied text corpora and guide the model toward different styles based on human principles. GraphRAG extracts and summarizes a knowledge graph globally to produce community-level strategies, which are then used to generate query-focused optimal strategies.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results. It states that the system shows strategic thinking, produces personified and stylized responses, and can be controlled by explicit factors.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, graph-derived strategies offer a route to controllable and personified conversational agents, and the authors deploy the system as a companion.

title: Pole or Vector? Encoders Capture Bangla Compound Verbs, but LLMs Read Them Literally
summary: In Bangla, a main verb is often followed by one of a small set of vector verbs. These verbs lose their own meaning and add a shade of meaning instead, such as completion. For example, likhe phello means that someone finished writing, not that they wrote and threw something. The same two verbs can also describe two separate events, so only the context shows which meaning is meant. This makes compound verbs a hard test of how language models handle multiword expressions. We present BanglaCV-Probe, a benchmark of 17 vector verbs with 1,044 minimal pairs, 204 entailment items and 197 pairs of correct and incorrect combinations, all checked by native speakers. We test 26 models (encoders, LLMs and translation systems) on four skills: telling the two meanings apart internally, understanding what a vector adds, preferring correct combinations and keeping the vector's meaning in translation. Probes on five encoders tell the two meanings apart and still reach up to 93% accuracy when trained on pairs without surface cues. Prompted models rarely use this knowledge. Entailment accuracy stays between 59% and 81%. Several LLMs answer Yes or No to almost every item, and nine of ten models miss that someone who ate up the rice left none. Most instruction-tuned LLMs translate vectors literally in 15-20% of vector sentences and in up to 55% for mora (die). On correct combinations, a small Bangla-only model (88%) matches BLOOM-7B1 (87%) and both beat Qwen2.5-7B (74%). Data and code: this https URL

AI.tldr: BanglaCV-Probe is a benchmark of 17 Bangla vector verbs that tests whether models separate the completive and literal meanings of compound verbs and translate them correctly. The authors find that encoders represent these distinctions, but prompted LLMs rarely use this knowledge.
AI.motivation: Bangla vector verbs lose their own meaning and add a shade such as completion, so only context shows the intended meaning. This makes compound verbs a hard test of multiword expression handling in language models.
AI.method: The benchmark has 1,044 minimal pairs, 204 entailment items and 197 pairs of correct and incorrect combinations, all checked by native speakers. Twenty-six models (encoders, LLMs and translation systems) are tested on four skills: distinguishing the two meanings internally, understanding what the vector adds, preferring correct combinations and keeping vector meaning in translation.
AI.result: Probes on five encoders separate the two meanings and reach up to 93% accuracy when trained on pairs without surface cues, but prompted models rarely use this knowledge. Entailment accuracy is between 59% and 81%. Nine of ten models miss that someone who ate up the rice left none. Most instruction-tuned LLMs translate vectors literally in 15-20% of vector sentences and up to 55% for mora (die). On correct combinations, a small Bangla-only model (88%) matches BLOOM-7B1 (87%) and both beat Qwen2.5-7B (74%).
AI.conclusion: Encoders capture Bangla compound verb meaning, but LLMs tend to read these verbs literally, which points to a gap in how they handle multiword expressions in this language.

title: DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Leaderboard: this https URL
summary: Existing evaluations of AI models on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real private equity (PE) and investment banking (IB) work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. We introduce DeepFinance, an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end PE and IB tasks that take a human professional an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files and is graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. We evaluate 22 model configurations, each in its native agent harness. The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.

AI.tldr: DeepFinance is an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end private equity and investment banking tasks, each with a data room and expert rubric grading. The best of 22 evaluated configurations satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of AI on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers and producing numerically correct outputs. Real PE and IB work also requires choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions and keeping every step auditable.
AI.method: Each of 21 tasks takes a human professional an average of 27.1 hours and pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files. Outputs are graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow and judgment. Each of 22 model configurations is run in its native agent harness.
AI.result: The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.
AI.conclusion: Current models remain far from reliable end-to-end financial diligence, with failures in source selection and in acting on evidence they have already found.

title: Gendered Misclassification from Surname-Based Race Imputation
summary: Researchers increasingly estimate political behavior based on race and gender from voter files, where race is imputed from surnames and geography. This only works where surnames suggest group membership, an assumption violated where surnames follow norms around marriage. Imputation is therefore biased against women who adopt their husband's surname, especially those who racially inter-marry, an outcome itself endogenous to partisanship. Using six US states recording self-reported race, I show that imputation is less accurate for Asian and Hispanic women, particularly those sharing the surname of a partner of another race, who differ politically from other women of their race. This violates assumptions behind downstream inference approaches, which nearly double the gender gap in partisanship among Asian voters. I derive an expression showing the bias is largest where a group is small. Using maiden rather than marriage-adopted surnames in North Carolina raises accuracy up to fourfold for women married across racial lines. Recovering maiden surnames, or omitting the married surname, removes much of the bias. In a national replication of a study of gender gaps in turnout, the correction more than triples the gap among Asian voters. In Lebanon, where wives register in their husband's locality, the error enters through geography.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that imputing race from surnames for voter files is biased against women who adopt a husband's surname, especially those married across racial lines. It derives an expression for the bias and tests corrections such as using maiden names.
AI.motivation: Political studies often impute race from surnames and geography, which assumes surnames signal group membership. This assumption fails where surnames follow marriage norms, which biases imputation against some women.
AI.method: Self-reported race data from six US states are used to measure imputation accuracy by race and gender. The paper derives an expression for the bias, tests maiden-name surnames in North Carolina, and runs a national replication of a turnout gender-gap study.
AI.result: Imputation is less accurate for Asian and Hispanic women, particularly those sharing a partner's surname of another race. Downstream methods nearly double the gender gap in partisanship among Asian voters. Using maiden surnames raises accuracy up to fourfold for women married across racial lines. In the national replication, the correction more than triples the turnout gender gap among Asian voters.
AI.conclusion: Surname-based imputation introduces gendered misclassification that can distort political inference, and recovering maiden surnames or omitting married surnames removes much of this bias. The bias is largest where a group is small.

title: Can small transformers learn the language of Coxeter groups?
comment: 13 pages, 13 figures, accepted as a poster at the 6th workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI; NeurIPS 2026, Atlanta; This version is updated from the camera-ready version which can be found at this https URL and this https URL
summary: The field of mechanistic interpretability is well-suited to collaborative projects between mathematicians and AI researchers. This work describes one such project. We trained a small transformer to learn the language of the Coxeter group affine A2, best known as the symmetries of the tiling of the Euclidean plane by equilateral triangles. We then formulated and proved a word-theoretic conjecture about affine A2 after observing the attention patterns of the trained model.

AI.tldr: The paper describes a collaboration in which a small transformer is trained to learn the language of the affine Coxeter group A2. The authors then prove a word-theoretic conjecture suggested by the model's attention patterns.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic interpretability is presented as a good area for collaboration between mathematicians and AI researchers.
AI.method: A small transformer is trained on the language of the affine Coxeter group A2, the symmetry group of the equilateral triangle tiling of the Euclidean plane. The attention patterns of the trained model are examined to formulate a conjecture, which is then proved.
AI.result: The abstract reports a proved word-theoretic conjecture about affine A2 suggested by the attention patterns. It gives no further quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Interpreting a small trained model can suggest mathematical conjectures that are then established by proof.

title: When Safety Becomes An Outlier: Understanding the Retention of LLM Safety Behaviors
summary: Safety-aligned large language models often lose their safety behaviors after fine-tuning, even when safety data are included. While this fragility is well documented, its underlying cause remains unclear. In this paper, we propose that formulaic refusal strings can function as outlier modes: narrow, weakly grounded response patterns that are easy to fit but vulnerable to subsequent updates. Controlled experiments support this account: fixed refusals are acquired much like arbitrary constant strings, in contrast to prompt-grounded natural responses. Motivated by these findings, we introduce Naturalness-Enhanced Safety Targets (NEST), a safety alignment framework that improves safety retention by constructing natural, context-aware safety targets that keep safety responses within the model's existing output distribution and grounded in semantics. We instantiate NEST in both supervised and preference-based alignment settings, using perplexity under the original model as a proxy for distributional support. Across multiple models and alignment regimes, natural safety targets improve both immediate safety and its retention under continued fine-tuning without sacrificing helpfulness. These findings suggest a practical principle for more durable safety alignment: construct safety targets that draw on the model's existing language capabilities and remain grounded in the meaning of each request.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that formulaic refusal strings act as outlier modes that are lost after fine-tuning, and proposes NEST, which builds natural, context-aware safety targets. NEST improves safety retention under continued fine-tuning without hurting helpfulness.
AI.motivation: Safety-aligned LLMs lose their safety behaviors after fine-tuning even when safety data are included, and the cause of this fragility was unclear.
AI.method: Controlled experiments compare how fixed refusals and prompt-grounded natural responses are acquired. NEST builds safety targets that stay within the model's existing output distribution and are grounded in request semantics, using perplexity under the original model as a proxy for distributional support. It is applied in supervised and preference-based alignment.
AI.result: Across multiple models and alignment regimes, natural safety targets improve immediate safety and its retention under continued fine-tuning without sacrificing helpfulness. Fixed refusals are acquired much like arbitrary constant strings.
AI.conclusion: Durable safety alignment should build safety targets from the model's existing language capabilities and keep them grounded in the meaning of each request.

title: SWEET: Mitigating Spurious Feature Reliance in LLM Reasoning via Weight Editing
summary: Reasoning in large language models can be disrupted by simple input perturbations (e.g. adding irrelevant distractors), suggesting reliance on spurious correlations. Identifying and suppressing the spurious features involved in long chain-of-thought reasoning remains challenging. We introduce Spurious-feature WEight EdiTing (SWEET), a training-free method that combines counterfactual interventions with mechanistic interpretability to identify and suppress spurious-features. SWEET extracts token- and sequence-level behavioral directions from activation contrasts between original problems and their counterfactual variants - capturing local and global patterns of spurious reasoning. It then localizes the responsible MLP neurons and attention heads and suppresses their contributions along these directions through weight edits. Using only 20 original-counterfactual pairs for direction extraction, SWEET improves accuracy by an average of 11.8 percentage points on perturbed inputs and 2 points on original inputs across five open-weight reasoning models and five reasoning benchmarks. It also reduces the relative gap between original and perturbed accuracies from 17.6% to 2.5%. Analyses identify two recurring forms of spurious reasoning, i.e. over-integrating irrelevant conditions and overthinking, and provide mechanistic evidence that SWEET improves reasoning robustness by suppressing both behavioral directions.

AI.tldr: SWEET is a training-free method that reduces reliance on spurious features in LLM reasoning by editing weights to suppress spurious-reasoning directions. It improves accuracy on perturbed and original inputs across five open-weight reasoning models.
AI.motivation: Simple input perturbations such as irrelevant distractors can disrupt LLM reasoning, which suggests reliance on spurious correlations. Identifying and suppressing these features in long chain-of-thought reasoning is difficult.
AI.method: Token- and sequence-level behavioral directions are extracted from activation contrasts between original problems and counterfactual variants. The responsible MLP neurons and attention heads are localized, and their contributions along these directions are suppressed by weight edits. Only 20 original-counterfactual pairs are used for direction extraction.
AI.result: SWEET improves accuracy by an average of 11.8 percentage points on perturbed inputs and 2 points on original inputs across five reasoning models and five benchmarks. The relative gap between original and perturbed accuracy falls from 17.6% to 2.5%. The two recurring spurious patterns identified are over-integrating irrelevant conditions and overthinking.
AI.conclusion: Suppressing these behavioral directions with weight edits improves reasoning robustness, as shown by mechanistic evidence.

title: Think or Remember: The Exchange Rate of Agentic Inference
summary: Agents built on reasoning models resend their growing transcript at every call. Two transacting parties, not the model, decide what that costs: the client keeps or edits messages; the server decides whether earlier reasoning returns in the prompt and what its cache reuses. We define a cost model whose counts match an instrumented engine exactly; the architecture charges $c$ per token processed and $\beta$ per pair attended. Their ratio $P^*=c/\beta$ is an exchange rate between thinking and remembering: per token, processing dominates below this context length, a thinking regime, and attention above it, a memory regime. A policy change has a mechanical cost, incurred even if the agent writes the same tokens, and a behavioral one: it writes different tokens, changing cost and outcome. Serving alone can flip which policy is cheaper: on recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74 times keeping it when the server reuses generated states and 0.34 times when it reuses nothing. In live reruns, dropping it cuts correct HotpotQA answers by 9-23 percentage points on four models, at lower point-estimate cost. Comparing context policies means comparing systems: architecture and serving set the cost of the history kept and the work it induces.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a cost model for agentic inference that treats context policy as an exchange rate between processing tokens and attending over history. Serving choices can change which policy is cheaper, and dropping earlier reasoning can cut correct answers.
AI.motivation: Agents resend a growing transcript at every call, and the client and server together decide what this costs, a decision that is often ignored when comparing policies.
AI.method: A cost model whose counts match an instrumented engine exactly charges c per token processed and beta per pair attended. The ratio P* = c/beta is treated as an exchange rate between a thinking regime below this context length and a memory regime above it. Recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs and live HotpotQA reruns on four models are analyzed.
AI.result: On recorded ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74 times as much as keeping it when the server reuses generated states, and 0.34 times when it reuses nothing. In live reruns, dropping earlier reasoning cuts correct HotpotQA answers by 9 to 23 percentage points on four models, at lower point-estimate cost.
AI.conclusion: Comparing context policies is also comparing systems, since architecture and serving determine the cost of the kept history and the work it induces.

title: Open Problems in Chatbots and Mental Health
summary: General-purpose chatbots are increasingly used for emotional and mental health support. They can be useful, but issues such as sycophancy, reinforcement of delusional beliefs, and poor crisis response create risks that are difficult for researchers to study and evaluate. In this paper, we review the most critical open problems for researchers and policymakers in the use of general-purpose chatbots and their effects on mental health. First, there are tractable problems in the controlled evaluation of chatbots: establishing the construct and ecological validity of evaluations, evaluating multi-turn interactions, and connecting evaluations to improvements in chatbot behavior. For example, conventional benchmarks that primarily rely on static datasets cannot establish chatbot safety, and novel simulation methods need validation. Second, researchers must connect their studies of chatbots and mental health to real-world evidence. This includes analyzing the chatbot products that AI companies and mental health practitioners have deployed, including their user interfaces and human review and escalation practices for user welfare concerns. However, clinical analysis opportunities afforded by real chat log data sharing are complicated by significant privacy concerns. Finally, we argue that researchers should take an active role in the construction and refinement of evidence-based policy through corporate and governmental decisions such as user protections, standards of care, protected access to user chat logs, data sharing between institutions, incident reporting, and post-deployment monitoring. Such behavioral evaluations, studies of real-world outcomes, and data governance depend on each other and must be addressed in tandem. We believe a coordinated research effort would have substantial real-world impact.

AI.tldr: This position paper reviews open problems in the use of general-purpose chatbots for emotional and mental health support, covering evaluation, real-world evidence and policy. It argues that these research efforts must proceed together.
AI.motivation: Chatbots are increasingly used for mental health support, but sycophancy, reinforcement of delusional beliefs and poor crisis response create risks that are difficult to study and evaluate.
AI.method: The paper is a review that identifies three groups of open problems: controlled evaluation (construct and ecological validity, multi-turn interactions, linking evaluation to behavior change), connections to real-world evidence (deployed products, user interfaces, escalation practices, chat log data sharing), and evidence-based policy (user protections, standards of care, incident reporting, post-deployment monitoring).
AI.result: The paper reports no empirical results. It argues that static benchmarks cannot establish chatbot safety and that novel simulation methods need validation.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral evaluation, real-world outcome studies and data governance depend on each other, and a coordinated research effort would have substantial real-world impact.

title: MoTo: Mixture of Tokenizers Towards Fair Multilingual Language Modeling
summary: Large language models rely on a single tokenizer that is chosen at training time and fixed thereafter. Most tokenizers are trained on English-dominant corpora, making them under-serve morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages, where they can produce fragmented representations, longer sequence lengths, and reduced information density during training. We propose Mixture of Tokenizers MoTo, a modular tokenization framework that trains dedicated per-language BPE tokenizers and composes them into a unified superset vocabulary, where tokens shared across languages are deduplicated into a common ID space. Each tokenizer maintains its own normalization policy, pre-tokenization rules, and vocabulary budget. Despite allocating significantly fewer entries to English, MoTo retains English performance while delivering consistent gains across 18 out of 21 typologically diverse languages spanning six scripts, with improvements most pronounced on morphologically complex and non-Latin-script languages that are systematically underserved by English-dominant tokenizer design. Our results suggest that modular subword tokenization is a practical and extensible alternative to monolithic tokenization for multilingual parity.

AI.tldr: MoTo is a modular tokenization framework that trains a BPE tokenizer for each language and merges them into one superset vocabulary with shared tokens deduplicated. It improves 18 of 21 typologically diverse languages while retaining English performance.
AI.motivation: A single tokenizer trained on English-dominant corpora under-serves morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages, producing fragmented representations, longer sequences and lower information density.
AI.method: Mixture of Tokenizers (MoTo) trains dedicated per-language BPE tokenizers and composes them into a unified superset vocabulary in a common ID space. Each tokenizer keeps its own normalization policy, pre-tokenization rules and vocabulary budget.
AI.result: Despite allocating significantly fewer entries to English, MoTo retains English performance and gives consistent gains across 18 of 21 languages spanning six scripts. The largest improvements are on morphologically complex and non-Latin-script languages.
AI.conclusion: Modular subword tokenization is a practical and extensible alternative to monolithic tokenization for multilingual parity.

title: Building and Auditing Chemical Datasets with LLMs: A General LLM-as-a-Judge Framework Applied to Homogeneous Catalytic PET Depolymerisation
summary: Large language models can rapidly extract structured multivariate experimental data from the chemistry literature, yet verifying thousands of generated records without ground truth remains difficult. We present a general, citation-grounded extraction and verification methodology centered on an independent "LLM-as-a-judge", applied to the literature on homogeneous catalytic poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) depolymerisation. In this pipeline, an extractor LLM generates schema-enforced records from research papers with citations to document chunks tagged with universally unique identifiers (UUIDs); an independent LLM judge then reads the full paper alongside each record, flags unsupported fields, and proposes cited corrections. Prompt ablations show that requiring chunk-level citations not only provides provenance down to specific paragraphs and tables but also improves extraction accuracy. Before deploying the judge at scale, we benchmarked it against manual evaluation on extractions from a hand-curated reference set of 295 ionic-liquid-catalysed PET glycolysis experiments. The judge agreed with human evaluation on 85.7% of reviewed records and was significantly more effective than a heuristic string-matching baseline at catching errors across related experiments. Deployed across 3,942 extracted records from 561 papers, the framework accepted 67.5% of them as written. Its proposed corrections concentrated on quantitative fields, where the extractor often conflated related experiments. We release the extracted dataset with the complete LLM judge audit logs, as well as the Chemistry Data Extractor Toolkit, an open-source application implementing this end-to-end pipeline in a code-free, browser-based environment for document parsing, customizable schema and prompt design, model-agnostic extraction and auditing, interactive provenance-highlighted review, and reproducible dataset bundling.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a citation-grounded extraction pipeline in which an independent LLM judge verifies records extracted from chemistry papers, applied to homogeneous catalytic PET depolymerisation. The judge agreed with humans on 85.7% of reviewed records, and 67.5% of 3,942 records were accepted as written.
AI.motivation: LLMs can extract structured experimental data quickly, but checking thousands of generated records without ground truth is difficult.
AI.method: An extractor LLM generates schema-enforced records with citations to UUID-tagged document chunks. An independent LLM judge reads the full paper with each record, flags unsupported fields and proposes cited corrections. The judge is benchmarked against manual evaluation on 295 ionic-liquid-catalysed PET glycolysis experiments, and chunk-level citation prompts are ablated.
AI.result: The judge agrees with human evaluation on 85.7% of reviewed records and beats a string-matching baseline at catching errors across related experiments. Across 3,942 records from 561 papers, 67.5% are accepted as written, and corrections concentrate on quantitative fields where the extractor conflated experiments. Chunk-level citations also improve extraction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: An LLM judge with citation grounding gives an auditable and scalable way to build chemistry datasets. The authors release the dataset, the judge audit logs and the open-source Chemistry Data Extractor Toolkit.

title: Room to Reconsider: Reply Length Decides Whether Pushback Makes Language Models Sycophantic or Self-Correcting
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Language models often abandon a correct answer when a user pushes back without giving a reason, and this behavior is usually studied as sycophancy to be suppressed. The same pushback, however, also leads models to revisit and sometimes repair a wrong answer. We measure both effects on multiple-choice questions from MMLU and ARC-Challenge with four open models from two families (Qwen3 1.7B, 4B and 8B, and OLMo-2 7B), reading the final answer exactly from option logits after a free-form reply. The reply budget changes the verdict. When Qwen3-4B may answer the challenge in at most 96 tokens, pushback leaves accuracy unchanged or slightly lower; with 1,024 tokens, it corrects 43% of its wrong answers and pushback raises accuracy by 5.7 points. Whether pushback helps overall follows a simple break-even rule in the cave and correction rates. Inside the model, caving can be partly predicted before the challenge: hidden states add about 0.04-0.06 AUROC over turn-1 confidence in three of our four probing runs. A probe trained only on self-correction cases predicts caving beyond confidence when replies are truncated, but not when the model can finish its reasoning. Activation steering never reduced caving selectively: where it worked, it suppressed self-correction as well. We conclude that sycophancy evaluations should allow full replies and report self-correction alongside caving.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the reply length budget determines whether pushback makes LLMs sycophantic or self-correcting. With short replies, pushback leaves accuracy unchanged or lower, while with full replies it corrects wrong answers and raises accuracy.
AI.motivation: Models often abandon correct answers under unexplained pushback, usually studied as sycophancy to suppress. The same pushback can also lead models to repair wrong answers, and this second effect is less studied.
AI.method: Multiple-choice questions from MMLU and ARC-Challenge are evaluated with four open models (Qwen3 1.7B, 4B and 8B, and OLMo-2 7B), reading the final answer from option logits after a free-form reply. Reply budgets are varied, and hidden-state probes and activation steering are tested for predicting and reducing caving.
AI.result: With Qwen3-4B limited to 96 tokens on the challenge set, pushback leaves accuracy unchanged or slightly lower. With 1,024 tokens, it corrects 43% of wrong answers and raises accuracy by 5.7 points. Hidden states add about 0.04 to 0.06 AUROC over turn-1 confidence in three of four probing runs. Activation steering that reduces caving also suppresses self-correction.
AI.conclusion: Sycophancy evaluations should allow full replies and report self-correction alongside caving.

title: Beyond Hard Labels: LLM Probabilities Improve Human-Assisted Regression
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text annotation, but their outputs are often reduced to a single categorical label before downstream analysis. This hardening step discards the model's relative support across categories, which may contain useful information when category boundaries are ambiguous. We study whether retaining the full probability vector improves downstream regression when LLM annotations are combined with a limited amount of human annotation. Using matched soft and hard representations from three LLMs across three social-science text datasets, we compare direct regression and human-assisted correction. Soft inputs are not uniformly better when used directly as outcomes, but after human correction, using the probability vector consistently improves regression efficiency across models and datasets. Analyses of repeated human judgments and controlled simulations further show that these gains arise when probability variation beyond the hard category carries useful information about the human-coded outcome. Our results identify output representation as an important design choice in LLM-assisted measurement and support preserving probability outputs for downstream statistical analysis. Code and reproducibility materials are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper shows that keeping the full probability vector from LLM annotations improves downstream regression after limited human correction, compared with using hard labels. The gains hold across three LLMs and three social-science text datasets.
AI.motivation: LLM text annotation usually reduces outputs to one categorical label, which discards information about relative support across categories that may matter when category boundaries are ambiguous.
AI.method: Matched soft and hard representations from three LLMs are compared across three social-science text datasets, using direct regression and human-assisted correction. Repeated human judgments and controlled simulations are used to explain the gains.
AI.result: Soft inputs are not uniformly better when used directly as outcomes. After human correction, the probability vector consistently improves regression efficiency across models and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Output representation is an important design choice in LLM-assisted measurement, and probability outputs should be preserved for downstream statistical analysis.

title: LongCap: Hour-Scale Timestamped Audio Captioning via Chunk-wise Processing
comment: 26 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail throughout the recording. We present LongCap, a framework for timestamped audio captioning (TAC), with the human-annotated LongCapBench and three diarization-inspired metrics: Timeline Error Rate (TER), Granularity Error Rate (GER), and Caption Similarity (tcpCapSim). LongCap interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context to support length extrapolation within a 1M-token inference context window. Event-level reannotation restores caption detail, while systematic studies examine model scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation. LongCap-Diar achieves strong benchmark results and extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings no longer than 40 minutes. Our TAC models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips, outperform evaluated baselines in caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons on LongCapBench-TAC-Long, and caption full recordings approaching two hours. On LongCapBench-TAC, 9B and 35B-A3B offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs, while 122B-A10B substantially improves event-dependency recovery. These findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.

AI.tldr: LongCap is a framework for timestamped audio captioning of hours of audio, using chunk-wise processing with relative timestamps and structured event captions. It extrapolates from training on recordings up to 40 minutes to 16 hours of concatenated audio.
AI.motivation: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail across the whole recording.
AI.method: Audio chunks are interleaved with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context within a 1M-token inference window. The authors add event-level reannotation and three diarization-inspired metrics (TER, GER and tcpCapSim), and study model scaling, dependency supervision and self-distillation. Results are reported on LongCapBench.
AI.result: LongCap-Diar extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings of at most 40 minutes. The models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips and outperform the evaluated baselines on caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons. The 122B-A10B model substantially improves event-dependency recovery, while the 9B and 35B-A3B models offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs.
AI.conclusion: The findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.

title: A Layer-wise Study of How Style Rewriting Breaks the Calibration of Zero-Shot LLM Fake-News Detectors
