summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked to judge whether a news article is true, and their stated confidence is often taken at face value. We test what happens to that confidence when an article's writing style, but not its facts, is manipulated, as in recent \emph{style attacks} on fake-news detectors. Tracing how the prediction and its confidence form layer by layer inside the network, we study three model families (LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B) on three fake-news benchmarks, and find the same three patterns in every model--dataset pairing. First, on the original articles the models are competent and largely honest judges: they settle on an answer, briefly become overconfident, and then correct their confidence in the final layers. Second, style-rewritten articles break this self-correction: the models become far less accurate, under the strongest attack, worse than random guessing, yet remain just as confident, so they are \emph{confidently wrong} precisely when a warning is most needed. Third, nearly all of the damage comes from rewriting into sensational or emotionally charged styles, while sober, neutral rewrites leave the models' honesty largely intact. The practical implication is that an LLM's confidence about veracity cannot be trusted as a safety signal when an article's style may have been manipulated.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that style rewriting, which changes writing style but not facts, makes zero-shot LLM fake-news detectors confidently wrong. Sensational or emotional rewrites cause nearly all of the damage across three model families and three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM confidence about whether a news article is true is often taken at face value, and recent style attacks on fake-news detectors raise the question of how that confidence behaves when only style is manipulated.
AI.method: Layer-by-layer analysis of how the prediction and its confidence form inside LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B on three fake-news benchmarks, comparing original articles with style-rewritten versions.
AI.result: On original articles, models settle on an answer, briefly become overconfident, and then correct their confidence in the final layers. Under style rewriting, accuracy drops, and under the strongest attack it falls below random guessing while confidence stays the same. Nearly all of the damage comes from sensational or emotionally charged rewrites, while neutral rewrites leave honesty largely intact.
AI.conclusion: An LLM's confidence about veracity cannot be trusted as a safety signal when an article's style may have been manipulated.

title: Saidzoda-Tajik-EmbeddingGemma-300M: Knowing Every Letter Is Not Reading Tajik
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables, 1 figure. Technical report. Model: this https URL
summary: EmbeddingGemma-300M is a small open embedder whose tokenizer represents every Tajik letter, and as released it is weak at Tajik retrieval: on our Tajik law test the right passage is in its top ten results for 49.3% of questions, on tax documents for 45.9%, and on the human-written Belebele Tajik set for 69.8%, against 98.6% on the Russian version of the same set. We present Saidzoda-Tajik-EmbeddingGemma-300M, the same model fully fine-tuned for one epoch on 235,140 question and passage pairs written by our own Tajik language model for laws, tax documents, Wikipedia and web text, with the same mined hard negatives, English and Russian replay, loss, global batch, learning rate and epoch as our earlier Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large (arXiv:2611.00592) and BGE-M3 models. After training, law reaches 92.4% and tax 91.7%; on Belebele, the one test written by people, recall@10 rises from 69.8% to 92.6% and the first result is right for 76.6% of questions instead of 51.7%. A checkpoint at step 100 of 466 already holds 88% of the law gain at recall@10. At recall@10 the result is no more than 2.8 points below the two 560M models trained on the same pairs on law, tax and Wikipedia, within the intervals, with 768-dimensional vectors and about half their parameters; at recall@1, for which we have no intervals, it stays 7.0 points behind the E5 model on Belebele. The cost is a drop of 3.0 and 2.8 points in Russian and English recall@1, larger than for the two earlier models. We also report that, according to our run notes, a bfloat16 test run produced a non-finite loss at step 3 which the training framework logged as zero, so training was done in fp32. Our generated test questions come from the same model as the training questions, so we treat those scores as an upper limit until questions written by Tajik speakers exist.

AI.tldr: Fine-tunes the small EmbeddingGemma-300M embedder on 235,140 Tajik question-passage pairs written by an in-house Tajik language model, raising Tajik retrieval recall sharply and approaching two 560M models trained on the same pairs.
AI.motivation: As released, EmbeddingGemma-300M is weak at Tajik retrieval (the right passage is in the top ten for 49.3% of law questions and 69.8% of Belebele Tajik questions, against 98.6% on the Russian Belebele set), although its tokenizer represents every Tajik letter.
AI.method: Full fine-tuning for one epoch with the same mined hard negatives, English and Russian replay, loss, global batch size, learning rate and epoch as the authors' earlier Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large and BGE-M3 models; training ran in fp32 because a bfloat16 test run produced a non-finite loss that the framework logged as zero.
AI.result: Law recall@10 reaches 92.4% and tax 91.7%; on Belebele recall@10 rises from 69.8% to 92.6% and recall@1 from 51.7% to 76.6%. At recall@10 the model is within 2.8 points of the two 560M models on law, tax and Wikipedia, with 768-dimensional vectors and about half their parameters, but at Belebele recall@1 it is 7.0 points behind the E5 model. Russian and English recall@1 drop by 3.0 and 2.8 points. Test questions come from the same model as the training questions, so the scores are an upper limit.
AI.conclusion: A small embedder can be adapted to a low-resource language with synthetic training pairs, but the gains are upper bounds until questions written by Tajik speakers exist, and they cost some accuracy in Russian and English.

title: Understanding When and Where Self-Supervised Speech Models Learn Phonemes and Prosodic Cues through Layer-Wise and Time-Resolved Probing
summary: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) encode a rich hierarchy of acoustic, prosodic, and phonetic information, yet when and where it emerges during pretraining remains unclear. We train frozen-encoder probes on every Transformer layer across pretraining checkpoints of two matched models: HuBERT-Base, whose stage 2 is a separately initialized model trained on new pseudo-label targets, and single-objective wav2vec 2.0-Base. Our five tasks span an acoustic-to-abstract gradient: absolute pitch (F0), speaker-relative pitch, lexical stress, phoneme boundaries, and 38-way phoneme identity. Acoustic-prosodic cues and phone boundaries are decodable from the earliest checkpoints and barely shift across layers, whereas phoneme identity is constructed during pretraining, re-localizing to upper-middle layers under HuBERT's stage-2 targets at a matched update count. Acquisition order therefore tracks abstraction from the acoustic surface, not the segmental/suprasegmental distinction, extending to prosody an account established for phonetic, lexical and syntactic structure; the no-switch wav2vec 2.0 shows no comparable re-localization.

AI.tldr: Layer-wise and checkpoint-wise probing of HuBERT-Base and wav2vec 2.0-Base shows that acoustic-prosodic cues and phone boundaries are learned early and stay across layers, while phoneme identity is built during pretraining and moves to upper-middle layers.
AI.motivation: It is unclear when and where self-supervised speech models acquire acoustic, prosodic and phonetic information during pretraining.
AI.method: Frozen-encoder probes are trained on every Transformer layer across pretraining checkpoints of HuBERT-Base, whose stage 2 uses a separately initialized model trained on new pseudo-label targets, and of single-objective wav2vec 2.0-Base, on five tasks: absolute F0, speaker-relative pitch, lexical stress, phoneme boundaries and 38-way phoneme identity.
AI.result: Acoustic-prosodic cues and phone boundaries are decodable from the earliest checkpoints and barely shift across layers. Under HuBERT's stage-2 targets, phoneme identity is constructed during pretraining and re-localizes to upper-middle layers at a matched update count, whereas the no-switch wav2vec 2.0 model shows no comparable re-localization.
AI.conclusion: Acquisition order tracks abstraction from the acoustic surface rather than the segmental versus suprasegmental distinction, which extends to prosody an account previously established for phonetic, lexical and syntactic structure.

title: WarBias: A Bilingual LLM Benchmark of Stereotypes About Internally Displaced People and Veterans
summary: This paper contains examples of stereotypes about veterans and displaced people that may be offensive or distressing. Social bias benchmarks for language models commonly examine categories such as gender, race, and religion, often drawn from lists of legally protected characteristics. Veterans and internally displaced people (IDPs) fall outside these lists, and stereotypes about them, which can undermine access to employment, housing, and social participation, remain largely absent from language model evaluation. We introduce WarBias, a Ukrainian--English benchmark of stereotypes about these two groups. Built from a taxonomy of 120 stereotype claims grounded in research and monitoring reports, WarBias contains 1,007 stereotype--counter-stereotype--unrelated sentence triplets and 240 multiple-choice questions per language. A Ukrainian language model selected in a blinded human pilot generated the Ukrainian triplets. At least two independent annotators reviewed each triplet in the annotation cohort. The authors revised items in response to the reviews, and the final release was machine-translated into English. Each claim carries a human severity rating. In a baseline evaluation of six models, four prefer stereotypical Ukrainian sentences about at least one group, most strongly about IDPs, while English scores are mostly balanced. WarBias supports complementary evaluations of stereotypical preferences and context-sensitive judgments, and provides paired forget/retain material for unlearning-based bias mitigation. We document the benchmark's construction, intended uses, and limitations, and offer its construction method as a template for analogous benchmarks in other conflict-affected societies.

AI.tldr: Introduces WarBias, a Ukrainian-English benchmark of 1,007 stereotype triplets and 240 multiple-choice questions per language about veterans and internally displaced people, and finds that four of six evaluated models prefer stereotypical Ukrainian sentences.
AI.motivation: Social bias benchmarks focus on legally protected characteristics, so stereotypes about veterans and internally displaced people (IDPs), which can undermine access to employment, housing and social participation, are largely absent from language model evaluation.
AI.method: Built from a taxonomy of 120 stereotype claims grounded in research and monitoring reports. A Ukrainian language model chosen in a blinded human pilot generated the Ukrainian stereotype, counter-stereotype and unrelated sentence triplets, which at least two annotators reviewed and the authors revised; the release was machine-translated into English. Each claim carries a human severity rating, and the benchmark provides paired forget and retain material for unlearning.
AI.result: In a baseline evaluation of six models, four prefer stereotypical Ukrainian sentences about at least one group, most strongly about IDPs, while English scores are mostly balanced.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark supports evaluation of stereotypical preferences and context-sensitive judgments and unlearning-based mitigation, and its construction method is offered as a template for benchmarks in other conflict-affected societies.

title: EASE-KV: Diagnosing the Gap Between Memory Availability and Effective Use
summary: Reusable key-value (KV) memory avoids repeatedly prefilling retrieved text, but stored and injected memories do not necessarily become usable evidence. We present EASE-KV, a controlled framework for understanding this gap under fixed candidates and a frozen language model. EASE-KV separates three interfaces: whether required relations are preserved during encoding, whether preserved memories receive appropriate influence during allocation, and whether outcome supervision can identify useful allocations. Matched experiments show that causal encoding improves compositional accuracy by 25.0 percentage points over block-diagonal encoding, while the tested inference-time bridging methods fail to recover the lost contextual information. With unchanged stored states, diagnostic evidence-guided allocation improves LongMemEval accuracy from 31.2% to 38.4%, demonstrating that memory influence can be controlled without re-encoding. However, controllability does not guarantee learnability: binary correctness provides informative reward contrast for 53.0% of sampled query groups, compared with 73.6% under the evaluated shaped-reward setting. These findings show that effective KV memory requires more than retrieval and injection: the required relations must be encoded, preserved memories must receive appropriate influence, and supervision must distinguish better allocations from worse ones.

AI.tldr: EASE-KV is a controlled framework showing that reusable key-value memory becomes usable evidence only when required relations are encoded, preserved memories receive appropriate influence, and supervision can tell better allocations from worse ones.
AI.motivation: Reusable key-value memory avoids repeated prefilling of retrieved text, but stored and injected memories do not necessarily become usable evidence for a frozen language model.
AI.method: Under fixed candidates and a frozen language model, the framework separates three interfaces: whether required relations are preserved during encoding (causal versus block-diagonal), whether preserved memories receive appropriate influence during allocation (diagnostic evidence-guided allocation without re-encoding), and whether outcome supervision can identify useful allocations (reward shaping).
AI.result: Causal encoding improves compositional accuracy by 25.0 percentage points over block-diagonal encoding, and the tested inference-time bridging methods do not recover the lost contextual information. With unchanged stored states, evidence-guided allocation raises LongMemEval accuracy from 31.2% to 38.4%. Binary correctness gives informative reward contrast for 53.0% of sampled query groups, against 73.6% under the evaluated shaped reward.
AI.conclusion: Controllability does not guarantee learnability, so effective KV memory needs relations encoded, memories given appropriate influence, and supervision that separates better allocations from worse ones, not just retrieval and injection.

title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track)
summary: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and this http URL directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and this http URL, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

AI.tldr: ScrapeBench is an agentic benchmark of AI agents' legal compliance with website terms of service and scraping directives, finding low compliance on sites that prohibit scraping and frequent over-refusal on sites that permit it.
AI.motivation: AI agents on the open web can take actions that may breach contract terms and computer security laws, and their compliance with website scraping policies had not been evaluated empirically.
AI.method: The first agentic benchmark of this kind, covering website terms of service and scraping directives, run on 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping and 269 that do not, across closed-weight and open-weight agents, with a human baseline of 180 participants.
AI.result: Most agents show compliance rates below 5% on prohibiting sites when instructed to scrape, even when they check the applicable policies. On permitting sites agents sometimes refuse lawful scraping, with Claude Opus 4.6 over-refusing 98.5% of the time. Humans comply at rates comparable to agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.
AI.conclusion: Agents do not reliably follow scraping policies, and their errors run in both directions, refusing lawful scraping while failing to respect prohibitions, so deployment needs calibrated compliance rather than blanket refusal or compliance.

title: AOP-Smart-Finder: A High-Throughput Human-AI Hybrid Framework for AOP Discovery and Evidence Mapping from Large-Scale Literature
summary: The rapid growth of scientific literature and the high heterogeneity of biological terminology and mechanistic descriptions make it difficult for researchers to integrate scattered research evidence, identify connections among biological events, and construct mechanistic networks. Here, we developed a high-throughput human-AI hybrid framework, AOP-Smart-Finder, for biological event discovery, relationship mining, and Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) construction and evidence mapping from large-scale literature. This framework integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), AOP-Smart retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) technology, and Python-based automation, supporting two analysis modes: one based on a single compound and the other based on a predefined set of biological events. In the di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) case, the system processed 12,983 articles within 30 min and included 1,093 of them, from which it extracted 1,589 biological events (including 458 official key events [KEs] and 1,131 candidate KEs) and 2,519 key event relationships (KERs). In the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) case, the system identified 55 stressors from 437 articles and extracted 278 biological events and 548 event relationships. Following manual curation and Weight of Evidence (WoE) evaluation, a mechanistic network comprising 16 KEs and 23 KERs was ultimately constructed. This framework can either use existing AOPs as knowledge guidance for mechanistic expansion and evidence supplementation, or discover novel event connections and construct mechanistic networks around user-specified research topics. It provides a high-throughput, traceable, human-AI hybrid methodology for complex biological mechanism elucidation and AOP discovery driven by large-scale literature.

AI.tldr: AOP-Smart-Finder is a human-AI hybrid pipeline that combines LLMs with retrieval-augmented generation to mine large literature sets for biological events and key event relationships, and to build adverse outcome pathway networks.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth and terminological heterogeneity of scientific literature make it hard for researchers to integrate scattered evidence, identify connections among biological events and construct mechanistic networks.
AI.method: An LLM and AOP-Smart retrieval-augmented generation pipeline with Python automation, supporting two modes: one starting from a single compound and one from a predefined set of biological events, followed by manual curation and Weight of Evidence evaluation.
AI.result: In the DEHP case, 12,983 articles were processed within 30 minutes, 1,093 were included, and 1,589 biological events (458 official key events and 1,131 candidate key events) and 2,519 key event relationships were extracted. In the ALS case, 55 stressors were identified from 437 articles, yielding 278 biological events and 548 event relationships; after curation and Weight of Evidence evaluation, a network of 16 key events and 23 key event relationships was built.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a high-throughput, traceable hybrid method for elucidating biological mechanisms and discovering AOPs from large-scale literature, either by extending existing AOPs or by exploring new event connections around user-specified topics.

title: Search-by-Answer Bias in Retrieval Models
summary: Dense retrievers are meant to select passages that match a query's semantic specification. We show they suffer from search-by-answer bias: they favor passages that mention answer objects the model knows (scores as likely), over passages that support valid alternative answers. We test this with controlled factual contrasts from LAMA/TREx. For each retriever, we measure how strongly the model scores the canonical object over an alternative object using a token-prediction head, and ask whether this score predicts passage rankings. Across eight retrievers, including DPR, Spider variants, Contriever, E5, and Qwen3-Embedding, larger token-prediction scores consistently predict higher retrieval scores for passages containing the corresponding object. This holds when passages differ only in the answer object, and even when the passage that mentions the high-scoring object expresses a wrong relation. Dense retrieval thus exhibits search-by-answer bias during passage selection, shaping which evidence is retrieved.

AI.tldr: Shows that dense retrievers, including DPR, Contriever, E5 and Qwen3-Embedding, rank passages higher when they mention answer objects the model itself predicts, even when those passages express a wrong relation.
AI.motivation: Dense retrievers are meant to select passages that match a query's semantic specification, yet they may instead favor passages that mention answer objects the model already knows.
AI.method: Controlled factual contrasts from LAMA/TREx. For each of eight retrievers, a token-prediction head measures how strongly the model scores the canonical object over an alternative object, and the authors test whether this score predicts passage rankings.
AI.result: Across eight retrievers, larger token-prediction scores consistently predict higher retrieval scores for passages containing the corresponding object. This holds when passages differ only in the answer object, and even when the passage mentioning the high-scoring object expresses a wrong relation.
AI.conclusion: Dense retrieval exhibits search-by-answer bias during passage selection, which shapes which evidence is retrieved.

title: Modeling individual and item differences in atypicality inferences with ACT-R
comment: Accepted as a conference paper at CogSci 2026
summary: Humans engage in pragmatic reasoning when encountering mentions of highly predictable events. Such mentions may appear redundant, leading comprehenders to infer that the event is atypical, and accommodate this inference with an explanation for why it is atypical. However, these inferences are not drawn uniformly across individuals, and experimental items vary in inference rates due to differences in event typicality. We show that these patterns can be predicted with a resource-rational cognitive model in which comprehenders select interpretation strategies based on individual exploration tendencies and item-level predispositions. These parameters are estimated independently from participants' Raven's Matrices score, event typicality rating and language model based accommodation likelihood. Taken together with recent findings from reference games, our results motivate a new perspective on the mechanisms that support pragmatic inferences.

AI.tldr: A resource-rational ACT-R model predicts individual and item differences in pragmatic atypicality inferences from comprehenders' exploration tendencies and items' typicality.
AI.motivation: When highly predictable events are mentioned, comprehenders may infer that the event is atypical, but these inferences are not drawn uniformly across individuals, and experimental items vary in inference rates.
AI.method: Comprehenders are modeled as selecting interpretation strategies based on individual exploration tendencies and item-level predispositions. These parameters are estimated independently from Raven's Matrices scores, event typicality ratings and language-model-based accommodation likelihoods.
AI.result: The model predicts the patterns of individual and item differences in atypicality inferences. The abstract reports no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Together with recent findings from reference games, the results motivate a new perspective on the mechanisms that support pragmatic inferences.

title: Vietnamese Legal Ontology: Every legal answer, traced to the article that grounds it
summary: A legal answer is only as good as the article it rests on. Vietnam's largest open legal corpus pairs 109,543 published questions and answers with 573,851 legal documents, yet its citations are free text: "Khoan 3 Dieu 101 cua Bo luat nay" ("Clause 3, Article 101 of this Code") names neither the code nor its version. Following the five stages of NVIDIA Auto Ontology, Discover, Ground, Validate, Expose and Learn, we turn four open datasets into a knowledge graph of 11.5 M nodes and 16.0 M edges in which every node and edge carries its source record and method, with no duplicate keys, dangling edges or schema violations. Of 67,868 cited provisions, 61,487 resolve to a dated law version, 51,694 to a parsed article, clause or point, and 19,012 are confirmed word for word. The ontology then shows what flat records hide. 36% of the 78,361 answers whose citations resolve now cite a law that is no longer in force; 2,525 verified citations point to an article number that says something else in the current law; 2,520 citations were re-versioned because their words match a different version than their date suggests; and 5,575 document numbers are shared by several local authorities, one of them by 72. Every number in this paper is computed from the graph.

AI.tldr: Builds an 11.5-million-node legal knowledge graph from Vietnam's open legal corpus that traces each citation to a dated law version, and shows that many answers cite laws no longer in force.
AI.motivation: Vietnam's largest open legal corpus pairs 109,543 published questions and answers with 573,851 legal documents, but its citations are free text that names neither the code nor its version.
AI.method: Following the five stages of NVIDIA Auto Ontology (Discover, Ground, Validate, Expose and Learn), four open datasets are turned into a knowledge graph in which every node and edge carries its source record and method, checked for duplicate keys, dangling edges and schema violations.
AI.result: The graph has 11.5 million nodes and 16.0 million edges. Of 67,868 cited provisions, 61,487 resolve to a dated law version, 51,694 to a parsed article, clause or point, and 19,012 are confirmed word for word. 36% of the 78,361 answers whose citations resolve cite a law no longer in force; 2,525 verified citations point to an article number that says something else in the current law; 2,520 citations were re-versioned; and 5,575 document numbers are shared by several local authorities, one of them by 72.
AI.conclusion: Provenance-tracked legal graphs expose errors and obsolescence in citations that flat records hide, so each legal answer can be traced to the article that grounds it.

title: Saidzoda-CA-EmbeddingGemma-300M: One Small Embedder for Tajik, Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz
comment: 12 pages, 6 tables, 2 figures. Technical report. Model: this https URL
summary: The small open embedder EmbeddingGemma-300M, used as released, finds the right passage first for only 51.7% to 60.8% of Belebele questions in Tajik, Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz. We present Saidzoda-CA-EmbeddingGemma-300M, one model for all four languages. It is our Tajik fine-tune of EmbeddingGemma-300M, trained for one more epoch on 279,904 pairs: questions in Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz that our own language model wrote about source passages, a Tajik refresher, and English and Russian replay. On Belebele, recall@1 rises by 14.4 to 26.0 points in each language, to between 75.2% and 77.7%. Against single-language models trained with the same settings, the one model stays within 2.8 points at recall@1 in Kazakh, Uzbek and Tajik, with overlapping recall@10 intervals, though it also had more training. It keeps the Tajik law recall@10 of its starting point (92.2 against 92.4) but loses 4.4 points of law recall@1. A model trained on one of these languages also improves the others on Belebele, but less than training on them. The model still trails the 560M XLM-RoBERTa embedders on Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz Belebele: the better of multilingual-e5-large-instruct and BGE-M3, used as released, is 9.4 to 10.2 points ahead at recall@1. Our scores of those released models agree with the published MTEB results within 2.4 points. Russian and English recall@1 fall by 3.0 and 4.2 points.

AI.tldr: Saidzoda-CA-EmbeddingGemma-300M is one embedder fine-tuned for Tajik, Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz that raises Belebele recall@1 by 14.4 to 26.0 points in each language, while still trailing 560M XLM-RoBERTa embedders on Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz.
AI.motivation: As released, EmbeddingGemma-300M finds the right passage first for only 51.7% to 60.8% of Belebele questions in Tajik, Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz.
AI.method: One more epoch of training on 279,904 pairs: questions in Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz that the authors' language model wrote about source passages, a Tajik refresher, and English and Russian replay, applied to the authors' Tajik fine-tune of EmbeddingGemma-300M.
AI.result: Belebele recall@1 rises to between 75.2% and 77.7% in each language. Against single-language models trained with the same settings, the one model stays within 2.8 points at recall@1 in Kazakh, Uzbek and Tajik, with overlapping recall@10 intervals, though it had more training. Tajik law recall@10 is 92.2 against 92.4 for its starting point, but law recall@1 falls by 4.4 points. The better of multilingual-e5-large-instruct and BGE-M3 is 9.4 to 10.2 points ahead at recall@1 on Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz Belebele. Russian and English recall@1 fall by 3.0 and 4.2 points.
AI.conclusion: One multilingual model can serve four Central Asian languages at a small cost against single-language models, though a gap to the 560M XLM-RoBERTa embedders remains on three of them.

title: THEATRON: A Benchmark for Evaluating Persona Persistence in Long-Horizon LLM Decision-Making
summary: Existing evaluations often test persona expression rather than whether persona information persists in extended decision-making. We introduce THEATRON, a controlled benchmark that uses financial replay to evaluate persona persistence in long-horizon sequential decision-making. In these environments, models conditioned on fixed behavioral-finance personas observe shared daily market evidence and trajectory-specific account-state feedback and make sequential decisions over multi-month trajectories. We evaluate Zero-Shot, One-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought persona injection across four LLMs, using cumulative-return and action trajectories to diagnose within-persona stability, cross-persona separability, and action collapse. Persona conditioning produces systematic behavioral shifts beyond a no-persona baseline, and persona-level separation generally exceeds the variation induced by semantically equivalent descriptions. Nevertheless, these shifts do not reliably form coherent persona-specific policies: apparently stable separation can arise from stereotyped action collapse, while diverse policies can exhibit noisy trajectory switching. These findings expose a gap between observable persona-induced behavior and persistent, context-sensitive persona-conditioned decision policies. Code and benchmark data are publicly available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: THEATRON is a financial-replay benchmark showing that persona-conditioned LLMs shift their decisions systematically but do not form coherent, persistent persona-specific policies over multi-month trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations often test persona expression rather than whether persona information persists through extended sequential decision-making.
AI.method: Models conditioned on fixed behavioral-finance personas observe shared daily market evidence and trajectory-specific account-state feedback and make sequential decisions over multi-month trajectories. Zero-Shot, One-Shot and Chain-of-Thought persona injection are compared across four LLMs, using cumulative-return and action trajectories to diagnose within-persona stability, cross-persona separability and action collapse.
AI.result: Persona conditioning produces systematic behavioral shifts beyond a no-persona baseline, and persona-level separation generally exceeds the variation induced by semantically equivalent descriptions. These shifts do not reliably form coherent persona-specific policies: apparently stable separation can arise from stereotyped action collapse, while diverse policies can show noisy trajectory switching.
AI.conclusion: There is a gap between observable persona-induced behavior and persistent, context-sensitive persona-conditioned decision policies.

title: TID System for Speech-COSER Challenge 2026: ASR Track
summary: We describe the system submitted by Telefónica Innovación Digital to the Speech-COSER Challenge 2026, which features spontaneous speech from elderly speakers recorded in rural Spain. For ASR, we perform CTC-based pseudo-forced alignment scores audio-text match quality to guide a two-stage LoRA curriculum, followed by post-hoc magnitude pruning of the LoRA matrices to enhance generalization. An ensemble of seven systems combined via ROVER achieves 36.25\% unnormalized and 22.17\% normalized WER.

AI.tldr: The Telefonica Innovacion Digital ASR system for the Speech-COSER Challenge 2026 combines CTC-based pseudo-forced alignment, a two-stage LoRA curriculum, LoRA magnitude pruning and a seven-system ROVER ensemble, reaching 36.25% unnormalized and 22.17% normalized WER on spontaneous speech from elderly rural Spanish speakers.
AI.motivation: The challenge's ASR track features spontaneous speech from elderly speakers recorded in rural Spain, and the system aims to enhance generalization on it.
AI.method: CTC-based pseudo-forced alignment scores audio-text match quality to guide a two-stage LoRA curriculum, followed by post-hoc magnitude pruning of the LoRA matrices; an ensemble of seven systems is combined via ROVER.
AI.result: The ensemble achieves 36.25% unnormalized and 22.17% normalized WER.
AI.conclusion: The abstract reports only the challenge WER result for this alignment-guided LoRA curriculum, pruning and ensemble system and makes no broader claim.

title: Does Merge Form a Hopf Algebra? Coproducts, Traces, and the Prospects of Algebraic Minimalism
summary: Marcolli, Chomsky, and Berwick (2025; henceforth MCB) formulate the Merge operation of Minimalism on a Hopf algebra of Connes-Kreimer type, and claim that language and physics obey the same algebraic structure. This paper separates their program into the working hypothesis H, that Merge on workspaces can be described as a Hopf algebra, and the claim P placed on top of it, that language and physics obey the same principle, and examines the validity of H. MCB employs two coproducts in formulating Merge, corresponding to two different translations of movement (Internal Merge): $\Delta_d$, which deletes the lower copy, and $\Delta_c$, which leaves a trace. MCB uses the former in syntax and the latter at the syntax-semantics interface, but $\Delta_d$ is not coassociative, and $\Delta_c$ is not connected under the gradings MCB gives and, moreover, not coassociative as long as the labels of traces are retained. Consequently, MCB's algebra is not a Hopf algebra, and the Birkhoff factorization is not a consequence of the Hopf-algebra theorem but of a weaker statement that requires neither coassociativity nor connectedness. There are four ways to recover a Hopf algebra, but none of them can distinguish different traces, and hence none is compatible with Heim-Kratzer-style formal semantics, which reads traces as indexed variables. Thus H does not hold at present, and under the current formulation, making Minimalism a Hopf algebra and preserving its connection with formal semantics are mutually exclusive. Finally, we indicate three directions in which algebraic Minimalism may proceed.

AI.tldr: Argues that Merge in the Marcolli, Chomsky and Berwick framework is not a Hopf algebra, because its coproducts fail coassociativity or connectedness, and that making Minimalism a Hopf algebra conflicts with formal semantics as currently formulated.
AI.motivation: Marcolli, Chomsky and Berwick (2025) formulate Merge on a Connes-Kreimer-type Hopf algebra and claim that language and physics obey the same algebraic structure; this paper examines whether the Hopf-algebra working hypothesis holds.
AI.method: Separates the program into a working hypothesis H, that Merge on workspaces is a Hopf algebra, and a claim P, that language and physics obey the same principle. It then analyzes the two coproducts used for Internal Merge, one that deletes the lower copy and one that leaves a trace, checking coassociativity, connectedness and the four routes to a Hopf algebra.
AI.result: The deleting coproduct is not coassociative, and the trace-leaving coproduct is not connected under the authors' gradings and is not coassociative once trace labels are retained, so the algebra is not a Hopf algebra. Birkhoff factorization follows from a weaker statement that requires neither property. None of the four ways to recover a Hopf algebra distinguishes different traces, so none is compatible with Heim-Kratzer-style formal semantics.
AI.conclusion: H does not hold in the current formulation, making Minimalism a Hopf algebra and preserving its link to formal semantics are mutually exclusive, and three directions for algebraic Minimalism are indicated.

title: When Should Diffusion Language Models Reconsider Their Commitments?
summary: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) are well known for fast text generation via parallel decoding. However, independent parallel sampling can commit to inconsistent predictions, and less is known about how to selectively revise these early token commitments. In this work, we introduce $\underline{\mathrm{P}}$lanned $\underline{\mathrm{U}}$nmasking-and-$\underline{\mathrm{R}}$evision Joint $\underline{\mathrm{L}}$earning (PURL) for MDMs, a training-based framework that seamlessly unifies parallel generation with selective token revision. We derive a normalized joint transition whose likelihood factorizes into edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction. These components are trained jointly on partially masked sequences constructed according to the model's own unmasking policy. During inference, all three decisions are supported by a single shared forward pass, enabling the model to decode masked tokens and revise noisy tokens. Across logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, PURL improves accuracy at matched unmask budgets, with relative gains up to 47.4% accuracy improvement and up to an $8\times$ reduction in scheduled decoding rounds. Beyond these gains, our analysis further reveals general principles of revisable decoding: token edits become more effective as context accumulates; early edits can steer unfinished trajectories, whereas later edits tend to remain localized; and effective edits therefore depend on both calibrating when to intervene and learning where and how to revise. Together, these suggest that effective parallel generation depends not on revising more tokens, but on making the right commitments revisable at the right time.

AI.tldr: PURL trains masked diffusion language models to unmask tokens and revise earlier commitments in one shared forward pass, improving accuracy on logic, math and code tasks at matched unmask budgets, with relative gains up to 47.4% and up to 8x fewer decoding rounds.
AI.motivation: Independent parallel sampling in masked diffusion models can commit to inconsistent predictions, and little is known about how to selectively revise those early token commitments.
AI.method: Planned Unmasking-and-Revision Joint Learning derives a normalized joint transition whose likelihood factorizes into edit selection, unmask selection and token prediction. These are trained jointly on partially masked sequences built from the model's own unmasking policy, and a single shared forward pass supports all three decisions at inference.
AI.result: Across logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning and code generation, PURL improves accuracy at matched unmask budgets, with relative gains up to 47.4% and up to an 8x reduction in scheduled decoding rounds.
AI.conclusion: Revisable decoding depends on timing: edits gain effectiveness as context accumulates, and early edits can steer unfinished trajectories, so effective parallel generation rests on making the right commitments revisable at the right time rather than revising more tokens.

title: Beyond the Transcript: Measuring and Improving the Use of Acoustic Information in Audio Language Models
summary: Audio language model benchmarks provide comprehensive evaluation across diverse tasks. However, some tasks can be answered from the transcript or even the question alone, and benchmark scores can therefore confound acoustic understanding with language modeling ability. We distinguish lexical tasks, for which the transcript usually suffices, from global-attribute and within-recording-structure tasks, which require the model to analyse the recording beyond its words, either as a whole, for properties such as the speaker and emotion, or within it, for patterns such as stress and intonation. We evaluated 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro on 92 tasks from 6 benchmarks and estimated the recording gain, the accuracy advantage of the original recording over references that retain its words, by comparing the recording with synthetic readings of its transcript and by adding it to the transcript. On attribute and structure tasks, the open models fall behind Gemini by 28.6 and 41.9 percentage points, and about half or more of each deficit lies in the recording gain. Nevertheless, linear probes in Gemma-4 12B and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B show that the acoustic information needed for answering is already readable in early language-model layers, while the readout of many cues declines in the layers that follow. We therefore constructed training data and trained LoRA adapters in these layers, with a content anchor, which raises attribute and structure accuracy by 12.8 to 44.4 points in the two models and keeps mean lexical accuracy within 1 point of the base model. Most of the improvement appears as larger recording gains. These results suggest that training improves the use of acoustic information that the models already encode.

AI.tldr: Shows that audio language models underuse acoustic information, measuring a recording gain across 92 tasks, and that LoRA adapters trained in early layers with a content anchor raise attribute and structure accuracy by 12.8 to 44.4 points.
AI.motivation: Audio language benchmarks can often be answered from the transcript or the question alone, so their scores confound acoustic understanding with language modeling ability.
AI.method: Lexical tasks are separated from global-attribute and within-recording-structure tasks. Nineteen open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro are evaluated on 92 tasks from 6 benchmarks, with recording gain estimated against synthetic readings of the transcript and against the transcript plus recording. Linear probes in Gemma-4 12B and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B locate where cues are readable, and LoRA adapters are then trained in those early layers with a content anchor.
AI.result: On attribute and structure tasks, open models trail Gemini by 28.6 and 41.9 percentage points, and about half or more of each deficit lies in recording gain. Probes show acoustic information is readable in early language-model layers while the readout of many cues declines in later layers. The LoRA training raises attribute and structure accuracy by 12.8 to 44.4 points in the two models and keeps mean lexical accuracy within 1 point of the base model, mostly through larger recording gains.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that training improves the use of acoustic information the models already encode.

title: Continuous modeling of manipulative participation for stance analysis: Online discourse on the 2024 Street Animal Law in Türkiye
comment: Submitted to Journal of Computational Social Science
summary: Studies of online political discourse commonly infer public opinion through stance analysis while implicitly assuming that observed user participation is authentic. Meanwhile, studies focusing on detecting manipulative participation are typically modeling it as a binary phenomenon, overlooking the varying degrees to which users may engage in coordinated or inauthentic behavior. This study proposes a continuous modeling approach for manipulative participation and examines its integration with stance analysis. Using online discourse on the 2024 Street Animal Law in Türkiye as a case study, we collected a dataset comprising 7,320,574 tweets from 537,994 users. From this corpus, 301 users were selected through a high-information sampling strategy and manually annotated by domain experts using a 10-criterion rubric that yields user-level continuous manipulative participation scores. Evaluation under a unified user-level cross-validation protocol showed that the proposed framework accurately estimates both manipulative participation and user stance, with gradient boosting methods providing the best manipulative participation estimates and BERTurk achieving the highest stance classification performance. External validation on an independently annotated user set demonstrated good generalization performance. The findings support modeling manipulative participation as a continuous construct rather than a binary label, providing a more informative basis for computational analyses of the relationship between manipulative participation and stance in online political discourse.

AI.tldr: Models manipulative participation as a continuous score from a 10-criterion rubric rather than a binary label, and integrates it with stance analysis of 7,320,574 tweets on Türkiye's 2024 Street Animal Law.
AI.motivation: Stance analysis of online discourse implicitly assumes that user participation is authentic, while manipulation detection typically treats manipulative participation as binary and ignores varying degrees of coordinated or inauthentic behavior.
AI.method: From tweets by 537,994 users, 301 users were chosen by high-information sampling and annotated by domain experts with a 10-criterion rubric yielding user-level continuous manipulative-participation scores. Models were evaluated under a unified user-level cross-validation protocol and on an independently annotated external user set.
AI.result: Gradient boosting methods give the best manipulative-participation estimates and BERTurk the highest stance classification performance, and external validation shows good generalization.
AI.conclusion: Manipulative participation is better treated as a continuous construct, which gives a more informative basis for analyzing its relation to stance in online political discourse.

title: Out of Parameters, Saved by Syntax: UD-PrMPT for Parser Augmented Low Resource Machine Translation
summary: Recent work advancing machine translation quality using LLMs for very low resource languages has relied on the injection of lexicon-based prompt components to expose vocabulary to models. However, these approaches run into a ceiling when models must guess sentence meaning purely from plausible combinations of possible word senses mapped to strings. In this paper we test UD-PrMPT, an approach using syntactic analyses in the Universal Dependencies formalism as prompt components to improve MT in five diverse low resource languages: Beja, Chintang, Chukchi, Coptic, and Xibe. Our results show additive improvements which stack on top of the lexicon based approach which are stronger for higher quality manual analyses but consistent for predicted parses as well.

AI.tldr: UD-PrMPT adds Universal Dependencies syntactic analyses to LLM prompts and improves machine translation for five low-resource languages (Beja, Chintang, Chukchi, Coptic and Xibe) on top of lexicon-based prompting.
AI.motivation: Lexicon-based prompt components reach a ceiling when models must guess sentence meaning from plausible combinations of word senses mapped to strings in very low-resource languages.
AI.method: Syntactic analyses in the Universal Dependencies formalism are used as prompt components to improve machine translation in five diverse low-resource languages, with manual and predicted parses compared.
AI.result: Syntactic prompting gives additive improvements that stack on top of the lexicon-based approach. The gains are stronger for higher-quality manual analyses and remain consistent for predicted parses.
AI.conclusion: Parser-augmented syntactic prompt components are a complementary route to better LLM-based machine translation for low-resource languages.

title: Perturbing Inputs Improves Pretraining Distillation
summary: Knowledge distillation trains a student language model to match a teacher's predictions on the training text. We ask whether learning the teacher's behavior beyond the training text can further improve the student. We investigate this using three input perturbations: additive token noise, blending two documents, and blending neighboring tokens. Specifically, for an early part of pretraining we perturb the inputs and train the student to match the teacher on them, and we spend the rest of the same token budget on ordinary distillation. When pretraining from scratch, the best method improves on standard distillation at both scales we tried, by 0.025 nats at 135M parameters and by 0.020 nats at 0.5B (mean of three seeds). At 135M this is 1.45 times the gain that distillation itself provides over next-token training. We also observe promising downstream transfer: at 0.5B, the best variant improves average zero-shot accuracy by about one percentage point across seven tasks. It also retains its validation-loss advantage after low-bit weight quantization. We also test a data-limited setting in which training data must be reused, and find that the gains persist. Finally, ablations suggest that, for additive noise, perturbing the teacher's inputs contributes most of the gain, while perturbing only the student's inputs yields much less.

AI.tldr: Perturbing inputs during an early phase of pretraining improves distillation, giving 0.025 nats over standard distillation at 135M parameters and 0.020 nats at 0.5B, with about one point of zero-shot gain at 0.5B.
AI.motivation: Knowledge distillation trains a student to match a teacher's predictions only on the training text, and the authors ask whether learning the teacher's behavior beyond that text can further improve the student.
AI.method: Three input perturbations are tested: additive token noise, blending two documents, and blending neighboring tokens. In an early part of pretraining the student is trained to match the teacher on perturbed inputs, and the rest of the same token budget goes to ordinary distillation.
AI.result: The best method improves on standard distillation by 0.025 nats at 135M and 0.020 nats at 0.5B (mean of three seeds); at 135M this is 1.45 times the gain distillation gives over next-token training. At 0.5B average zero-shot accuracy improves by about one percentage point across seven tasks. The validation-loss advantage survives low-bit weight quantization, and the gains persist when training data must be reused. For additive noise, perturbing the teacher's inputs contributes most of the gain.
AI.conclusion: Input perturbation during early distillation gives the student a consistent, if modest, improvement over standard distillation at the two scales tested.

title: The Average Patient: Do Simulated Psychiatric Patients Answer Like Real People?
summary: Language models are used as simulated psychiatric patients to train clinicians and evaluate AI therapists, and are judged by plausibility or total scores. We give a framework for simulated respondents: an information budget bounds how much simulated patients can differ, and an average-patient hypothesis, that a model answers each item at the level typical of the named condition and severity, implies little variation, a full profile of the condition's typical symptoms and totals at or above the top of the stated severity band. We examine these implications at matched totals on item-level data from eight human samples, including a clinical and an instructed-feigning sample. Across 17 models, simulated patients vary 1.5 to 11 times less than real respondents with the same total and on most questionnaires endorse nearly every symptom at a middling level; on the PHQ-9 their symptoms covary less like real ones. People, honest or feigning, answer "not at all" about as often as genuine patients with the same totals, and more often than every model. Single answers are highly concentrated, and prompt changes, published personas, larger models and reasoning reduce the pattern without removing it. In interviews, patients told a severity are rated as having nearly every symptom, so an assessment agent's recognition of absent symptoms goes untested, and scored against the stated severity the agent places a quarter of them in their band, against about half of patients given a real symptom profile. Having the model word such a profile restores half to two thirds of the variation.

AI.tldr: Shows that language models simulating psychiatric patients answer questionnaires with far less variation than real respondents, endorsing nearly every symptom at a middling level, so they do not behave like realistic simulated patients.
AI.motivation: Language models are used as simulated psychiatric patients to train clinicians and evaluate AI therapists, but they are typically judged only by plausibility or total scores.
AI.method: A framework in which an information budget bounds how much simulated patients can differ, and an average-patient hypothesis predicts little variation and full symptom profiles at totals at or above the stated severity band. It is examined at matched totals on item-level data from eight human samples, including a clinical and an instructed-feigning sample, and 17 models.
AI.result: Simulated patients vary 1.5 to 11 times less than real respondents with the same total, and on most questionnaires endorse nearly every symptom at a middling level; on the PHQ-9 their symptoms covary less like real ones. People answer "not at all" about as often as genuine patients with the same totals, and more often than every model. Prompt changes, published personas, larger models and reasoning reduce the pattern without removing it. When told a severity, simulated patients are rated as having nearly every symptom, and an assessment agent places a quarter of them in the stated band, against about half of patients given a real symptom profile. Having the model word such a profile restores half to two thirds of the variation.
AI.conclusion: Simulated respondents must be checked against the variation and symptom structure of real people, since current models fail that test, and an assessment agent's recognition of absent symptoms goes untested with them.

title: Language model capabilities fail in a shared, predictable order under compression and perturbation
comment: 45 pages (34 main text with Methods and Extended Data, 11 Supplementary Information), 4 figures, 6 Extended Data figures. Code, protocols and data: this https URL ; interactive summary: this https URL
summary: Compression can preserve a language model's average accuracy while selectively degrading individual capabilities. Whether these losses follow method-specific patterns or a transferable order is unclear. We applied seven perturbation and compression methods to eight instruction-tuned models, scoring 16 tasks in four answer formats against preregistered predictions. Short-answer capabilities failed in nearly the same order under four random perturbations with different mechanisms (median correlation 0.90) and, within each model, under pruning and quantization (0.875). Intact answer margin, answer frequency and answer format predicted this order. Fragility profiles measured under random perturbation predicted which tasks and facts compression removes first and, after four-task calibration, held-out task accuracy (median absolute error 0.11-0.12, against 0.20-0.21 for uniform decline); profiles borrowed from other model families did almost as well. The order did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization or hold for long-form tasks. Within short answers, what compression removes is predictable before deployment.

AI.tldr: Shows that compression and perturbation remove short-answer capabilities of instruction-tuned models in a largely shared, predictable order, which can be estimated from fragility profiles measured before deployment.
AI.motivation: Compression can preserve average accuracy while selectively degrading individual capabilities, and it is unclear whether these losses follow method-specific patterns or a transferable order.
AI.method: Seven perturbation and compression methods are applied to eight instruction-tuned models, and 16 tasks in four answer formats are scored against preregistered predictions. Intact answer margin, answer frequency and answer format are tested as predictors of the order, and fragility profiles measured under random perturbation are calibrated on four tasks to predict held-out task accuracy.
AI.result: Short-answer capabilities fail in nearly the same order under four random perturbations with different mechanisms (median correlation 0.90) and, within each model, under pruning and quantization (0.875). Fragility profiles predict held-out task accuracy after four-task calibration with median absolute error 0.11 to 0.12, against 0.20 to 0.21 for uniform decline, and profiles borrowed from other model families do almost as well. The order does not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization and does not hold for long-form tasks.
AI.conclusion: Within short answers, what compression removes is predictable before deployment, though the order does not transfer across models under GPTQ and does not extend to long-form tasks.

title: Explaining and interrupting collective misalignment in language model systems
summary: In collectives, language model agents can exchange individually innocuous messages that together support a policy violation. Understanding and preventing collective misalignment requires answering the question of which messages sufficiently influenced and necessarily enabled the violation. Collective Dependence Analysis (CDA) operationalises necessity and sufficiency to explain decisions and find the fewest removals interrupting support within tested combinations. Tests covered constructed violations, unscripted agent conversations, and recorded interactions, with selected message removals reducing violations from 93% to 6% in controlled cases. Using O(N) model evaluations for N messages, CDA achieves the same violation reduction with half the deletions of a frontier LLM judge given the transcript and asked for all supporting messages in eligible operational cases. CDA also proposes the mechanism through which the collective misalignment emerged. Nonetheless, complete explanations remain difficult on unfamiliar tasks and some removals can inadvertently disrupt correct decisions. CDA unifies explanations of collective misalignment with experimentally tested interventions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Collective Dependence Analysis (CDA), which finds the fewest message removals that interrupt the support for a policy violation among language model agents, and shows that removing selected messages cuts violations from 93% to 6% in controlled cases.
AI.motivation: Language model agents in collectives can exchange individually innocuous messages that together enable a policy violation, and understanding or preventing this collective misalignment requires knowing which messages were sufficient and necessary for it.
AI.method: CDA operationalises necessity and sufficiency of messages to explain decisions, using O(N) model evaluations for N messages to find the fewest removals that interrupt support within the tested combinations, and it also proposes the mechanism by which the misalignment emerged.
AI.result: On constructed violations, unscripted agent conversations and recorded interactions, selected removals reduce violations from 93% to 6% in controlled cases; CDA matches this reduction with half the deletions of a frontier LLM judge given the transcript in eligible operational cases, though complete explanations remain hard on unfamiliar tasks and some removals can disrupt correct decisions.
AI.conclusion: CDA unifies explanations of collective misalignment with experimentally tested interventions, offering a practical way to explain and interrupt such violations, with its limits on unfamiliar tasks acknowledged.

title: BridgeKV: Large-Model Prefill and Small-Model Decoding for LLM Inference via KV Cache Translation
summary: LLM inference has two phases with different bottlenecks: LLM prefill runs once per request and is compute-intensive. Decoding repeats for every output token and is limited by memory bandwidth. To address the challenges associated with this issue, different solutions have been proposed. All of these solutions use the same model for both prefill and decode phases. We propose BridgeKV, which uses a larger model for prefill and a smaller model of the same family for decoding. A lightweight KV-stitching module translates the larger model's prompt cache into the smaller model's cache layout. It handles differences in cache shape and representation through learned local layer mixing and separate nonlinear maps for keys and values. With both models frozen, we train the module to align their caches and make the smaller model follow the larger model's next-token predictions. A second training stage adds low-rank adapters when further task adaptation is needed. Across six model pairs and five datasets, BridgeKV outperforms fine-tuned small-model baselines with matched trainable parameter budgets in all 30 settings. It closes up to 80% of the quality gap to using the larger model for both phases. On one A40 GPU, Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B achieves 3.0X faster requests than the larger model alone, with latency close to the smaller model alone. BridgeKV can improve the hardware and system solutions that separate prefill and decode phases across GPUs. A separate serving simulation models request arrivals, queues, and cache transfer. For Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B, it predicts up to 33.86X faster requests and 27.5X lower energy use than using the larger model for both prefill and decode phases.

AI.tldr: BridgeKV speeds up LLM inference by running a larger model for prefill and a smaller model of the same family for decoding, connected by a lightweight KV-stitching module that translates the large model's prompt cache into the small model's cache layout.
AI.motivation: Prefill is compute-intensive and decoding is memory-bandwidth-limited, yet existing acceleration solutions use the same model for both phases, so they cannot exploit a larger model's prefill quality together with a smaller model's cheap decoding.
AI.method: With both models frozen, a KV-stitching module with learned local layer mixing and separate nonlinear maps for keys and values is trained to align the two caches and make the smaller model follow the larger model's next-token predictions; a second stage adds low-rank adapters for task adaptation when needed.
AI.result: Across six model pairs and five datasets, BridgeKV beats fine-tuned small-model baselines with matched trainable parameter budgets in all 30 settings and closes up to 80% of the quality gap to the larger model; on one A40 GPU, Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B is 3.0X faster than the larger model alone, and a serving simulation predicts up to 33.86X faster requests and 27.5X lower energy for Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B.
AI.conclusion: BridgeKV shows that cache translation between models of one family can capture much of the benefit of a large model at near small-model latency, and it can improve systems that split prefill and decode across GPUs.

title: ChemInsight: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating and Diagnosing Chemistry Understanding and Reasoning in Large Language Models
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures. Changyu Hu, Yiming Zou, and Xin Tang contributed equally. Corresponding authors: Zhenduo Zhang, Wang Ren, and Xiao Li
summary: We introduce ChemInsight, a benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on chemistry tasks that require multi-step reasoning and structured chemical understanding. We propose a two-dimensional scoring system (scope and depth) to assess both task coverage and reasoning completeness. ChemInsight consists of 203 challenging chemistry questions organized into 50 bundles, which support the two-dimensional scoring evaluation scheme. We evaluate ten representative LLMs using ChemInsight and observe consistently low performance across models, with scope scores below 30% and depth scores below 11%, substantially lower than human expert performance. We then proceed to ask (1) What factor limits the advancement of current LLMs in chemistry? (2) To what extent are statistically driven language-model training methods effective at modeling chemistry symbolic language such as SMILES? And (3) Can LLM performance in chemistry be improved through intensive training on large, domain-specific corpora?

AI.tldr: ChemInsight is a benchmark of 203 chemistry questions in 50 bundles that scores LLMs on scope and depth of multi-step chemical reasoning, and finds consistently low performance across ten evaluated LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations do not adequately measure whether LLMs can handle chemistry tasks requiring multi-step reasoning and structured chemical understanding, nor how complete their reasoning is.
AI.method: The authors introduce a two-dimensional scoring system, scope for task coverage and depth for reasoning completeness, applied to 203 challenging questions organised into 50 bundles that support this scheme.
AI.result: Ten representative LLMs score below 30% on scope and below 11% on depth, substantially lower than human expert performance, and the paper examines what limits progress, how well statistical language-model training handles SMILES, and whether intensive training on domain corpora helps.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate that current LLMs remain far from expert-level chemistry reasoning, and the benchmark and two-dimensional scoring provide a diagnostic tool for identifying where they fail.

title: HiddenPathQA: A Benchmark for Knowledge Graph Question Answering When Questions Hide Their Paths
summary: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) systems are typically evaluated on questions whose surface tokens lexically expose the gold KG path. Users, however, may ask questions without knowing the underlying schema: "Which condition could Andrew have due to family history?" compresses a 4-hop chain "Andrew --[father]--> parent --[father]--> grandparent --[medical condition]--> disease --[subclass of]--> hereditary disorder" into a single phrase (family history) that names none of those relations. We identify this collapse of path-question alignment as a blind spot in existing KGQA evaluation. Three major LLM-KG paradigms, hop-by-hop exploration, plan-then-retrieve, and similarity-based retrieval, implicitly rely on such lexical cues, an assumption rarely tested in practice. We make three contributions. (i) We introduce HiddenPathQA, a manually verified benchmark of 1,055 questions spanning 2-6 hops and multiple domains, constructed so that question wording does not reveal the gold path's relations. (ii) We propose Holistic Path Selection, which compares questions against candidate relation chains in the local subgraph as complete units, replacing irreversible per-hop relation scoring with globally informed chain-level reasoning. We develop two implementations, TieredHolistic and FlatHolistic. (iii) We conduct a pseudoword stress test that replaces entity names with meaningless placeholders to distinguish KG-grounded reasoning from entity-level memorization. Holistic Path Selection outperforms six strong KGQA baselines (ToG, PoG, FiDeLiS, R2-KG, KAPING, and KARPA) by 8.8-17.9 accuracy points across two LLM backbones and both original and pseudoword settings. Its advantage under pseudoword replacement shows that the gains cannot be explained by entity-level memorization alone.

AI.tldr: HiddenPathQA is a benchmark of 1,055 knowledge graph questions whose wording does not reveal the gold path, and Holistic Path Selection, which scores whole candidate relation chains, outperforms six KGQA baselines by 8.8 to 17.9 accuracy points.
AI.motivation: Existing KGQA evaluations use questions whose surface words expose the gold KG path, a lexical cue that paradigms such as hop-by-hop exploration, plan-then-retrieve and similarity-based retrieval implicitly rely on, so their performance on realistic questions is untested.
AI.method: The authors build HiddenPathQA with manually verified questions spanning 2 to 6 hops, propose Holistic Path Selection in TieredHolistic and FlatHolistic implementations that compares questions with candidate relation chains as complete units, and run a pseudoword stress test that replaces entity names with placeholders.
AI.result: Holistic Path Selection outperforms ToG, PoG, FiDeLiS, R2-KG, KAPING and KARPA by 8.8 to 17.9 accuracy points across two LLM backbones and both original and pseudoword settings, and its advantage under pseudoword replacement suggests the gains are not due to entity memorisation alone.
AI.conclusion: Path-question alignment is a blind spot in KGQA evaluation, and chain-level, globally informed path selection is a more robust way to ground LLM answers in knowledge graphs than per-hop relation scoring.

title: CaseLaw: A Policy-Decoupled Framework for Training-Free Content Moderation
summary: Content moderation is inherently policy-dependent: moderation boundaries are often subtle, subjective, and frequently updated, while conventional rule based or fine-tuning based systems require costly rule rewriting, model retraining, or system redeployment. We propose CaseLaw, a policy-decoupled and training-free framework for adaptive content moderation. CaseLaw reformulates moderation as precedent-based retrieval and voting, where multimodal content is transformed into evidence-preserved structured semantics, embedded into a stable semantic space, and classified by thresholded voting over retrieved precedent labels. We train NoteCap on a large-scale corpus of structurally annotated notes to ensure consistent semantic extraction and freeze it during subsequent policy adaptation, which requires no additional training. Policy adaptation is achieved by updating the semantic case library, including case labels and mappings, without retraining models or modifying prompts. To evaluate CaseLaw, we construct MFO-RedNotes, a benchmark for the male-female opposition risk domain. We additionally provide a five category CoPro comparison. Experiments show that CaseLaw consistently outperforms competing baselines in both precision and recall across policy-dependent risk levels and broader safety categories, with category-wise precision/recall reaching up to 86.8%/90.1% on MFO-RedNotes across both policy settings and 94.5%/92.3% on CoPro. Our work highlights the potential of precedent-based reasoning for policy adaptive content moderation and offers a practical direction toward more stable, transparent, and training-free moderation systems.

AI.tldr: CaseLaw is a training-free content moderation framework that classifies content by thresholded voting over retrieved precedent labels in a semantic case library, so policy changes require only updating that library rather than retraining or redeploying.
AI.motivation: Content moderation boundaries are subtle, subjective and frequently updated, while rule-based or fine-tuned systems need costly rule rewriting, retraining or redeployment whenever the policy changes.
AI.method: Multimodal content is converted into evidence-preserved structured semantics by NoteCap, a model trained on structurally annotated notes and frozen afterwards, embedded in a stable semantic space, and classified by thresholded voting over retrieved precedent labels; policy adaptation updates case labels and mappings without touching models or prompts.
AI.result: CaseLaw outperforms competing baselines in precision and recall across policy-dependent risk levels and broader safety categories, reaching up to 86.8% precision and 90.1% recall on the authors' MFO-RedNotes benchmark across both policy settings and 94.5% precision and 92.3% recall on CoPro.
AI.conclusion: Precedent-based reasoning offers a practical route to policy-adaptive moderation that is stable, transparent and training-free, although the evaluation is limited to the authors' benchmarks and the male-female opposition risk domain.

title: Improving Confidence Estimation in Language Models with Linear Representations of Ambiguity
summary: As language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed in downstream applications, accurately estimating their likelihood of success on a given example is critical. However, confidence estimates from LMs are poor predictors of their likelihood of success. Accurate confidence estimation is linked in part to the detection of aleatoric uncertainty; we hypothesize that LMs possess representations of at least some aspects of this uncertainty in the form of representations of the inherent ambiguity of the input. Using difference-in-means on minimal pairs of ambiguous and unambiguous sentences, we derive ambiguity representations in LM activations, and find that steering with them selectively (albeit weakly) modulates LMs' judgments of the input's ambiguity. We then propose DART, a fine-tuning method that encourages updates to lie within the span of the ambiguity directions, and penalizes changes to the LM activations outside of this subspace. DART greatly improves calibration, encodes these improvements into the model parameters, and maintains model accuracy on multiple-choice and generative QA tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper finds linear ambiguity representations in LM activations and proposes DART, a fine-tuning method that constrains updates to the span of these directions, which greatly improves calibration while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Confidence estimates from language models are poor predictors of their success, and accurate confidence may depend on detecting aleatoric uncertainty, which the authors hypothesise LMs represent as the inherent ambiguity of an input.
AI.method: Difference-in-means on minimal pairs of ambiguous and unambiguous sentences yields ambiguity directions in LM activations, and DART is a fine-tuning method that encourages updates within the span of these directions while penalising changes to activations outside that subspace.
AI.result: Steering with the ambiguity representations selectively but weakly modulates LM judgments of input ambiguity, and DART greatly improves calibration, encodes the improvement into model parameters, and maintains accuracy on multiple-choice and generative QA tasks.
AI.conclusion: Language models contain usable representations of input ambiguity, and constraining fine-tuning to them is a way to improve calibration without sacrificing accuracy, although the steering effect is described as weak.

title: A Large-Scale Dataset for Cross-Lingual Multi-Jurisdiction Patent Drafting from Patent Cooperation Treaty Applications
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Accepted to INLG 2026
summary: Securing patent protection across countries requires drafting claims separately for each national patent office, in the relevant language and according to its legal and stylistic conventions. Patent claims can therefore differ across languages and jurisdictions because of translation, target-office drafting practices, and prosecution-stage changes. We formulate cross-lingual patent drafting as generating plausible candidate claim sets for a specified target language, jurisdiction, and prosecution stage from a source claim set in another language. The task models jurisdiction- and stage-specific transformations beyond content-preserving translation. We construct a large-scale Japanese-English dataset by linking Japan Patent Office (JPO) and United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) records through 884,179 Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT)-derived patent families. Across six released configurations, these families yield 4,067,168 directional claim-set instances; four core configurations form the main benchmark. Commercial machine translation and zero- and few-shot prompting capture part of the task, while supervised adaptation provides the strongest overall baseline, showing that task-specific patterns can be learned from linked cross-jurisdictional claim sets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces cross-lingual, multi-jurisdiction patent claim drafting as a task and releases a Japanese-English dataset of 884,179 PCT-derived patent families yielding over four million directional claim-set instances.
AI.motivation: Patent claims must be drafted separately for each national office in its language and conventions, and they differ across languages because of translation, office practice and prosecution changes, which content-preserving translation does not capture.
AI.method: The authors link Japan Patent Office and USPTO records through PCT-derived families to build the dataset, and formulate the task as generating plausible candidate claim sets for a target language, jurisdiction and prosecution stage from a source claim set in another language.
