AI.result: Across six released configurations the families yield 4,067,168 directional claim-set instances, with four core configurations forming the main benchmark; commercial machine translation and zero- and few-shot prompting capture part of the task, while supervised adaptation gives the strongest overall baseline.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific patterns in linked cross-jurisdictional claim sets can be learned, so the dataset provides a resource for jurisdiction- and stage-aware patent drafting beyond translation.

title: ShopMind: A Mental World Model for Personalized and Realistic E-commerce User Simulation
summary: Large language models are widely used in e-commerce user simulation, providing a foundation for understanding users and predicting human decisions. However, existing simulators still struggle to achieve both personalization and behavioral realism. Most methods predict the next action directly from interaction histories and the current context, without accounting for the evolving mental world that underlies user behavior. Theory of Mind suggests that behavior is driven by mental states, including beliefs, uncertainties, and intentions. Users may interpret the same information in distinct ways, leading to divergent behaviors, while an individual's mental state evolves through interaction and shapes subsequent actions. Ignoring this process prevents simulators from faithfully capturing individual differences and realistic behavior patterns, and undermines its effectiveness in downstream applications. To address this, we propose ShopMind, a Mental World Model for e-commerce user simulation that captures how consumers interpret shopping information and how their mental states evolve, better reflecting individual users and real-world behavior patterns. We further use behavior-mental state pairs synthesized by ShopMind to train a Mental State Reconstruction (MSR) model, which infers consumers' latent mental states from observable behavior. Experiments show that ShopMind improves personalization by 18.0% and behavioral realism by 19.6% over the strongest alternatives. Moreover, MSR improves performance on consumption value measurement and CTR prediction, showing the utility of ShopMind for understanding and predicting real user behavior.

AI.tldr: ShopMind is a mental world model for e-commerce user simulation that models how shoppers interpret information and how their mental states evolve, and it improves personalisation by 18.0% and behavioural realism by 19.6% over the strongest alternatives.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based e-commerce simulators predict the next action directly from interaction history and context, ignoring the evolving beliefs, uncertainties and intentions that drive individual and divergent user behaviour.
AI.method: ShopMind captures how consumers interpret shopping information and how their mental states change, and its synthesised behaviour-mental state pairs train a Mental State Reconstruction (MSR) model that infers latent mental states from observable behaviour.
AI.result: ShopMind improves personalisation by 18.0% and behavioural realism by 19.6% over the strongest alternatives, and MSR improves consumption value measurement and CTR prediction.
AI.conclusion: Modelling latent mental states gives simulators better fidelity to individual users and makes them more useful for downstream tasks such as understanding and predicting real user behaviour.

title: Adaptive Entropy-Sparing for Efficient Reasoning
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) produce explicit chains of thought to improve transparency, but they frequently overthink, generating long yet inefficient reasoning chains that inflate computational costs and risk introducing errors. While numerous reinforcement learning methods struggle to penalize verbosity to achieve conciseness, they typically apply the penalty uniformly across lengthy sequences, which leads to credit confounding, that is, the failure to distinguish essential reasoning steps from superfluous ones. In this paper, we study a measurable proxy for this confounding: high-entropy tokens that often coincide with surface transition points where reasoning re-enters verification. Based on this insight, we propose Adaptive Entropy-Sparing (AES), which selectively spares high-entropy tokens that occur before an efficient in-group reference, while penalizing overlength high-entropy suffix tokens associated with superfluous branching. Our AES thereby navigates the suppression-exploration trade-off, reducing overthinking while preserving average reasoning accuracy. We also present an entropy-length model that motivates why local uncertainty can serve as a proxy for future reasoning cost. Across eight reasoning benchmarks, AES reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% while increasing mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over the base models, consistently outperforming existing efficiency-oriented methods. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Entropy-Sparing (AES) reduces overthinking in large reasoning models by sparing high-entropy tokens before an efficient reference and penalising overlength high-entropy suffix tokens, cutting reasoning length by up to 52.9% while raising mean accuracy by up to 3.8%.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning penalties for verbosity apply uniformly across long reasoning chains and confound essential reasoning steps with superfluous ones, and high-entropy tokens at transition points into verification serve as a measurable proxy for this confounding.
AI.method: AES selectively spares high-entropy tokens that occur before an efficient in-group reference and penalises overlength high-entropy suffix tokens linked to superfluous branching, and an entropy-length model motivates using local uncertainty as a proxy for future reasoning cost.
AI.result: Across eight reasoning benchmarks AES reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% while increasing mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over the base models, consistently outperforming existing efficiency-oriented methods.
AI.conclusion: Targeting credit assignment at high-entropy tokens navigates the suppression-exploration trade-off, so conciseness can be gained without sacrificing average reasoning accuracy.

title: BharatSynthQA: A Context-Grounded Question Answering Dataset on Indian Temples and Religious Heritage
summary: India's temples and other places of worship are among its richest repositories of cultural heritage, bringing together religious tradition, history, architecture, and art. Due to the widespread curiosity, people increasingly turn to Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistants for information about them. Current models are rarely trained or evaluated on this domain. We present BharatSynthQA, a passage grounded question answering (QA) dataset focused on Indian temples, which also covers other religious sites connected to them. Our pipeline crawls Wikipedia from topics seeded by authentic heritage sources, filters articles for topical relevance, and locations in India. Further it generates Boolean, factoid, and explanatory QA pairs with a fewshot prompted LLM. An LLM judge filters the pairs on answer correctness, retaining 98,677 of 131,494 generated pairs. Additionally, 300 human-annotated pairs are released separately as a reference set. Human evaluation of the subsample of this dataset showed 89.83% of the questions were formed correctly. Benchmarking five current LLMs shows that factoid token F1 is only 0.18-0.30 without the source passage but 0.73-0.77 with it, indicating that this domain is poorly captured in model knowledge. The dataset is available at this https URL to support research on culturally grounded QA and retrieval-augmented generation for Indian heritage.

AI.tldr: BharatSynthQA is a passage-grounded question answering dataset on Indian temples and related religious sites, generated from Wikipedia and filtered by an LLM judge to 98,677 pairs, with a 300-pair human-annotated reference set.
AI.motivation: AI assistants are increasingly asked about Indian temples and religious heritage, but current models are rarely trained or evaluated on this domain.
AI.method: The pipeline crawls Wikipedia from seeded heritage topics, filters articles for topical relevance and location in India, generates Boolean, factoid and explanatory QA pairs with a few-shot prompted LLM, and keeps pairs that an LLM judge verifies for answer correctness.
AI.result: The judge retains 98,677 of 131,494 generated pairs, human evaluation finds 89.83% of the questions well formed, and factoid token F1 for five LLMs is only 0.18 to 0.30 without the source passage but 0.73 to 0.77 with it.
AI.conclusion: The domain is poorly captured in model knowledge but well handled when the source passage is supplied, which supports the dataset for culturally grounded QA and retrieval-augmented generation for Indian heritage.

title: When Audio and Video Mislead: Evaluating Multimodal AI for Conversational Emotion Recognition
comment: 40 pages, 3 figures, 24 tables. Full version with appendices of a paper accepted at AICompS 2026 (Springer CCIS). Code and data: this https URL
summary: Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation (MERC) combines lexical, acoustic, visual and conversational cues, but accepting audio and video does not establish their effective or robust use. We audit off-the-shelf Omni models while holding the target transcript and prior textual context fixed and adding, removing or replacing target audio and video. In the primary evaluation of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Baichuan-Omni-1.5 and MiniCPM-o 2.6 on MELD and the full five-session six-class IEMOCAP set, T+A improves Accuracy in all six model-dataset pairs, with four gains significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Across three source mappings, unrelated A/V (RandA/V) lowers Accuracy relative to Full in all 18 comparisons; all 18 remain significant under dialogue-cluster inference and BH-FDR correction, both on common-valid pairs and when invalid/OOM outcomes are treated as incorrect. Comparisons with modality-omission baselines further distinguish replacement penalties from mismatch-specific harm. A Qwen/MELD case study finds significantly greater gold-vs-best-candidate margin recovery in Late than Early or Middle under decision-query audio knockout, relative to an edge-count-matched Video-Sham control, using Holm-corrected tests. These results distinguish genuine-modality benefit from sensitivity and vulnerability to misleading input.

AI.tldr: The paper audits off-the-shelf Omni models on multimodal emotion recognition in conversation and finds that audio and video can help or mislead, with unrelated audio-visual input lowering accuracy in all 18 comparisons.
AI.motivation: Accepting audio and video does not guarantee that models use them effectively or robustly, so it is unclear whether multimodal emotion recognition genuinely benefits from acoustic and visual cues.
AI.method: With the target transcript and prior text context held fixed, the authors add, remove or replace target audio and video for Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Baichuan-Omni-1.5 and MiniCPM-o 2.6 on MELD and the five-session six-class IEMOCAP set, comparing against unrelated audio-visual input and modality-omission baselines.
AI.result: Adding audio and video improves accuracy in all six model-dataset pairs, with four gains significant after FDR correction, and unrelated audio-visual input lowers accuracy relative to Full in all 18 comparisons, all significant under dialogue-cluster inference and BH-FDR correction; a Qwen/MELD case study finds greater gold-versus-best-candidate margin recovery in Late fusion than Early or Middle under audio knockout.
AI.conclusion: The results separate genuine benefit from modality use from sensitivity to misleading input, showing that multimodal emotion models can be vulnerable to mismatched audio and video.

title: EmoHarness: Boosting Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Meta-Harness Evolving
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Project page: this https URL. Code: this https URL
summary: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.

AI.tldr: EmoHarness boosts a small frozen multimodal student model on emotion recognition by wrapping it in an evolving harness of prompts, settings and verification code, raising task-macro Recognition by 7.6 to 13.4 points over a video-only call.
AI.motivation: Small multimodal models misjudge emotion when words, voice and visual cues conflict, and the authors ask whether the surrounding prompts and verification code can help them weigh these cues.
AI.method: A human-written scaffold numbers visual observations, transcript and prosody descriptions as citable evidence, and in Meta-Harness Evolving a stronger Builder LLM reads errors and traces offline and edits the harness, with static checks and validation gates deciding which edits are kept and the Builder never seeing evaluation items.
AI.result: On 5,507 MME-Emotion items EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6 to 13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders; transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of the boost (+5.38 to +10.71), evolved edits add at most +0.95, and no evolved increment survives Holm correction.
AI.conclusion: EmoHarness mainly helps small multimodal students by supplying and organising audio-derived evidence rather than through the evolved edits, and its emotion context transfers to IntentQA only with small, uncorrected gains.

title: Robust Domain-Mixture Scheduling for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) merges the capabilities of multiple domain-expert teachers, such as mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, into a single compact student. Since all domains share a limited training budget, how to allocate it across domains directly determines the quality of distillation. Existing methods allocate the budget by each domain's learning progress, but offer no guarantee for lagging domains. We therefore introduce distributionally robust optimization (DRO) into MOPD to prioritize the worst-performing domain. However, the per-domain training signals are estimated from a few rollouts and are inherently noisy, so directly applying DRO mistakes noise for the worst case, lets occasional spikes hijack the budget, and protects inherently hard domains rather than truly regressing ones. To address these issues, we propose RDS-MOPD, which keeps the DRO objective and redesigns its three parts: it shifts the allocation only when differences clearly exceed the noise, bounds the influence of any single anomaly, and defines the worst case as the regression from each domain's own best level, all with theoretical guarantees. Experiments show that RDS-MOPD outperforms recent competing methods and ranks first on most mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks.

AI.tldr: RDS-MOPD applies distributionally robust optimisation to budget allocation in multi-teacher on-policy distillation, redesigning the worst-case objective to tolerate noisy per-domain signals, and ranks first on most math, code and instruction-following benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation must split a limited training budget across domains, and existing progress-based allocation gives no guarantee for lagging domains, while naive DRO is misled by noisy few-rollout estimates, letting spikes hijack the budget and protecting hard domains instead of regressing ones.
AI.method: RDS-MOPD keeps the DRO objective but shifts allocation only when differences clearly exceed noise, bounds the influence of any single anomaly, and defines the worst case as regression from each domain's own best level, with theoretical guarantees.
AI.result: RDS-MOPD outperforms recent competing methods and ranks first on most mathematical reasoning, code generation and instruction-following benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Robust, noise-aware worst-case allocation is a practical way to protect lagging domains in multi-teacher distillation without being misled by noise or hard domains.

title: A generalized transition framework for identifying reduction domains in non-binary constituency parsing
summary: Direct non-binary constituency parsing must identify an ordered sequence of children at each phrase-level reduction. We extend our earlier delimiter-guided bottom-up construction to a common calculus for top-down, in-order, and bottom-up parsing. At reduction, the rightmost delimiter marks the left boundary, the nonterminal marker supplies the mother label, and the completed items in the delimited segment determine the children and arity. We use a stack invariant to prove soundness and completeness and derive the exact length of the static oracle's action sequence. A projection-and-lifting theorem shows that each delimiter-guided system and its canonical counterpart generate the same set of trees under both the structural and grammar-licensed transition relations. In controlled experiments on PTB and CTB, the delimiter-guided parsers achieve similar labeled accuracy to their canonical counterparts across all traversal orders. For bottom-up parsing, delimiter guidance reduces the number of action classes and increases the number of supervised decisions per tree.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a common transition calculus for top-down, in-order and bottom-up non-binary constituency parsing, with delimiter guidance that yields the same trees as canonical systems and reduces the action classes in bottom-up parsing.
AI.motivation: Direct non-binary constituency parsing must identify an ordered sequence of children at each phrase-level reduction, and the authors aim to extend their earlier delimiter-guided bottom-up construction to all traversal orders with a single formal account.
AI.method: At reduction the rightmost delimiter marks the left boundary, the nonterminal marker gives the mother label and the completed items in the delimited segment determine children and arity; a stack invariant proves soundness and completeness, the exact length of the static oracle's action sequence is derived, and a projection-and-lifting theorem links delimiter-guided and canonical systems.
AI.result: On PTB and CTB the delimiter-guided parsers achieve labeled accuracy similar to their canonical counterparts across all traversal orders, and for bottom-up parsing delimiter guidance reduces the number of action classes and increases the number of supervised decisions per tree.
AI.conclusion: Delimiter guidance preserves the generated trees and accuracy while changing the action inventory, offering a unified and provably correct framework for non-binary parsing across traversal orders.

title: SMO: Compiling Natural Language Skills into Graphs of Reusable State-Move-Outcome Bricks
summary: Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable natural-language skills, yet growing skill collections remain accumulations of isolated text artifacts that are difficult to compare, deduplicate, and compose. We argue that the reusable content of a skill lies not in its surface wording but in its procedural transitions: which operation to execute under a given state and which observable outcome to produce. Based on this observation, we propose State-Move-Outcome (SMO), a compilation-like framework that decomposes raw skills into reusable procedural bricks and organizes admitted bricks as an externalized symbolic structure. When compiling a skill, SMO first retrieves and composes existing bricks, dynamically connects them through Outcome-to-State conditions, and creates a candidate brick only for an uncovered procedure; the candidate becomes reusable only after validation and admission. Experiments on SkillsBench v1.1 demonstrate that SMO represents 232 rawSkills from 87 underlying tasks with 95 shared bricks, reducing the corresponding skill representations from 366,472 to 149,154 tokens--a $\mathbf{59.3}\times$ reduction and $\mathbf{2.46}\times$ compression. Across 232 skill-conditioned evaluation instances, SMO raises the average task score from $\mathbf{0.6379}$ to $\mathbf{0.7478}$ and increases 5/5 Pass instances from $\mathbf{138}$ to $\mathbf{164}$, while matching or outperforming rawSkill on $\mathbf{208}$ of $\mathbf{232}$ instances. It also reduces average runtime token consumption by $\mathbf{38.38\%}$. These results show that compiling natural-language skills into shared procedural units can jointly improve skill reuse, representation efficiency, and downstream execution.

AI.tldr: State-Move-Outcome (SMO) compiles natural-language skills into shared, reusable procedural bricks, reducing skill representations from 366,472 to 149,154 tokens while raising average task score from 0.6379 to 0.7478 on SkillsBench v1.1.
AI.motivation: Growing collections of LLM agent skills are isolated text artifacts that are hard to compare, deduplicate and compose, although their reusable content lies in procedural transitions between states, operations and outcomes rather than in wording.
AI.method: SMO decomposes raw skills into procedural bricks and organises admitted bricks as an externalised symbolic structure; when compiling a skill it retrieves and composes existing bricks, connects them through Outcome-to-State conditions, and creates a candidate brick only for an uncovered procedure, admitting it after validation.
AI.result: On SkillsBench v1.1, SMO represents 232 raw skills from 87 tasks with 95 shared bricks, a 59.3x reduction in representation tokens and 2.46x compression; across 232 evaluation instances it raises average task score from 0.6379 to 0.7478, increases 5/5 Pass instances from 138 to 164, matches or outperforms the raw skill on 208 of 232 instances, and cuts average runtime token consumption by 38.38%.
AI.conclusion: Compiling natural-language skills into shared procedural units can jointly improve skill reuse, representation efficiency and downstream execution.

title: MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System
comment: Code available at this https URL
summary: Long-term memory lets LLM agents personalize, stay consistent, and reuse what worked before. Parametric memories need training, consolidation can lose details for good, and keeping every record leaves a growing store to search. We present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks. It reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, where it leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points, and with AutoDream disabled it gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA. As procedural memory, it yields the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% for MetaClaw's skill library. Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, and a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence a question inspects does not grow with the history. AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path without rewriting any record, and it distills task sessions into skills. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks. It needs no fine-tuning, runs with closed and open models, and its code is public.

AI.tldr: MIRIX-2.0 is a multi-agent long-term memory system for LLM agents that reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks, and answers faster than HyperMem when AutoDream is disabled.
AI.motivation: Parametric memories need training, consolidation can permanently lose details, and keeping every record makes the store expensive to search, so the authors seek long-term memory that is practical, accurate and efficient at once.
AI.method: Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows, retrieval runs under explicit budgets, and AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path and distils task sessions into skills.
AI.result: MIRIX-2.0 leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points on LongMemEval-S, gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA with AutoDream disabled, gives the highest mean success on ALFWorld and WebShop among compared memory methods, and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench against 44.0% for MetaClaw's skill library.
AI.conclusion: The system needs no fine-tuning, works with closed and open models, and its code is public, showing that complete records with budgeted retrieval can serve as both episodic and procedural memory.

title: SadaqahStories: A Verified English-Arabic Corpus of Charity Stories for Children, with an Audit of Errors in AI-Drafted Religious Narratives
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Data and code: this https URL Website: this https URL
summary: We present SadaqahStories, a parallel English-Arabic corpus of 41 illustrated four-page stories about charitable giving in Islam (Sadaqah, Zakat and Waqf), written for readers aged 7 to 18. The stories were first drafted with large language model (LLM) assistance, then audited against hadith collections, Qur'an references and historical sources, and finally rewritten for children and signed off by an Islamic scholar. Every story carries an evidence label and links to its sources. We release all three versions of each story (AI-assisted draft, audited text, final child-oriented text) together with the correction log, so the corpus can be used to study how AI drafts of religious and historical content go wrong. The audit found substantive errors in 39 of the 41 drafts. The most frequent were unsupported specific details (dates, figures, prices, names), invented quotations, institutions or anecdotes, and conflation of separate events or people; six drafts contained errors in the wording, grading or ruling of a religious text. Rewriting cut the estimated Flesch-Kincaid grade of the English text from 14.0 to 6.1. We also release an 81-entry charity lexicon covering Modern Standard Arabic and Qatari Arabic, and describe the free, account-free website that serves the corpus (this https URL).

AI.tldr: SadaqahStories is a verified English-Arabic parallel corpus of 41 illustrated charity stories for children, released with its AI-drafted versions and correction log, and an audit found substantive errors in 39 of the 41 AI drafts.
AI.motivation: LLMs can produce fluent but wrong religious and historical narratives, and the authors want a corpus that shows how AI drafts of such content go wrong and can be used to study it.
AI.method: Stories were drafted with LLM assistance, audited against hadith collections, Qur'an references and historical sources, rewritten for children and signed off by an Islamic scholar, with an evidence label and source links for each story, and all three versions and the correction log are released alongside an 81-entry charity lexicon.
AI.result: The audit found substantive errors in 39 of 41 drafts, most often unsupported specific details such as dates, figures, prices and names, invented quotations, institutions or anecdotes, and conflation of separate events or people, with six drafts containing errors in religious wording, grading or ruling; rewriting cut the estimated Flesch-Kincaid grade of the English text from 14.0 to 6.1.
AI.conclusion: The corpus, with its correction log, can be used to study how AI drafts of religious and historical content go wrong, and the audited versions are released for that purpose.

title: Lost in Rounding: bf16 Recurrent State Makes Hybrid Reasoning Models Think Longer
summary: Hybrid reasoning models interleave attention with recurrent mixers such as Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, whose state is cached between decoding steps. Prior work showed that storing this state in FP16 or INT8 with round-to-nearest (RTN) makes Mamba-2 and GDN hybrids more verbose, and that stochastic rounding (SR) fixes it. We study the other 16-bit format that serving engines expose, bf16, on six open hybrid reasoning models and 590 competition-math problems. With bf16 RTN state, five of six models reason longer (geometric-mean length 1.07x to 1.27x; also under greedy decoding in the two models tested) and hit the 32K token cap more often. On Qwen3.5-9B, cap hits rise from 118 to 223 and accuracy falls from 85.6% to 70.8%. On LiveCodeBench, both models tested also reason longer and lose 12.6 and 13.4 points of pass@1. Rerunning the capped items with a 128K budget halves the accuracy gap but does not close it (93.6% vs. 86.6%): bf16 runs that never finish are twice as common, and 85% of them are exact repetition loops. On Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2, by contrast, 30 of 31 extra caps finish at 128K, so the cost there is mostly extra tokens (exploratory). Same-width bf16 SR removes the length increase in four of five affected models, restores Qwen3.5-9B to 87.6% and brings code length and pass@1 near FP32 levels, so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution. With an integer-hash random generator, SR on Qwen3.5-9B matches FP32 on cap hits and accuracy (113 vs. 118; 85.6% for both) at the memory and decoding speed of bf16 RTN. In the Nemotron-Nano-v2 lineage, SR on 25% of heads (an intermediate-decay band) removes the effect, while random heads and the top teacher-forced-KL octiles do not; in Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5-9B the effect is spread across heads. We recommend that evaluations of hybrid models report the state dtype, cap rate and output length alongside accuracy.

AI.tldr: Storing the recurrent state of hybrid reasoning models in bf16 with round-to-nearest rounding makes five of six models reason longer and hit the token cap more often, and the failure is mostly rounding bias that stochastic rounding largely removes.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that FP16 and INT8 recurrent-state storage with round-to-nearest makes Mamba-2 and GDN hybrids more verbose and that stochastic rounding fixes it, but the bf16 format that serving engines expose had not been studied.
AI.method: The authors evaluate six open hybrid reasoning models on 590 competition-math problems and on LiveCodeBench, comparing bf16 round-to-nearest state with stochastic rounding, same-width bf16 stochastic rounding, FP32, a 128K budget rerun of capped items, and head-level stochastic rounding ablations.
AI.result: With bf16 round-to-nearest state, five of six models produce geometric-mean lengths of 1.07x to 1.27x and hit the 32K cap more often; on Qwen3.5-9B cap hits rise from 118 to 223 and accuracy falls from 85.6% to 70.8%, while same-width stochastic rounding restores Qwen3.5-9B to 87.6% and brings code length and pass@1 near FP32 levels.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid model evaluations should report state dtype, cap rate and output length alongside accuracy, because bf16 rounding bias can silently inflate reasoning length and reduce accuracy.

title: Blind Variation, Selective Retention: Improving Creative Idea Generation in AI Scientists
summary: Scientific discovery requires ideas that are original, useful, and non-obvious. Yet AI scientists are typically given as much task information as possible during idea generation, which can anchor generation toward familiar approaches. Inspired by the cognitive framework of Blind Variation and Selective Retention (BVSR), we propose a discovery framework that separates these two roles of information: it generates proposals under deliberately limited task information to broaden exploration, then learns from proposals previously verified on the same task and their outcomes to retain promising candidates for costly empirical evaluation. We evaluate BVSR across five proposer models and 12 scientific tasks. Limiting task information substantially increases proposal originality and non-obviousness, and produces a larger share of highly creative and high-utility proposals than existing state-of-the-art prompting-based baselines. Learning from prior proposal outcomes on the task further improves candidate selection, discarding half of the candidates while retaining most top-performing proposals. When incorporated into existing AI-scientist workflows, BVSR achieves stronger discoveries across gene expression analysis, drug response prediction, anomaly detection, scaling law discovery, and brain activity prediction. These results suggest that effective AI scientists should use information differently across stages of discovery: constrain task-specific information during exploration while exploiting accumulated empirical experience on the task.

AI.tldr: BVSR separates information use in AI scientists by generating proposals under deliberately limited task information and then retaining candidates using outcomes of proposals previously verified on the same task, and it yields more original and useful ideas across five proposer models and 12 scientific tasks.
AI.motivation: AI scientists are usually given as much task information as possible, which can anchor idea generation toward familiar approaches, and the authors draw on Blind Variation and Selective Retention to argue that exploration and selection need different information.
AI.method: The framework generates proposals with limited task information to broaden exploration, then learns from proposals previously verified on the same task and their outcomes to choose which candidates are worth costly empirical evaluation.
AI.result: Limiting task information substantially increases proposal originality and non-obviousness and gives a larger share of highly creative and high-utility proposals than prompting baselines, learning from prior outcomes discards half of the candidates while retaining most top proposals, and BVSR strengthens existing AI-scientist workflows across five tasks including gene expression analysis and drug response prediction.
AI.conclusion: Effective AI scientists should constrain task-specific information during exploration and exploit accumulated empirical experience when selecting candidates.

title: The Deception Archive as a repository of standardized datasets for large-scale verbal deception detection research
summary: Computational advances in natural language processing and machine learning have substantially expanded the use of automated approaches in verbal deception research. However, existing verbal deception datasets remain fragmented across disciplines, as they are often difficult to identify, access, and reuse, limiting cross-study comparisons and the development of robust computational models. We present the Deception Archive, a curated and standardized repository of publicly available verbal deception datasets built upon a large-scale systematic review. Eligible datasets were retrieved, manually inspected, and standardized following a structured data curation workflow. The current repository comprises 41 publicly available datasets containing 387,995 truthful or deceptive statements. The archive represents a heterogeneous repository (e.g., in data size, topic of investigation, ground-truth, etc.) and a living resource for integrating newly available deception datasets over time. By providing centralized access to standardized datasets and accompanying metadata, the Deception Archive facilitates dataset discovery, cross-dataset validation, and reproducible evaluation of computational models.

AI.tldr: The Deception Archive is a curated, standardised repository of 41 publicly available verbal deception datasets containing 387,995 truthful or deceptive statements, built from a large-scale systematic review to support dataset discovery and reproducible evaluation.
AI.motivation: Verbal deception datasets are fragmented across disciplines and are often hard to identify, access and reuse, which limits cross-study comparison and the development of robust computational models.
AI.method: Eligible datasets were retrieved from a systematic review, manually inspected and standardised through a structured data curation workflow, and accompanied by metadata in a centralised repository designed to grow as new datasets appear.
AI.result: The current repository holds 41 publicly available datasets with 387,995 truthful or deceptive statements, a heterogeneous collection in data size, topic and ground truth.
AI.conclusion: Centralised, standardised access to deception datasets with metadata facilitates dataset discovery, cross-dataset validation and reproducible evaluation of computational deception-detection models.

title: TrajLift: Lifting Memory Recall Trajectories with Latency-Modulated Heat Diffusion
summary: Verbal memory retrieval carries rich diagnostic information for Alzheimer's disease through the order, hesitation, and categorical organization of recalled words, yet computational modeling of this retrieval process remains largely unexplored. A key challenge is that timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled: the diagnostic meaning of retrieval timing depends on its hierarchical context. We propose TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a hierarchical graph. Our central mechanism is latency-modulated heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy, a unified operator that lifts each recalled word into a representation of both multi-scale hierarchical structure and continuous retrieval timing. Formal analysis shows that the resulting representation is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchical levels. On synthetic benchmarks requiring structure-time interaction, TrajLift stays near-perfect on deep hierarchies where all baselines fail. On real-world clinical data, we show that TrajLift outperforms diverse baselines by jointly modeling timing and semantic structure, with gains that grow as retrieval timing becomes more informative.

AI.tldr: TrajLift models verbal memory recall as timed trajectories on a semantic hierarchy, using latency-modulated heat diffusion to lift each recalled word into a joint structural and temporal representation for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Verbal recall order, hesitation and categorical organization carry diagnostic information for Alzheimer's disease, but computational models of this retrieval process are largely unexplored, and timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled.
AI.method: A spectral framework in which heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy is modulated by retrieval latency, producing a per-word representation that is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchy levels.
AI.result: TrajLift stays near-perfect on synthetic deep hierarchies where all baselines fail, and on real clinical data it outperforms diverse baselines, with gains that grow as retrieval timing becomes more informative.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling timing and semantic structure is needed to extract diagnostic value from verbal recall, and the benefit depends on how informative the timing signal is.

title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
summary: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.

AI.tldr: The paper compares two state-of-the-art one-shot expert compression methods for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs, REAP (expert pruning) and REAM (expert merging), on five multilingual production tasks and finds pruning clearly better.
AI.motivation: REAP and REAM were evaluated only on academic benchmarks, while serving MoE models in production depends on their behaviour on real multilingual tasks.
AI.method: Both methods are applied with the same calibration data to two 30B-parameter models, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning, at 25% and 50% of experts removed, and outputs are compared on five production tasks from a web-hosting company.
AI.result: REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2; at 25% REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality versus 62.5% for REAM, although on benchmarks the two are within a point. Most losses on email templates come from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and cross-perplexity, logit divergence and repetition-loop rate track production quality while n-gram diversity does not.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark rankings do not reflect production quality, and the authors give practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production based on output-contract failures.

title: MNN-Pocket-0.3B Technical Report
summary: This technical report presents MNN-Pocket-0.3B, a compact 300M-parameter dense language model designed for efficient on-device deployment and supporting context lengths of up to 32K tokens. With an INT4 deployment footprint of only 173 MB and decoding throughput of up to 466 tokens/s on iPad Pro M5 (Metal), it can be seamlessly integrated into applications on edge devices such as smartphones and smart glasses. MNN-Pocket-0.3B is developed through the co-design of its architecture, data, training pipeline, and inference system. Hardware-aware architecture selection and dependency-aware vocabulary pruning balance model capability with on-device memory and compute constraints. A four-stage pre-training pipeline covering approximately 4.1 trillion high-quality Chinese and English tokens equips the model with broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. This is followed by a three-stage post-training pipeline comprising instruction fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and quantization-aware training. Finally, hardware-specific optimizations in the MNN inference engine enable fast, memory-efficient inference and long-context processing. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MNN-Pocket-0.3B achieves frontier-level performance among models of comparable size, with particularly strong results in Chinese and English knowledge and reasoning, mathematics, coding, and instruction following. It consistently outperforms similarly sized open-source models and even surpasses several 0.5B-parameter models on instruction-following benchmarks. We release MNN-Pocket-0.3B with open weights and ready-to-use MNN deployment packages. We hope it will provide a practical foundation for capable, responsive, and memory-efficient edge applications while advancing research and development in on-device language models.

AI.tldr: MNN-Pocket-0.3B is a 300M-parameter dense language model with a 32K context, designed for on-device use, with an INT4 footprint of 173 MB and up to 466 tokens/s decoding on iPad Pro M5.
AI.motivation: Capable language models are needed for edge devices such as smartphones and smart glasses, where memory and compute are tightly constrained.
AI.method: The model is co-designed across architecture, data, training and inference, with hardware-aware architecture selection and dependency-aware vocabulary pruning, a four-stage pre-training pipeline on about 4.1 trillion Chinese and English tokens, and a three-stage post-training pipeline of instruction fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation and quantization-aware training, followed by hardware-specific MNN inference optimizations.
AI.result: The model reaches frontier-level performance among comparably sized models in knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, coding and instruction following, consistently outperforms similarly sized open-source models, and surpasses several 0.5B-parameter models on instruction-following benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The release of open weights and MNN deployment packages is meant to provide a practical base for responsive, memory-efficient on-device language models.

title: More Than Just Style: Benchmarking Personality Influence in Large Language Models
summary: In addition to the effects of explicit input prompts and instructions, large language model outputs are influenced by underlying behavioral preferences similar to human personality tendencies. These tendencies can affect how models interpret situations and make decisions. However, their influence is difficult to disentangle from the effects of model capabilities and instructions. Therefore, we introduce SPACE, a benchmark framework combining a controlled evaluation protocol with complementary datasets for personality verification, capability assessment, and hierarchical situational tasks. Controlled comparisons across guidance conditions help distinguish personality influence from measured capability changes and immediate instruction effects. Experimental results demonstrate that although prompting can shift generation style, models' internal personality tendencies are persistent and not readily overridden by opposing instructions. Furthermore, these underlying tendencies have an observable influence on LLM task performance, highlighting the need for greater attention to these characteristics and potential applications. Training code and SPACE benchmark specifications are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SPACE is a benchmark framework that separates an LLM's internal personality tendencies from prompt-induced style and capability effects, and finds that these tendencies are persistent and affect task performance.
AI.motivation: LLM outputs are influenced by behavioural preferences resembling personality, but this influence is hard to disentangle from model capability and explicit instructions.
AI.method: SPACE combines a controlled evaluation protocol across guidance conditions with complementary datasets for personality verification, capability assessment and hierarchical situational tasks.
AI.result: Prompting can shift generation style, but models' internal personality tendencies are persistent and not readily overridden by opposing instructions, and these tendencies have an observable influence on task performance.
AI.conclusion: Personality-like tendencies deserve more attention in LLM evaluation and deployment, since instructions alone do not control them.

title: BDBBQ: A Human-AI Collaborative Benchmark for Bengali Social Bias in LLMs
summary: Despite growing attention to social bias in large language models (LLMs), existing bias benchmarks provide limited coverage of culturally grounded evaluation in Bengali, particularly within Bangladesh's sociocultural context. To address this gap, we develop a bilingual extension of BanglaBBQ comprising 61,312 question-answering instances across 12 social categories in English and Bengali. The benchmark incorporates balanced answer permutations, contrasting question framings, and both ambiguous and disambiguated contexts to systematically examine model performance and stereotype-aligned bias across languages. We validate the dataset through structural checks, 220 statistical tests, and expert annotation of 150 instances by four annotators, achieving strong inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' \k{appa}=0.8349). We evaluate eight LLMs across 490,496 instances and identify five key findings. First, disambiguated contexts yield substantially greater accuracy improvements in Bengali (+36.59 percentage points) than in English (+17.71). Second, all evaluated models exhibit lower accuracy in Bengali, although Mistral-Nemo shows the smallest cross-lingual accuracy gap (5.12 percentage points). Third, stereotype-aligned bias exhibits language and model dependent variation, increasing in Bengali for Gemma 2 9B but decreasing for Mistral-Nemo. Fourth, higher accuracy does not necessarily correspond to lower stereotype-aligned bias. Finally, bias varies considerably across social categories, with Qwen 2.5 7B exhibiting stronger stereotype alignment in Bengali for Politics and Physical Appearance. These findings demonstrate that cross-lingual performance and social bias are distinct dimensions of LLM behavior and underscore the importance of culturally grounded, language-sensitive benchmarks for evaluating fairness beyond English-centric settings.

AI.tldr: BDBBQ is a bilingual English and Bengali extension of BanglaBBQ with 61,312 question-answering instances across 12 social categories for measuring social bias in LLMs, applied to eight LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing bias benchmarks give limited coverage of culturally grounded evaluation in Bengali, particularly within Bangladesh's sociocultural context.
AI.method: The benchmark uses balanced answer permutations, contrasting question framings, and ambiguous and disambiguated contexts, validated by structural checks, 220 statistical tests and expert annotation of 150 instances by four annotators (Fleiss' kappa 0.8349).
AI.result: Across 490,496 instances, disambiguated contexts improve Bengali accuracy by 36.59 points versus 17.71 in English, all models are less accurate in Bengali, Mistral-Nemo has the smallest cross-lingual gap (5.12 points), and stereotype-aligned bias varies by language, model and social category; higher accuracy does not imply lower bias.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual performance and social bias are distinct dimensions of LLM behaviour, so culturally grounded, language-sensitive benchmarks are needed for fairness evaluation beyond English.

title: Path-Level Structural and Semantic Alignment for Hierarchical Multi-Label Text Classification
summary: Hierarchical multi-label text classification (HMTC) requires models to capture both structural dependencies among labels and the fine-grained semantics of labels at different hierarchy levels. Existing methods often model hierarchy through prediction constraints or representations of individual labels and local relations. Structural and semantic supervision, however, are usually formulated separately. We instead use complete root-to-node label paths as a shared unit for both. Our framework introduces two auxiliary training objectives while retaining a standard multi-label classifier at inference. PathSimNCE aligns document representations with hierarchical paths using hierarchy-aware contrastive targets. These targets provide graded supervision for structurally related paths while preserving explicit supervision for the ground-truth paths. The complementary semantic objective uses LLM-generated, document-conditioned descriptions of the same positive paths. It thereby provides context-specific label semantics beyond static label representations. Experiments on three benchmarks show consistent improvements: structural alignment is particularly beneficial in deeper hierarchies, while semantic alignment provides additional gains for fine-grained labels.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training framework for hierarchical multi-label text classification that uses root-to-node label paths as the shared unit for a path-level structural contrastive objective and an LLM-generated semantic objective, keeping a standard classifier at inference.
AI.motivation: Existing HMTC methods model hierarchy through prediction constraints or individual label representations, and structural and semantic supervision are usually formulated separately.
AI.method: Two auxiliary objectives are added during training: PathSimNCE aligns document representations with hierarchy-aware contrastive targets over label paths, and a semantic objective aligns documents with LLM-generated, document-conditioned descriptions of the positive paths.
AI.result: Experiments on three benchmarks show consistent improvements, with structural alignment especially helpful in deeper hierarchies and semantic alignment giving additional gains for fine-grained labels.
AI.conclusion: Modelling label paths as a shared unit for both structural and semantic supervision improves hierarchical classification without changing inference.

title: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?
summary: Scientific research has long been driven by substantial human effort, from reviewing prior work and identifying research gaps to designing specific solutions. Recent advances in harness-based agent systems have given rise to increasingly capable Auto Researchers, which can autonomously carry out these tasks and, increasingly, entire end-to-end research workflows. Yet despite their rapidly growing capabilities, how closely the research decisions and outputs produced by auto researchers align with those of human experts remains underexplored. We investigate this gap through the lens of research reconstruction and study: Given comparable research context, how similar are the research decisions and outputs produced by Auto Researchers to those of human researchers in AI research? To answer this question, we introduce AutoResearcher-Human Research Similarity (AutoHRS), a stage-wise evaluation framework for assessing how faithfully auto researchers reconstruct human research artifacts across different stages of the scientific workflow. Using 152 ICLR oral papers as our corpus, we generate 456 research trajectories spanning different stages of the research process. Applying AutoHRS to these trajectories, we find that current Auto Researchers frequently fail to recover key research decisions and their resulting artifacts across multiple stages of the research process.

AI.tldr: AutoHRS is a stage-wise evaluation framework that measures how faithfully AI auto researchers reconstruct human research decisions and artifacts, and it finds that current systems often fail to recover key decisions across stages.
AI.motivation: How closely the research decisions and outputs of increasingly capable auto researchers match those of human experts is underexplored.
AI.method: Using 152 ICLR oral papers as the corpus, the authors generate 456 research trajectories across stages of the research process and score them with AutoHRS under comparable research context.
AI.result: Current auto researchers frequently fail to recover key research decisions and their resulting artifacts across multiple stages of the workflow.
AI.conclusion: Auto researchers are not yet reliable reconstructions of human research, and faithfulness to human decisions should be measured stage by stage.

title: Phrase-Level Speculative Decoding on a Frozen Target
summary: Speculative decoders raise throughput by banking more target tokens per forward pass, and Medusa, EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark all do it the same way: more candidates that survive verification. All of them draft in the target's own vocabulary, so one node of the candidate tree is one target token, and the tokenizer makes that unit look like a constant. It is not. BPE's pretokenizer splits on whitespace before merges are learned, so no multi-word string can ever become a single token: in Qwen3-4B, "United States of America" is four tokens and no adjacent pair of them exists as one entry, so a phrase is out of reach of any method drafting in the target's vocabulary. We change the unit. A small MLP head reads the frozen target's hidden state and predicts a one- to three-word phrase as one entry in a separate draft vocabulary; greedy longest-match expansion maps it back into the target's own tokens, and N candidates are verified in one forward pass behind a prefix-tree mask, so the change is orthogonal to tree depth and width. The target and its tokenizer stay frozen and a candidate is accepted only while it matches the target's own argmax, so the served output is identical to greedy decoding up to floating-point tie-breaking. On one A5000 at batch 1, against HuggingFace generate(), a 21.94M head (0.545% of Qwen3-4B) reaches 2.391x on GSM8K, 2.444x on MATH-500 and 1.544x on MT-Bench. Because the head's output layer is one row of 257 parameters per entry, the draft vocabulary size is the parameter budget: an 8,000-entry head is 3.434M parameters, 0.0854% of the target and 64x smaller than EAGLE-3's drafter, and keeps 92.3% of the larger head's GSM8K tokens per pass. With EAGLE-3 run on same prompts and baseline, our 21.94M head is ahead of tree-16 on both maths sets and behind tree-60 on every set.

AI.tldr: Phrase-level speculative decoding drafts one- to three-word phrases with a small MLP head on a frozen target's hidden state, using a separate draft vocabulary, and verifies candidates in one forward pass while keeping greedy-equivalent output.
AI.motivation: Existing speculative decoders such as Medusa, EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark draft in the target's own vocabulary, where BPE tokenization prevents any multi-word string from being a single token, so phrases are out of reach.
AI.method: A small MLP head predicts a phrase as one entry in a separate draft vocabulary, greedy longest-match expansion maps it to target tokens, and N candidates are verified with a prefix-tree mask; the target stays frozen and a candidate is accepted only if it matches the target's argmax.
AI.result: On one A5000 at batch 1 against HuggingFace generate(), a 21.94M-parameter head reaches 2.391x on GSM8K, 2.444x on MATH-500 and 1.544x on MT-Bench; an 8,000-entry head with 3.434M parameters keeps 92.3% of the larger head's GSM8K tokens per pass, and the 21.94M head is ahead of EAGLE-3 with tree-16 on both maths sets but behind tree-60.
AI.conclusion: Changing the drafting unit from tokens to phrases is orthogonal to tree depth and width and gives strong speedups with a very small parameter budget, though larger candidate trees still outperform it.

title: Detecting AI-Authored Text in Authentic Student Writing: Evidence from PISA 2025
summary: AI-text detectors reach near-perfect scores in evaluations that contrast fully human-written texts with texts generated from researcher-designed prompts. In authentic student writing, however, AI use is voluntary and often partial. We study this setting with the PISA 2025 FLA dataset, in which 15-year-olds in Germany wrote English argumentative essays with and without access to a gpt-4o-mini-based chatbot. Keystroke, clipboard and chat logs let us trace every character of the final essay to its origin. From this provenance, we derive text- and sentence-level labels for human-written, AI-generated and mixed text, and for text written after chatbot use without traceable AI material. We evaluate a feature-based detector and a classifier on frozen Llama-3.1-8B embeddings, both adapted from top-ranked shared-task systems. Both separate AI from human text reliably (macro-F1 up to 0.96 for texts and 0.95 for sentences), independently of spelling errors. The feature-based detector, however, relies on lexical complexity, which a simple student-style rewriting prompt removes (AI recall 0.92 $\to$ 0.60 with gpt-4o-mini, 0.41 with Qwen3). The embedding-based detector stays robust for whole texts (AI recall $\geq$ 0.94) but not for single sentences (AI recall as low as 0.59). Mixed text falls between the two classes, and text without traceable AI material is classified as human-written in about 95\% of texts.

AI.tldr: Using PISA 2025 essays with keystroke, clipboard and chat logs that give exact provenance, the paper shows that AI-text detectors work well on authentic student writing but are fragile to simple rewriting and to single sentences.
AI.motivation: AI-text detectors score near-perfectly when human texts are contrasted with researcher-prompted AI texts, but in authentic student writing AI use is voluntary and partial.
AI.method: Provenance traces each character of 15-year-old German students' English essays to human, AI or mixed origin, yielding text- and sentence-level labels, and a feature-based detector and a classifier on frozen Llama-3.1-8B embeddings are evaluated.
AI.result: Both detectors separate AI from human text (macro-F1 up to 0.96 for texts and 0.95 for sentences), but the feature-based detector's AI recall falls from 0.92 to 0.60 with gpt-4o-mini rewriting and 0.41 with Qwen3; the embedding detector keeps AI recall of at least 0.94 for whole texts but drops to 0.59 for single sentences, and about 95% of texts without traceable AI material are classified as human.
AI.conclusion: Detectors are reliable for whole texts in authentic settings but not for single sentences, and lexical-complexity cues are easily removed by student-style rewriting.

title: Text Grouping Changes Completion-Time Comparisons in Long-Form Simultaneous Speech Translation
summary: Does grouping translation updates before speech synthesis change the measured completion gap between two translators? We compare StreamAtt with its fixed-audio-history baseline on ten English-German talks. For each translation, we keep the intended text and its availability times fixed and vary how updates are grouped for synthesis. Four-second grouping increases StreamAtt's mean completion lead from 106.6 to 229.1 seconds with XTTS-v2, but reduces it from 169.5 to 146.5 seconds with Piper. Both produce shorter audio; different changes in playback idle account for the opposite effects. These directions recur on a separately selected twenty-talk panel. In continuing CosyVoice 3 sessions, grouping instead leaves paired audio unchanged and delays completion on nineteen of twenty blocks. A speech-timing comparison therefore needs to specify how text enters synthesis, not just which synthesizer is used. Recognition and automatic word timing describe the outputs, but do not establish translation accuracy or intelligibility.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that grouping translation updates before speech synthesis changes the measured completion-time gap between two simultaneous speech translators, and the direction of the effect depends on the synthesizer.
AI.motivation: Speech-timing comparisons of simultaneous translation may depend on how text is grouped before synthesis, which is rarely specified.
AI.method: StreamAtt and its fixed-audio-history baseline are compared on ten English-German talks with intended text and availability times held fixed, varying four-second grouping for synthesis with XTTS-v2, Piper and continuing CosyVoice 3 sessions, and checked on a separately selected twenty-talk panel.
AI.result: With XTTS-v2 grouping raises StreamAtt's mean completion lead from 106.6 to 229.1 seconds, with Piper it reduces the lead from 169.5 to 146.5 seconds, and with CosyVoice 3 it leaves paired audio unchanged and delays completion on nineteen of twenty blocks.
AI.conclusion: A speech-timing comparison must specify how text enters synthesis as well as which synthesizer is used, and recognition and word-timing measures do not establish translation accuracy or intelligibility.

title: Language Defaults Before Content: A Causal Layer Map of Multilingual Generation
summary: Multilingual generation requires large language models (LLMs) to determine both what to say and in what language to say it, yet these two commitments are difficult to disentangle from model outputs alone. We use translation as a controlled probe: for multi-parallel segments that a model translates well in one language direction but poorly in another, content is held fixed while language varies. Using activation patching, we write residual-stream states from successful runs into failing ones and compare content-matched states with content-independent controls, allowing us to trace content-specific and language-related signals across layers. Across three LLMs of different scales and architectures, we find a consistent three-stage pattern of multilingual generation. Intermediate layers first express a default English signal; content information becomes causally available one layer later; and the final target language is resolved only at later layers. The ordering of the English default before content also appears in a reading-comprehension task. Our sparse autoencoder analyses reveal a further dissociation: the intermediate language signal is only weakly represented by sparse features, whereas a later language distinction is clearly sparse, but resists intervention at the patched position. These results provide a mechanistic account of how language selection and content information emerge and interact during multilingual generation.

AI.tldr: Using activation patching on translation tasks, the paper finds that LLMs first express a default English signal in intermediate layers, then make content causally available one layer later, and resolve the target language only in later layers.
AI.motivation: It is hard to tell from outputs alone how multilingual LLMs decide what to say and in which language to say it, since content and language are entangled.
AI.method: For multi-parallel segments translated well in one direction and poorly in another, residual-stream states from successful runs are patched into failing ones and compared with content-matched states and content-independent controls, with sparse autoencoder analyses across three LLMs.
AI.result: A consistent three-stage pattern appears across three LLMs of different scales and architectures, with the English default preceding content, which also appears in a reading-comprehension task; the intermediate language signal is weakly represented by sparse features, while a later language distinction is clearly sparse but resists intervention at the patched position.
AI.conclusion: The paper gives a mechanistic account of how language selection and content information emerge and interact during multilingual generation, with English acting as a default before content is resolved.

title: AgentOPSD: Turn-Level Credit Assignment via Recursive Belief Revision
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ordinarily spreads a single advantage over a whole trajectory, a granularity too coarse to isolate the few decisions on which success in a long, multi-turn interaction actually turns. Privileged self-distillation supplies denser supervision, but it leaves unanswered how a set of local teacher-student discrepancies should be converted into credit along a sequence. We introduce AgentOPSD, a critic-free scheme that assigns credit recursively, one interaction turn at a time. Inside a turn, the token-level log-probability gaps between a skill-conditioned self-teacher and the student are summed, and that sum acts as evidence in a recursive Bayesian update carried out in log-odds space; the resulting revisions reallocate the outcome-derived advantage across turns through a multiplier that is bounded and preserves its sign. With Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B as policy backbones on ALFWorld, the method improves consistently on GRPO and on self-distillation baselines, and attains 89.1% success at the 7B scale. Ablations attribute the gain to aggregating evidence at turn boundaries and to making the belief revision depend on history, rather than to the local gap by itself.

AI.tldr: AgentOPSD is a critic-free credit assignment scheme for multi-turn reinforcement learning that converts token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into a recursive Bayesian belief revision over turns, reallocating the trajectory advantage across turns.
AI.motivation: RLVR spreads one advantage over a whole trajectory, which is too coarse for long multi-turn interactions, and privileged self-distillation gives denser signals without saying how local discrepancies should become credit along a sequence.
AI.method: Per turn, token-level log-probability gaps between a skill-conditioned self-teacher and the student are summed as evidence in a recursive log-odds Bayesian update, and the revisions set a bounded, sign-preserving multiplier that redistributes the outcome-derived advantage across turns.
AI.result: With Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B on ALFWorld, the method improves consistently over GRPO and self-distillation baselines and reaches 89.1% success at the 7B scale; ablations attribute the gain to aggregating evidence at turn boundaries and to history-dependent belief revision rather than the local gap alone.
AI.conclusion: Turn-level credit assignment built from aggregated, history-dependent evidence helps multi-turn agent training more than local teacher-student discrepancies do.

title: Fairness in Explainable AI Narratives: Decomposing Social Disparities in LLM-Generated Explanations
comment: 25 pages, 8 figures, 9 tables. Code, prompts, narratives and extractions available at this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate technical explainable AI (XAI) artefacts such as SHAP into explanatory narratives (XAINs) for lay users. In high-risk domains, these explanations are often the main resource through which individuals can understand and contest adverse decisions. Yet LLMs are known to reproduce social bias, even from proxy variables alone, and fairness in XAINs remains unstudied. Because XAINs are bound to a ground-truth artefact, fairness concerns not only what a narrative says and how, but also whether it is equally faithful across social groups. We introduce fairness in XAINs as a new field of research and propose a framework that generates narratives under three conditions (protected attribute disclosed, withheld, or counterfactually swapped), allowing five comparisons that pinpoint the cause of disparities. We apply it to adversely classified instances from four datasets in credit scoring, education and employment, generating narratives with five LLMs, and evaluate faithfulness, feature coverage and sentiment. We find significant disparities across all datasets, metric families and models, arising in two ways. Faithfulness disparities result from feature values: LLMs make plausible but false statements, triggered by values that are unequally distributed across social groups. Feature coverage and sentiment disparities stem from the protected attribute itself: once it is disclosed, LLMs give less explanation to, or frame more negatively the narratives of, groups that have historically been discriminated against or are stereotypically associated with worse outcomes. A more faithful model removes the faithfulness disparities, and withholding protected attributes mostly removes the others, but neither suffices on its own. Fairness in XAINs should therefore be audited separately from the predictive model and its XAI artefact.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces fairness in explainable AI narratives, a framework that generates LLM explanations of SHAP results under three protected-attribute conditions and finds significant disparities across credit, education and employment datasets.
AI.motivation: LLMs translate XAI artefacts into narratives that lay users rely on to contest adverse decisions, but whether these narratives are equally faithful and equally framed across social groups has not been studied.
AI.method: For adversely classified instances from four datasets, narratives are generated with five LLMs under three conditions (protected attribute disclosed, withheld or counterfactually swapped), enabling five comparisons, and evaluated for faithfulness, feature coverage and sentiment.
AI.result: Disparities appear across all datasets, metric families and models; faithfulness disparities arise from feature values that are unequally distributed across groups, while coverage and sentiment disparities arise from disclosing the protected attribute, which leads to less explanation or more negative framing for historically discriminated groups; a more faithful model removes faithfulness disparities and withholding attributes mostly removes the others, but neither suffices alone.
AI.conclusion: Fairness in XAI narratives should be audited separately from the predictive model and its XAI artefact.

title: Unmasking Four Knapsack Problems in the Traveling Thief Benchmark
summary: The traveling thief problem (TTP) asks a thief to choose a tour and a packing together, and the benchmark of 9,720 instances of Polyakovskiy et al. (2014) is the standard test set for comparing TTP heuristics. We show that four of these instances are not TTP instances at all. Their files give a renting rate of 0.00, so the tour has no effect on the objective and each instance reduces to a 0-1 knapsack problem. One of them belongs to the 60 categorized instances on which new methods are usually compared, and on it five of nine published methods report exactly the same value. The cause is the format of the files, which keep the renting rate with two decimals, while the rule of the generator gives a rate close to 0.003 on these instances. The same rounding may shift the rate of 949 other instances by more than 1%. Since the tour and the packing used by the generator were not published, the original rates cannot be recovered. We therefore define new rates with the same rule, applied to a fully specified reference solution that we publish, and we show with a published heuristic that the corrected instances behave as TTP instances again. We also give reference results on the corrected instances and recommendations for future studies. Finally, we present ttplib, a new open-source Python library that loads any of the 9,720 instances, including the corrected ones, without downloading the whole benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that four instances in the standard Traveling Thief Problem benchmark have a renting rate of 0.00, so they reduce to 0-1 knapsack problems, and it defines corrected rates, reference results and an open-source Python library ttplib.
AI.motivation: The 9,720-instance TTP benchmark is the standard test set for heuristics, and rounding of renting rates in the instance files may have corrupted some instances.
AI.method: The authors identify instances with zero renting rate, show that the rounding of two-decimal rates shifts the rate of 949 further instances by more than 1%, define new rates by the generator's rule on a published reference solution, and check the corrected instances with a published heuristic.
AI.result: One of the four affected instances is among the 60 categorized instances usually used for comparison, where five of nine published methods report exactly the same value; the corrected instances behave as TTP instances again, and reference results are provided.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark needs correction and clearer reporting, and the paper recommends practices for future studies and releases ttplib to load any instance, corrected or original.

title: Adapting Small Language Models to Romanized Nepali: Tokenizer Fertility, Reference Likelihood, and Generation Metrics
summary: Romanized Nepali, Nepali written in Latin script, is common in digital communication but has no standard spelling and few resources, and it is unclear how reliably small open language models can be adapted to it. We adapt three 2-3B base models from different families, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Gemma-2-2B, with QLoRA on 9,000 instruction examples produced by deterministic transliteration of Nepali instruction data. Each model is trained with one shared recipe and three seeds and evaluated on 1,000 held-out examples with reference-overlap metrics, byte-normalized reference likelihood (bits per byte, BPB), and an output audit, against zero-shot baselines under two prompts. Fine-tuning raises chrF++ from 10-14 to 29.0-30.6 and lowers BPB from 2.23-2.41 to 0.78-0.84; most zero-shot outputs (54-92%) are English-like. Likelihood and overlap disagree on how far apart the models are. Llama-3.2-3B has the lowest BPB in every seed, 0.042 below Qwen2.5-3B (95% CI 0.039-0.046), yet the two cannot be separated on chrF++ (30.51 and 30.61) or BLEU, even with paired item-level tests. Gemma-2-2B, whose tokenizer splits Romanized Nepali words least (2.72 tokens per word), scores worst on every measure. Which model gains most over its zero-shot baseline depends on the zero-shot prompt. In a supplementary comparison with an identical tokenizer, Llama-3.1-8B lowers BPB by 0.053 (0.050-0.056) relative to Llama-3.2-3B, while chrF++ and BLEU rise by only 0.68 and 0.58 points. Lower fertility and higher reference likelihood therefore did not identify the model whose outputs were closest to the references.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts three 2-3B base models to Romanized Nepali with QLoRA and finds that likelihood and n-gram overlap metrics disagree about which model is best, so lower tokenizer fertility and higher reference likelihood do not identify the closest outputs.
AI.motivation: Romanized Nepali has no standard spelling and few resources, and it is unclear how reliably small open models can be adapted to it.
AI.method: Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma-2-2B are fine-tuned with QLoRA on 9,000 instruction examples from deterministic transliteration, with one recipe and three seeds, and evaluated on 1,000 held-out examples with chrF++, BLEU, bits per byte and an output audit against zero-shot baselines.
