AI.result: On 100K-token coding sessions with Qwen3-8B and a 2,048-token budget, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV, and either component alone reaches 63%. In 1M and 2M-token sessions PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks while holding under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147 to 295 GB. Renumbering adds 9% wall time and no measurable perplexity cost.
AI.conclusion: Keeping the right tokens resident is not sufficient for long-horizon agents; retrievability also depends on positional distance, and planner foresight plus bounded positions are both needed.

title: Do large language models rank moral values? A transitivity test of moral competence
summary: LLMs are increasingly used to support decisions that require moral consideration. While LLMs perform well on morality benchmarks from psychology and philosophy, producing appropriate outputs on these benchmarks (moral performance) does not establish that an LLM weighs competing moral values at stake in a decision (moral competence). We test a minimal, necessary condition for such weighing: that an ordinal ranking can represent LLM moral choices. Such a ranking requires transitivity. To assess transitivity, we presented LLMs with pairwise trade-offs among moral value violations in vignette choice sets and extracted resulting choice probabilities from first-token distributions. Tested against three stochastic transitive choice models, most choice sets admitted weak or unstable orderings. Aggregating an LLM's responses, a common practice in LLM moral evaluation, produced transitive structure that matched no individual choice set. Evaluations of AI morality should establish that choices are structured before asking whether they are aligned.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether LLM moral choices are structured enough to be represented as an ordinal ranking by checking transitivity over pairwise trade-offs among moral value violations. Most choice sets admit only weak or unstable orderings.
AI.motivation: Good performance on moral benchmarks does not show that an LLM weighs competing moral values in decisions, so a minimal necessary condition for such weighing is needed.
AI.method: LLMs are presented with pairwise trade-offs among moral value violations in vignette choice sets, choice probabilities are taken from first-token distributions, and the results are tested against three stochastic transitive choice models.
AI.result: Most choice sets admit only weak or unstable orderings. Aggregating responses across an LLM, a common practice in moral evaluation, yields transitive structure that matches no individual choice set.
AI.conclusion: Moral evaluations of AI should first establish that choices are structured before asking whether they are aligned with human values.

title: How Much Is Left Matters: False Positives and False Negatives in Partial-Prompt Contamination Tests
summary: Partial-prompt completion, where a model receives the first part of a benchmark problem and is checked for whether it reproduces the rest, is a widely used test for benchmark contamination. We audit this test on seven open-weight models using MATH-500 and recent AIME 2025/2026 problems, which serve as true negatives. Memorization flags depend strongly on how much text remains: for every model, problems with at most 8 leftover words are flagged several times more often than problems with at least 25 (31.5% vs. 5.5% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), and half to three-quarters of all ROUGE-based flags come from short leftovers. On true negatives, a ROUGE-L >= 0.75 threshold flags up to 6.7% of problems at a 60% prefix, and at an 80% prefix even exact match flags 8.6% (pooled over models; 6.2% on AIME 2026, which postdates every model), against 0% at 40-60%. The test also misses contamination upstream: models distilled from Qwen2.5-Math, whose base is heavily flagged in prior work, show almost no model-specific recall. Calibrating each model against models from other families removes most flags while isolating a consistent Qwen2.5-specific signal at every prefix length. We recommend length-stratified reporting, prefixes of at most 60%, style-matched post-cutoff controls, and cross-family calibration.

AI.tldr: The paper audits the partial-prompt completion test for benchmark contamination and shows that its false positive and false negative rates depend strongly on prefix length and on the leftover text. It recommends length-stratified reporting, prefixes of at most 60%, post-cutoff controls and cross-family calibration.
AI.motivation: Partial-prompt completion is widely used to detect benchmark contamination, but its reliability on true negatives and for contamination inherited through distillation has not been checked.
AI.method: Seven open-weight models are tested on MATH-500 and on recent AIME 2025 and 2026 problems, which serve as true negatives. The analysis stratifies flags by leftover word count and prefix length, compares ROUGE-based and exact-match flags, and calibrates each model against models from other families.
AI.result: Problems with at most 8 leftover words are flagged several times more often than those with at least 25 words (31.5% vs. 5.5% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). On true negatives a ROUGE-L of at least 0.75 flags up to 6.7% at a 60% prefix, and at an 80% prefix exact match flags 8.6%, against 0% at 40 to 60%. Models distilled from Qwen2.5-Math show almost no model-specific recall, and cross-family calibration removes most flags while keeping a Qwen2.5-specific signal.
AI.conclusion: Contamination claims from partial-prompt tests need length-stratified reporting, short prefixes and cross-family calibration, since many flags come from short leftovers rather than memorization.

title: Police Behavior Patterns Through Radio Analysis
comment: 10 pages (14 with SI), 6 figures (8 with SI)
summary: In the United States, most police departments communicate using police radio, which allows for officer-to-officer and officer-to-dispatch communication without depending on cellular network or WiFi availability. While some departments use encrypted digital radio, many continue to transmit in the clear, and are legally monitored by public citizens with `police scanners.' Because police radio is intended for internal police use and represents real-time communication, it may offer valuable insight into patterns of law enforcement activities without the potential bias and filtering introduced by a press release after the fact. In this study, we collect and examine over 14 million radio transmissions representing over 100,000 hours of speech by officers in 34 cities across the United States from July 2025 through July 2026; to our knowledge the largest scale analysis of Broadcast Police Communication (BPC) to date. We highlight both typical patterns of police communication and categorize anomalous activity that represents incidents including protests and major weather events. We present this dataset as a starting point for an array of police communication studies, conduct our own preliminary analysis, and propose several further areas of inquiry.

AI.tldr: The paper collects over 14 million transmissions, about 100,000 hours of speech, from police radio in 34 US cities between July 2025 and July 2026 and presents it as a dataset for studying police communication. It also reports typical patterns and anomalous activity such as protests and weather events.
AI.motivation: Police radio is real-time and unfiltered by press releases, so it may reveal law enforcement activity without the bias introduced by after-the-fact reporting, yet it has not been studied at scale.
AI.method: The authors record and transcribe unencrypted police scanner traffic from 34 cities, release the corpus, and run a preliminary analysis that identifies typical communication patterns and categorizes anomalous episodes.
AI.result: The corpus contains over 14 million transmissions and more than 100,000 hours of officer speech, which the authors describe as the largest analysis of Broadcast Police Communication to date. Anomalous activity is linked to protests and major weather events.
AI.conclusion: The dataset is offered as a starting point for a range of police communication studies, with several further lines of inquiry proposed.

title: Two-Sided Conformal Evidence Sets for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026). 8 pages
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can surface passages that support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it, yet existing calibrated grounding methods are typically one-sided and model only supporting evidence. We introduce Conformal Evidence Sets (CES), a two-sided framework that returns separate support and refutation sets with finite-sample inclusion coverage of at least $1-\alpha$ on each side under exchangeability; a Bonferroni union yields joint coverage of at least $1-2\alpha$. On labeled candidate pools from the contrastive VitaminC benchmark, CES closely tracks nominal coverage across $\alpha\!\in\!\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30\}$, with maximum deviations of $3.0$ percentage points for support and $5.4$ for refutation, and reaches essentially the same empirical coverage--size frontier as a test-tuned fixed-threshold heuristic without any test exposure. Stress tests mark the boundary of that guarantee: under FEVER distribution shift both sides under-cover, by up to $12.7$ percentage points, and support-side group-stratified recalibration substantially reduces the support gap. Scorer swaps, hard-negative retrieval, cross-dataset transfer, and a live end-to-end pilot expose a clear separation: when exchangeability holds and relevant evidence is retrieved, evidence inclusion remains calibrated even with an imperfect scorer, whereas the support/refute verdict tracks scorer quality directly. Calibrated evidence coverage and reliable verdicts are therefore distinct properties and should be reported separately.

AI.tldr: Conformal Evidence Sets (CES) is a two-sided conformal framework for RAG that returns separate support and refutation sets, each with finite-sample inclusion coverage of at least 1 minus alpha under exchangeability. A Bonferroni union gives joint coverage of at least 1 minus 2 alpha.
AI.motivation: Existing calibrated grounding methods are one-sided and model only supporting evidence, so they cannot certify retrieved passages that refute a claim.
AI.method: CES builds conformal sets for supporting and refuting passages over labeled candidate pools from VitaminC, with a Bonferroni union for joint coverage. Stress tests include FEVER distribution shift, group-stratified recalibration, scorer swaps, hard-negative retrieval, cross-dataset transfer and a live end-to-end pilot.
AI.result: Empirical coverage tracks nominal levels for alpha in {0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30}, with maximum deviations of 3.0 points for support and 5.4 points for refutation. Under FEVER shift both sides under-cover by up to 12.7 points, and support-side group-stratified recalibration substantially reduces the support gap.
AI.conclusion: Evidence inclusion stays calibrated with an imperfect scorer when exchangeability holds and relevant evidence is retrieved, but the support or refute verdict depends directly on scorer quality, so the two properties should be reported separately.

title: Collaboration Signatures: Tracking Long-Horizon Dynamics of Cross-Meeting Collaboration Networks
summary: Enterprise platforms have received increasing attention as a core component of social networks and the Web. However, existing work mostly relies on fragmented logs of small units of work, like emails and chats, and focuses on who connects with whom without sufficient account of collaboration content and dynamics. This work systematically explores tracking collaborations across sequences of meetings as a new approach to interpreting their long-horizon dynamics. Linking 45,426 meetings in a large multinational technology company based on full transcripts and 1.6 million extracted agenda items, we establish a cross-meeting collaboration network of 6,065 collaborations. The network recovers the natural shapes of workplace collaborations: meetings, as snapshots of ongoing collaboration, link into largely tree-shaped structures, while the work content forms nested directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Further, we explore how these networks evolve over time, examining three established perspectives: task division, team composition, and temporal continuity. Each explains part of the dynamics but does not capture the distinctness of long-horizon workplace collaboration: e.g., work flows in a consistent direction between a few pairs of subjects, yet a collaboration's subject explains little of how its meetings are conducted. Instead, accumulating the agenda, interaction, and language of meetings along each tree yields a signature of the collaboration, a distinctive profile that picks out the collaboration of a held-out meeting at 4.5 times chance. The signature models collaboration better than team or task views, individually or combined, in next-meeting prediction and tree-level fitting. We discuss the implications of these cross-meeting dynamics for designing office applications and support tools, and call for next-generation Web systems that represent collaborations over their long horizon.

AI.tldr: The paper links 45,426 meetings at a large multinational technology company into a cross-meeting collaboration network and shows that a collaboration signature built from agenda, interaction and language identifies held-out meetings better than team or task views. The network is largely tree-shaped, and its work content forms nested DAGs.
AI.motivation: Enterprise collaboration research relies on small fragmented logs such as emails and chats and focuses on who connects with whom, without modeling collaboration content and long-horizon dynamics.
AI.method: Meeting transcripts and 1.6 million extracted agenda items are used to link meetings into 6,065 collaborations. Three perspectives are compared, task division, team composition and temporal continuity, against a signature obtained by accumulating agenda, interaction and language along each tree.
AI.result: The signature picks out the collaboration of a held-out meeting at 4.5 times chance. It outperforms team or task views, individually or combined, in next-meeting prediction and tree-level fitting.
AI.conclusion: Collaboration is better described by an accumulated signature than by team or task structure, with implications for office applications and for next-generation Web systems that represent collaborations over time.

title: SituRecBench: Evaluating Frontier Models as Situated Recommendation Assistants in 3D Environments
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track
summary: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.

AI.tldr: SituRecBench is an interactive benchmark that evaluates frontier vision-language models as situated recommendation assistants in high-fidelity 3D shopping environments, where the assistant shares the user's egocentric view. Experiments show persistent difficulty with spatial grounding and preference elicitation.
AI.motivation: Recommender research largely ignores the combination of spatial navigation, visual grounding and multi-turn social interaction that a physically situated assistant requires.
AI.method: Recommendation is reformulated as a situated assistance process in which the assistant converses with the user, elicits preferences, grounds recommendations in the environment and guides the user to locations. Dialogue quality, recommendation utility and navigation effectiveness are scored under one interactive protocol in simulated supermarkets and home furnishings stores.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on frontier VLMs reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, and limitations in integrating global context with local observations. The abstract does not report specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark is presented as a rigorous foundation for developing situated recommendation assistants in the real world.

title: In Search of Lost Time: Temporal Competence in Large Language Models
summary: Today's large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with time: AI agents schedule tasks, coordinate with people and other AI systems, and even decide how long to think. Yet LLMs only ever encounter time secondhand---in descriptions rather than experience. Does this hinder their reasoning and decisions that involve time? Our paper traces this question from a model's knowledge to its actions through four successive evaluations. We find that models know the rules of time, which can be read, but struggle to predict durations, which must be lived; while they are highly accurate (92.0-97.5\%) on a collection of questions built from the theorems of various time-related literatures, they underestimate their own completion times by up to 99.5\% and fail to identify which tasks will take them longer to run. And while they are better at estimating durations of human tasks, their duration judgments change based on how an event is worded, magnifying similar human biases by up to 1.3$\times$. Moving from estimation to action, we find that some LLMs disregard time costs completely when answering user queries, ignoring a 1,200-fold increase in wait time entirely. Together, our experiments reveal new challenges posed to LLMs as they navigate a dimension they cannot directly perceive, and highlight how their blind spots can even be simple cognitive abilities that humans take for granted.

AI.tldr: Through four evaluations, the paper finds that LLMs know the rules of time but cannot predict durations, underestimate their own completion times by up to 99.5%, and sometimes ignore time costs when answering users. Their blind spots include basic cognitive abilities that humans take for granted.
AI.motivation: LLMs learn about time only secondhand from descriptions, and it is unclear whether this limits reasoning and decisions that depend on time, even as they increasingly schedule tasks and decide how long to think.
AI.method: Four successive evaluations trace the question from knowledge to action. They cover accuracy on questions built from time-related theorems, self-estimation of completion times, judgments of human task durations under different wordings, and whether models account for wait times when answering user queries.
AI.result: Models are highly accurate (92.0 to 97.5%) on theorem-based time questions, but underestimate their own completion times by up to 99.5% and fail to identify which tasks will take longer. Duration judgments shift with wording, magnifying similar human biases by up to 1.3 times. Some LLMs ignore a 1,200-fold increase in wait time entirely.
AI.conclusion: Temporal competence is a distinct gap, since LLMs can state the rules of time yet act poorly on durations they cannot directly perceive, which raises new challenges for agents that operate over time.

title: What Do Collusion Probes Read? Three Pitfalls in Evaluating Multi-Agent Collusion Monitors
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL ; data: this https URL ; archive: doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23636508
summary: Activation probes look like near-perfect monitors for secret collusion among large language model (LLM) agents. We show that they mostly detect that an agent was told to collude, not that it decided to. Our benchmark (2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes) adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it, separating instruction from decision. Published detectors barely tell colluders from these refusers, and our best probe separates them mostly by reading the instruction: without it, agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Two further pitfalls inflate reported results: scored after the vote, a rule that only reads the votes reaches AUROC 0.990 but finds nothing before it; and in 57% of attempts no colluder argues for the target in public. The decision is still there: a probe trained on agents' own choices reads it (AUROC 0.73 without the instruction), and probes find colluders whose goal was fine-tuned into the weights (AUROC 0.995; pre-registered). We turn the controls into a protocol for testing any collusion monitor, and adapt scan statistics into an online monitor for groups of any size.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that activation probes for secret LLM-agent collusion mostly detect whether an agent was instructed to collude rather than whether it decided to. It also identifies two evaluation pitfalls and offers controls and an online monitor.
AI.motivation: Activation probes appear to be near-perfect monitors for collusion, but the benchmark does not separate an agent receiving a collusion instruction from an agent deciding to collude.
AI.method: A benchmark of 2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it. The authors test published detectors and a trained probe, examine a rule that scores only after the vote, and check public arguments for the target, then adapt scan statistics into an online monitor.
AI.result: Published detectors barely separate colluders from refusers. Without the instruction, the best probe's agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Scoring after the vote gives AUROC 0.990 for a rule that finds nothing before the vote, and 57% of attempts have no colluder arguing for the target publicly. A probe trained on agents' own choices reaches AUROC 0.73 without the instruction, and probes detect fine-tuned goals with AUROC 0.995.
AI.conclusion: Reported collusion detection is inflated by instruction leakage and by post-vote scoring, so the controls in the paper should be used as a protocol for testing any collusion monitor.

title: Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention: Closed-Loop Quality Control for Long-Context LLM Decoding
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 35 pages, 12 figures, 35 tables
summary: Sparse attention accelerates long-context decoding by reading a subset of the KV cache, but existing methods are open-loop: the kernel commits to its selection with no signal indicating whether enough attention mass was preserved and no recovery path when it was not. The needed signal already exists inside the kernel. The fraction of softmax mass on the selected tokens, which we call coverage, satisfies an exact algebraic equality with per-step output error and serves a dual role as the acceptance criterion and the interpolation weight for recovery. Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention (CVSA) turns coverage into a training-free, closed-loop verify-then-correct decode loop that accepts high-coverage drafts and recovers only the heads that fall short, with no sampling, no draft model, and no speculative-decoding infrastructure. Quality varies by only $0.14$ points across the threshold sweep; budget and scheduling ablations characterize the deployed operating point. On LongBench at 7B and 70B, CVSA comes within $1.13$ points of dense attention, statistically matching it at 70B, and it loses $0.8$ points on RULER; measured median decode-step speedup reaches $6.21\times$ at 128K context.

AI.tldr: Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention (CVSA) is a training-free decode loop that measures the softmax mass captured by a sparse selection, accepts high-coverage drafts and recovers only the heads that fall short. It stays close to dense attention on LongBench and RULER while decoding faster at long context.
AI.motivation: Existing sparse attention methods are open-loop: they commit to a KV subset without knowing whether enough attention mass was preserved and without a recovery path.
AI.method: Coverage, defined as the fraction of softmax mass on the selected tokens, has an exact algebraic relation to per-step output error and is used both as the acceptance criterion and as the interpolation weight for recovery. The method runs a verify-then-correct loop without sampling, a draft model or speculative-decoding infrastructure.
AI.result: Quality varies by only 0.14 points across the threshold sweep. On LongBench at 7B and 70B CVSA comes within 1.13 points of dense attention and statistically matches it at 70B, and it loses 0.8 points on RULER. The measured median decode-step speedup reaches 6.21 times at 128K context.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop coverage verification gives sparse attention a quality guarantee signal without extra training, with a favorable quality and speed trade-off for long-context decoding.

title: Same Contacts, Different Rooms:Meeting Format Shapes LLM Group Influence Beyond Pairwise Contact Counts
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Simulations of LLM agent collectives usually summarise interaction as a pairwise contact network. We test that summary with a contact-matched intervention: the members, their initial stances and every pairwise contact count stay fixed while the meetings are reorganised, and each member gives a one-step support readout after reading the arguments of everyone present. Across six open-weight LLMs and 14 debate topics, merging triads into five-person meetings (resize) moves group support more than reshuffling who meets in triads (regroup), although both move the same 60 dyadic exposures. The root-mean-square change is 4.36 versus 2.59 percentage points (pp), larger for resize in all six models and in 81 of 84 model-topic cells. Resizing also has a consistent direction: it amplifies the initial majority of the merged members by 1.72 pp, in every model, whereas regrouping has no direction (<= 0.03 pp). A contact network cannot represent regrouping at all, yet pairwise rules applied meeting by meeting explain up to 76% of its effect, and with identical weights they raise resize R^2 by 0.51-0.58 for two models. We show that the gap between the two placements is an exact Jensen gap of the sigmoid readout, bounded by how much a member's predicted logits vary across meetings; this dispersion tracks the gap with log-log r=0.97 and tells a modeller when contact counts are a safe summary. Meeting format is a first-class variable for LLM social simulation.

AI.tldr: Using contact-matched interventions on LLM debate groups, the paper shows that the format of meetings, whether triads are merged into five-person meetings or reshuffled, shifts group support more than the pairwise contact counts predict. A contact network cannot represent this regrouping effect.
AI.motivation: LLM agent simulations usually summarize interaction as a pairwise contact network, and this summary may hide how meeting format shapes group influence.
AI.method: The members, initial stances and pairwise contact counts are held fixed while meetings are reorganized, either by resizing triads into five-person meetings or by regrouping them. Each member then gives a one-step support readout after reading the arguments of everyone present, across six open-weight LLMs and 14 debate topics.
AI.result: Resizing moves group support more than regrouping, with root-mean-square changes of 4.36 versus 2.59 percentage points, and resize is larger in all six models and in 81 of 84 model-topic cells. Resizing amplifies the initial majority of merged members by 1.72 points in every model, while regrouping shows no direction. Pairwise rules applied meeting by meeting explain up to 76% of the resize effect.
AI.conclusion: Meeting format is a first-class variable in LLM social simulation, and the gap between placements is a Jensen gap of the sigmoid readout that tells modelers when contact counts are a safe summary.

title: Pandemonium: Longform Target-Speaker Speech Recognition with Cross-Speaker Interactions
summary: Diarization-conditioned target-speaker ASR (TS-ASR), in particular Diarization-conditioned Whisper (DiCoW), is an accurate and data-efficient approach to multi-talker transcription. It has, however, three structural limitations: the model transcribes each speaker independently, operates on short (30 s) windows, and optimizes its diarization and TS-ASR components separately. We address the first two. We integrate the diarization conditioning into a longform Parakeet backbone (DiCoP) and add cross-speaker attention, which lets the model attend across the speaker dimension so that speakers are no longer decoded in isolation, and an STNO mask refiner that re-estimates the diarization-derived conditioning. As conversational data with genuine multi-speaker interaction is scarce, we scale training with a pseudo-labeling pipeline that mines 5.4k hours of in-the-wild multi-speaker audio from YODAS2. Combining these with synthetic and real data yields state-of-the-art results across several meeting benchmarks. We open-source the resulting models, DiCoP and Pandemonium, and the pseudo-labeled data.

AI.tldr: Pandemonium extends diarization-conditioned Whisper (DiCoW) to longform multi-talker speech recognition with a Parakeet backbone (DiCoP), cross-speaker attention and a mask refiner, and reports state-of-the-art results on several meeting benchmarks. Models and pseudo-labeled data are released.
AI.motivation: Diarization-conditioned target-speaker ASR has three limits: it transcribes speakers independently, works only on 30-second windows and trains diarization and ASR separately. The paper addresses the first two.
AI.method: The diarization conditioning is integrated into a longform Parakeet backbone (DiCoP), with cross-speaker attention across the speaker dimension and an STNO mask refiner that re-estimates the conditioning. Training uses synthetic and real data plus 5.4k hours of multi-speaker audio mined from YODAS2 with a pseudo-labeling pipeline.
AI.result: The combination yields state-of-the-art results across several meeting benchmarks. The abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Modeling cross-speaker interaction in longform audio improves multi-talker transcription, and the authors open-source DiCoP, Pandemonium and the pseudo-labeled data.

title: Machine Hearing: Can Audio LLMs Generalize Beyond Human Auditory Perception?
summary: Multimodal LLMs have made remarkable progress in perceiving the physical world, while their perceptual scope remains largely human-centric, focusing on what humans can directly see or hear. This progress raises the prospect of perception beyond human limits, such as extending hearing to sounds that are inaudible to humans. More broadly, the physical world is full of waves, vibrations, and oscillations, only a small fraction of which are directly audible to humans. This invites the extension of multimodal LLMs toward a broader form of machine hearing, which remains largely underexplored. To investigate this direction, we introduce the Machine Hearing Benchmark (MHB), comprising 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains. MHB spans highly heterogeneous input regimes, with sampling rates from approximately $10^{-5}$ to $10^6$ Hz, sequence lengths from $10^1$ to $10^6$ samples, and both single- and multi-channel inputs. Evaluations of current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs (ALLMs) reveal limited zero-shot transfer to machine hearing. Supervised adaptation on machine-hearing data alone does not close this gap, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond data exposure to a systematic mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs. To address this mismatch, we introduce MachEar, a lightweight encoder extension that complements the pretrained Audio LLM for machine-hearing inputs. The results show that MachEar equips a pretrained Audio LLM with stronger machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving its existing audio understanding performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Machine Hearing Benchmark (MHB) for audio LLMs on signals beyond human hearing, from about 10^-5 to 10^6 Hz. Current audio LLMs transfer poorly, and the proposed MachEar encoder extension improves machine-hearing performance while largely preserving general audio understanding.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs are human-centric in their perception, and extending them to waves and vibrations inaudible to people is largely unexplored.
AI.method: MHB contains 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains, with sampling rates from about 10^-5 to 10^6 Hz, sequence lengths from 10 to 10^6 samples and single- and multi-channel inputs. MachEar is a lightweight encoder extension added to a pretrained audio LLM.
AI.result: Open-source and proprietary audio LLMs show limited zero-shot transfer, and supervised adaptation on machine-hearing data alone does not close the gap. MachEar gives the pretrained model stronger machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving its existing audio understanding. The abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: The gap stems from a systematic mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs, so front-end design rather than data exposure alone is needed.

title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind
comment: 36 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (E&D). Code and dataset: this https URL
summary: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. The consensus diagnosis is conceptual, prescribing new belief-reasoning modules. We argue the dominant bottleneck is perceptual: not what the model cannot reason about, but what it cannot see. We propose a five-condition dissociation protocol that holds the reasoning task constant while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and quantify the result with the Perceptual Contribution Ratio, the share of the visual-to-text gap a given fidelity closes. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider--Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning. Whereas scaffolds built by automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. The most common error in the visual-only condition is \emph{reality bias}, which accounts for 60\% of false-belief failures. Models report where an object actually is, not where an absent agent believes it is. This points to a perceptual front-end that fails to track which agents were present at each moment. Under the evaluated protocol, structured visual scene-state extraction, rather than belief inference, is the dominant bottleneck for visual ToM.

AI.tldr: Vision-language models lose over twenty points on visual false-belief tasks compared with text, and the paper argues the main cause is perception rather than reasoning. A dissociation protocol and a Perceptual Contribution Ratio show that structured visual scene-state extraction is the dominant bottleneck.
AI.motivation: The prevailing explanation is conceptual and calls for new belief-reasoning modules, but the authors argue the bottleneck is what the model cannot see, not what it cannot reason about.
AI.method: A five-condition dissociation protocol holds the reasoning task fixed while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and the Perceptual Contribution Ratio measures the share of the visual-to-text gap each fidelity closes. Tests use abstract 2D Heider-Simmel panels and 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower across seven VLMs and about 159,000 API calls.
AI.result: Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting and match or exceed text-only reasoning on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM, while scaffolds from automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. Reality bias accounts for 60% of false-belief failures in the visual-only condition, with models reporting where an object actually is rather than where an absent agent believes it is.
AI.conclusion: Under the evaluated protocol, perceptual scene-state extraction rather than belief inference is the dominant bottleneck for visual theory of mind, pointing to a front end that tracks which agents were present at each moment.

title: Generating Diverse and Verified Synthetic Clinical Notes with Labels by Construction
comment: Accepted at the GenAI for Health Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026. 38 pages including appendix. Code: this https URL
summary: Under strict privacy regulations in the clinical domain, de-identification is necessary to enable the use of clinical data such as for natural language processing. However, we currently lack sophisticated ways to tell which de-identification models actually are suitable. Specifically, we need benchmarks that are challenging, diverse, and clinically plausible, all while ensuring label correctness. To this end, we present SPARCLING, an LLM-based pipeline to generate synthetic discharge letters with character-exact PHI span annotations. Our pipeline combines structured attribute sampling, template generation, and red teaming to obtain diverse PHI-labeled discharge letters. In our experiments, we demonstrate this superior content diversity over existing public datasets. Further, we show SPARCLING's downstream utility as a benchmark to uncover failure modes of de-identifiers in the German clinical domain. Finally, our experiments show that training on our synthetic data can yield more capable de-identifiers than training on the scarce public data alone. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SPARCLING is an LLM-based pipeline that generates synthetic German discharge letters with character-exact PHI span annotations, producing diverse, label-correct data for de-identification. The data serves as a benchmark that exposes de-identifier failure modes and can train stronger de-identifiers than scarce public data alone.
AI.motivation: Clinical de-identification is required before clinical text can be used, yet there are few challenging, diverse and clinically plausible benchmarks with reliable labels for judging de-identification models.
AI.method: The pipeline combines structured attribute sampling, template generation and red teaming to produce PHI-labeled discharge letters. Diversity is compared with existing public datasets, and the data is used both as a benchmark and as training data for de-identifiers.
AI.result: The synthetic letters show higher content diversity than existing public datasets. The benchmark uncovers failure modes of de-identifiers in the German clinical domain, and training on the synthetic data yields more capable de-identifiers than training on scarce public data alone. The abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Label-correct synthetic clinical notes are a useful substitute for scarce privacy-restricted data, both for evaluating and for training de-identification models.

title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
summary: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.

AI.tldr: Auditing LLM responses to users disclosing suicidal ideation or distress with identity information, the paper finds models often attribute distress to presumed identity-related adversity, especially when marginalized identities are disclosed. The authors frame this as a harm of compassionate othering.
AI.motivation: Disclosed identities are not necessarily causes of distress, yet LLMs may treat them as explanations for suffering, which can misrepresent individuals' experiences in supportive contexts.
AI.method: Paired counterfactual interventions are applied to six LLMs across two suicidal ideation and distress datasets, with 16 identity and control conditions and two prompting protocols.
AI.result: Models transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives that attribute distress to identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. The abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Interpretations of distress should be grounded in what individuals disclose rather than unsupported identity-linked assumptions, since such assumptions are a form of harm.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
summary: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

AI.tldr: Deletion Tuning zeroes fewer than 0.05% of a pretrained LLM's weights through a learned binary mask on the gate projection and matches full fine-tuning across three post-training regimes. It forgets much less than full fine-tuning, LoRA or random sparse fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: The paper asks how little of a pretrained LLM must change to acquire new capabilities, and whether such minimal change also reduces forgetting, a central problem in continual learning.
AI.method: A binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks is learned while no other weights are modified. It is tested under reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation, and the learned weight changes are analyzed with stable rank, spectrum drift and principal-weight overlap.
AI.result: The trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding full fine-tuning checkpoint. Under reinforcement learning, prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while full fine-tuning, LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. Deletion Tuning is closest to full fine-tuning on all three geometry measures compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Masking alone can suffice for new capabilities with far less forgetting, and its weight-change geometry resembles that of full fine-tuning.

title: DM-Call: Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling with Cumulative Verification Feedback
summary: Reliable function calling requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to select appropriate functions and generate arguments consistent with user intent. However, syntactically valid calls may still be semantically incorrect due to inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments. In this paper, we propose Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that combines local schema validation with separate decision-model verification of function selection and argument correctness. For rejected candidates, DM-Call accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across attempts. A hybrid feedback representation further combines numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels to guide iterative refinement without executing external tools. Extensive evaluation across BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) demonstrates DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy versus direct generation, at modest additional cost.

AI.tldr: DM-Call is a function-calling framework in which a separate decision model verifies function selection and argument correctness, and cumulative verification feedback guides iterative refinement without executing tools. It improves accuracy over direct generation on BFCL and API-Bank first calls at modest extra cost.
AI.motivation: Syntactically valid function calls can still be semantically wrong because of inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments, and local schema validation alone does not catch these errors.
AI.method: Local schema validation is combined with decision-model verification of selection and arguments. For rejected candidates the framework accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments and schema errors, and a hybrid feedback representation pairs numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation on BFCL and API-Bank first-call settings shows that DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy over direct generation at modest additional cost. The abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Decision-model verification with accumulated feedback is a practical way to improve semantic correctness of function calls without tool execution.

title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure. Code: this https URL
summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems face two costs that research comparisons rarely measure: building the graph, and removing documents from it. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions carrying chunk-level provenance. Indexing makes one language-model call per passage, retrieval makes none, and deleting a document is a database operation with no model calls. On the full 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus we verify that, after deleting 10% of the documents, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. We compare Lightfoot with HippoRAG 2, LightRAG and fast-graphrag under identical extraction, answer and embedding models on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA. Lightfoot builds the cheapest index on all three datasets, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2 and 3-6x below LightRAG and fast-graphrag. Against HippoRAG 2 it is significantly better on MuSiQue retrieval (+2.8 points recall@5 and +4.3 recall@10 on a held-out split) and on HotpotQA answers (+7.7 points exact match), and significantly worse on 2WikiMultiHopQA (-3.9 recall@2, -8.4 F1). Deleting the same documents took LightRAG 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours; fast-graphrag has no deletion path. Code and per-question results: this https URL

AI.tldr: Lightfoot is a GraphRAG system whose graph is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions with chunk-level provenance, so deleting a document is a database operation with no model calls. It builds the cheapest index among compared systems and matches a fresh index after deletion.
AI.motivation: Deployed GraphRAG systems face costs that research comparisons rarely measure, namely building the graph and removing documents from it.
AI.method: Indexing makes one language-model call per passage and retrieval makes none. Each entity, link, fact and synonym edge is derived deterministically from the per-passage extractions. Lightfoot is compared with HippoRAG 2, LightRAG and fast-graphrag under identical extraction, answer and embedding models on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA.
AI.result: After deleting 10% of the 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. Lightfoot's index is 26 to 31% cheaper than HippoRAG 2 and 3 to 6 times cheaper than LightRAG and fast-graphrag. It is significantly better than HippoRAG 2 on MuSiQue retrieval (+2.8 recall@5 and +4.3 recall@10) and HotpotQA exact match (+7.7 points), and significantly worse on 2WikiMultiHopQA (-3.9 recall@2, -8.4 F1). Deleting the same documents took LightRAG 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours, and fast-graphrag has no deletion path.
AI.conclusion: Making graph construction deterministic and provenance-tracked yields cheap indexing and exact, model-free deletion, at a cost in multi-hop 2WikiMultiHopQA accuracy relative to HippoRAG 2.
